checks.requirement: Microscopes are clean, adequate (eg, low, high dry and oil immersion lenses as appropriate for the intended use), optically aligned, and properly maintained with records of preventive maintenance at least annually.
checks.subject: Microscope Maintenance
checks.note: NOTE: Koehler illumination must be maintained for optimal resolution. Phase contrast microscopy should be available when indicated (eg, manual platelet counting, urinalysis microscopy).
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a policy for microscope maintenance as evidenced by 'FS1009.0v1_Motic AE2000 Microscope Operation_Maintenance SOP.pdf' and 'Motic AE2000 Microscope Operation_Maintenance SOP.docx', which cover cleaning, operational procedures, and phase contrast microscopy requirements. However, the requirement mandates records of preventive maintenance at least annually. A review of the provided documentation confirms that while the SOP exists, no records of preventive maintenance performed at least annually were provided or verified. The current SOP states maintenance is performed on an 'as needed' basis, which does not explicitly satisfy the CAP requirement for at least annual preventive maintenance records.
corrective_actions: 1) Establish a formal preventive maintenance schedule to ensure all microscopes undergo documented maintenance at least annually.
2) Maintain a log or record for each microscope documenting the date, specific maintenance performed, and the individual performing the task to ensure compliance with COM.30680.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30680**: The Motic AE2000 Microscope Operation/Maintenance SOP, document FS1009.0v1_Motic AE2000 Microscope Operation_Maintenance SOP, outlines procedures for cleaning and maintenance. Instrument maintenance should be performed as needed based on usage. Lenses and filters are to be cleaned by first removing dust with an air blower, then with a soft brush or gauze if dust persists. A soft gauze or lens tissue lightly moistened with 70% ethanol should be used for grease or fingerprints. When not in use, the microscope should be covered with a dust cover and stored in a low-humidity environment. The SOP also details operational procedures including adjusting eyepieces, cleaning the stage, focusing, and adjusting illumination and objective lenses. The Motic AE2000 Microscope Manual provides guidance on brightfield and phase contrast microscopy, including the use of aperture diaphragms and annular rings. However, records of preventive maintenance performed at least annually were not found in the provided documents.

checks.requirement: The microscopes used for fluorescence testing are monitored to ensure sufficient light source intensity, and are used with filters and slides appropriate to, and verified in conjunction with, the test(s) being performed.
checks.subject: Microscopes for Fluorescence Testing
checks.note:
NOTE: Having a process to track the length of time the bulb is in use and limit bulb usage based on the manufacturer's recommendations (as applicable), is an example of an acceptable process to monitor the adequacy of the source intensity. 
  
  The use of filters or slides not matched properly to the assay(s) performed can lead to erroneous results. Written procedures must specify the excitation and emission filters used for fluorescence microscopy. Fluorescence microscopes should be used in an area where ambient lighting can be minimized.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of microscope monitoring
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established operational procedures for the SpectraMax iD3 and Motic AE2000 microscope, including IQOQ documentation (IQOQ_373702658_27Jun2023.pdf) and software-based optimization settings (softmax-pro-user-guide-v7-2.pdf). However, the requirement for ongoing monitoring of light source intensity is not fully met. While the SpectraMax iD3 utilizes self-calibration, no records were provided to demonstrate routine monitoring of the Motic AE2000 bulb usage or intensity. Furthermore, the written procedures for the Motic AE2000 (Motic AE2000 Microscope Operation_Maintenance SOP.docx) do not explicitly specify the excitation and emission filters used for fluorescence microscopy as required by the note in COM.30685.
corrective_actions: 1) Implement and maintain a log to track bulb usage hours for the Motic AE2000 microscope to ensure intensity adequacy.
2) Update the Motic AE2000 SOP to explicitly document the specific excitation and emission filters utilized for fluorescence testing.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30685**: The SpectraMax iD3 Multi-Mode Microplate Reader utilizes a xenon flash lamp with a two-year or 1-billion-flash lifespan and features self-calibration via built-in fluorescence standards. Users optimize fluorescence intensity assays through SoftMax Pro software by adjusting PMT voltage, emission cutoff filters, and wavelengths in 1 nm increments from 250 nm to 850 nm. For FilterMax F3 and F5 readers, interchangeable slides hold up to six filters each, with the software supporting definitions for 31 excitation and 31 emission slides. Users must update the Filter Settings dialog whenever filter configurations change to prevent data errors. Regarding the Motic AE2000 microscope, the operation and maintenance SOP requires aligning the condenser with the objective lens and adjusting light intensity via the brightness control knob, though no monitoring records were provided.

Operation Procedure: Initial Setup Place the microscope on a stable and flat surface. Connect the power cord to the microscope and plug it into a power outlet. Turn on the microscope using the power switch located at the base. Adjusting the Microscope Eyepieces: Adjust the interpupillary distance by sliding the eyepieces closer or further apart. Set the diopter adjustment to match your vision. Stage: Ensure the stage is clean and free of obstructions. Place the specimen slide on the stage and secure it with the stage clips. Focusing: Start with the lowest magnification objective lens. Use the coarse focus knob to bring the specimen into view. Fine-tune the focus using the fine focus knob. Using the Microscope Illumination: Adjust the light intensity using the brightness control knob. Ensure the condenser is aligned and adjusted to match the objective lens in use. Objective Lenses: Rotate the nosepiece to select the desired objective lens. Always start with the lowest magnification and work your way up. Viewing: Look through the eyepieces and adjust the focus as needed.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Chapter 3: Collecting Data 5305581 A 167 Optimizing Fluorescence Intensity Assays
The optimal instrument settings for detection of a particular fluorophore depend on a number of
different factors. Settings you can adjust for assay optimization include the excitation and
emission wavelengths, emission cutoff filter, reads per well, the PMT voltage, and the
temperature of the read chamber. Another important factor that is independent of the instrument but can affect assay optimization
is the Stokes shift, which is the difference between the wavelengths of the excitation and
emission maxima. When the Stokes shift is very small, optimizing the excitation and emission
wavelengths and correct cutoff filter choices are very important. Excitation and Emission Wavelengths
The excitation and emission wavelengths can be set in 1 nm increments between 250 nm
and 850 nm. The available wavelengths are dependent on the instrument. For more
information about the available wavelengths, see the documentation for the instrument you
are using. A procedure to optimize excitation and emission wavelengths for a given assay is outlined
in Spectral Scanning on page 167. Emission Cutoff Filter
The emission cutoff filters assist in reducing background. Sources of background include
stray excitation light and native fluorescence of plate materials, sample constituents, and
solvents (including water). The default setting lets the instrument and the software
determine which cutoff filter to use for the endpoint and kinetic read types.

Operation Procedure: Initial Setup Place the microscope on a stable and flat surface. Connect the power cord to the microscope and plug it into a power outlet. Turn on the microscope using the power switch located at the base. Adjusting the Microscope Eyepieces: Adjust the interpupillary distance by sliding the eyepieces closer or further apart. Set the diopter adjustment to match your vision. Stage: Ensure the stage is clean and free of obstructions. Place the specimen slide on the stage and secure it with the stage clips. Focusing: Start with the lowest magnification objective lens. Use the coarse focus knob to bring the specimen into view. Fine-tune the focus using the fine focus knob. Using the Microscope Illumination: Adjust the light intensity using the brightness control knob. Ensure the condenser is aligned and adjusted to match the objective lens in use. Objective Lenses: Rotate the nosepiece to select the desired objective lens. Always start with the lowest magnification and work your way up. Viewing: Look through the eyepieces and adjust the focus as needed.

Chapter 3: Collecting Data 5305581 A 167 Optimizing Fluorescence Intensity Assays
The optimal instrument settings for detection of a particular fluorophore depend on a number of
different factors. Settings you can adjust for assay optimization include the excitation and
emission wavelengths, emission cutoff filter, reads per well, the PMT voltage, and the
temperature of the read chamber. Another important factor that is independent of the instrument but can affect assay optimization
is the Stokes shift, which is the difference between the wavelengths of the excitation and
emission maxima. When the Stokes shift is very small, optimizing the excitation and emission
wavelengths and correct cutoff filter choices are very important. Excitation and Emission Wavelengths
The excitation and emission wavelengths can be set in 1 nm increments between 250 nm
and 850 nm. The available wavelengths are dependent on the instrument. For more
information about the available wavelengths, see the documentation for the instrument you
are using. A procedure to optimize excitation and emission wavelengths for a given assay is outlined
in Spectral Scanning on page 167. Emission Cutoff Filter
The emission cutoff filters assist in reducing background. Sources of background include
stray excitation light and native fluorescence of plate materials, sample constituents, and
solvents (including water). The default setting lets the instrument and the software
determine which cutoff filter to use for the endpoint and kinetic read types.

checks.requirement: A certified biological safety cabinet (BSC) is available and used when appropriate.
checks.subject: Biological Safety Cabinet
checks.note:
NOTE: The biological safety cabinet must be certified when installed, whenever moved, and at least annually to ensure that filters are functioning properly and that airflow rates meet specifications. 
  
  A BSC is used when protection of personnel, product, and/or the environment is needed for certain types of testing or procedures, including: 
  
  * Handling specimens potentially containing infectious pathogens considered highly transmissible by airborne routes or with potential for aerosolization or risk of splashes 
  * Prevention of DNA/RNA contamination for molecular testing procedures 
  * Maintaining sterility of cell cultures. 
  
  The laboratory director is responsible for ensuring a risk assessment is conducted, and for defining and implementing work practice controls to minimize identified risks, including installation and proper use of the appropriate type of biological safety cabinet. 
  
  The 6th edition of Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories provides guidance for safe conduct of work from a biosafety perspective. It can be used as a tool for assessing and mitigating risk. Refer to Section II - Biological Risk Assessment, Appendix N - Clinical Laboratories, Section IV - Laboratory Biosafety Level Criteria and Table 1. Summary of Laboratory Biosafety Levels (BSLs) for specific information.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Defined work practice controls appropriate for the assessed level of risk AND 
  * Maintenance and function check schedule AND 
  * Records of testing and certification

checks.ai_evidence_summary:
**COM.30695**: The laboratory utilizes Class II Type A2 Biological Safety Cabinets (BSCs) for processing patient and clinical samples in the PCR lab and for microbes in the antigen lab. These BSCs provide protection for the analyst, samples, and the environment through inward airflow, HEPA-filtered downward laminar airflow, and HEPA-filtered exhaust air. The FS1002.0V2_Biological Safety Cabinets SOP and maintenance document outlines the purpose, responsibilities, and safety precautions for BSC use, including processing all patient and clinical samples within a BSC.

BSCs are certified annually by an outside vendor to ensure proper filter function and airflow rates. HEPA filters are replaced every 4-5 years. Daily maintenance procedures include ensuring the hood is on for 15 minutes prior to use, cleaning surfaces with 70% ethanol before and after each use, and disinfecting with UV for 30 minutes daily. Installation Qualification (IQ) records for BioSafety Cabinet #1 and BioSafety Cabinet #2 confirm that recertification is required annually, upon relocation, when performance is suspected, or after major maintenance. The G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program also specifies that Class II biological safety cabinets should be used as containment devices for sample preparation.

checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established policy F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program.pdf and identified NIST-traceable standard devices in W17597 Therm Traceability.pdf. While Thermometer 4 Verification.docx provides evidence of a verification procedure and a specific 2022 verification result, the current records do not demonstrate that the reference standard itself is within its active calibration/certification period. Per the requirement note, devices must be recalibrated or replaced prior to expiration, or treated as non-certified after two years from the certificate date. The provided documentation lacks current, unexpired certificates of accuracy for the reference thermometers listed in W17597. Verification of the current calibration status of the reference standards is required to ensure compliance.
corrective_actions: 1) Obtain and attach current, unexpired NIST-traceable calibration certificates for all reference thermometers listed in W17597.
2) Update the equipment log to include the expiration dates for all thermometric standard devices to ensure timely recalibration or replacement per COM.30700.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30700**: Laboratories must maintain thermometric devices traceable to NIST standards, ensuring recalibration or replacement before expiration or within two years of certification. Non-certified thermometers require annual verification against a certified reference. Equipment must be monitored during use, with thermometers calibrated at least annually and inspected for damage. Document W17597 Therm Traceability.pdf identifies NIST-calibrated serial numbers, such as #7713700 for temperatures below -30°C and #878758 for 250°C to 300°C, and confirms Easy-Read® thermometers conform to ISO 17025 and NIST Special Publication 1088, maintaining an accuracy of ±1 division for the -20 to 150°C range. Per Thermometer 4 Verification.pdf, a verification conducted on August 18, 2022, yielded a T-test result of <0.05, confirming no significant difference between the control and working thermometer, necessitating a correction factor of +0.64.

checks.requirement:
The laboratory monitors and records temperatures using a calibrated thermometer as defined in written procedure for the following: 
  
  * Temperature-dependent storage devices (eg, refrigerators, freezers, incubators) 
  * Temperature-dependent equipment (eg, water baths, heat blocks) 
  * Temperature-dependent environments (eg, ambient reagent or specimen storage, conditions for instrument operation and test performance)
checks.subject: Temperature Checks
checks.note:
NOTE: Temperature-dependent storage devices and temperature-dependent environments where reagents, supplies, and patient/client specimens are stored within a specified temperature range must be checked daily. Temperature-dependent environments refer to areas of the laboratory where specific instruments, equipment, kits, or supplies have manufacturer or laboratory specified ambient temperature ranges for proper operation, storage, or use. Please refer to more stringent requirements in the Transfusion Medicine, Reproductive Laboratory Medicine and Biorepository Checklists for storage requirements for blood components, tissues, and biorepository specimens. 
  
  Use of a continuous monitoring device or a minimum/maximum thermometer satisfies the requirement for daily temperature recording, including during laboratory closures (eg, weekends, holidays), as long as the monitoring data is evaluated on the next business day prior to use. For use of minimum/maximum thermometers during laboratory closures, this includes resetting the device prior to the monitoring period and recording both low and high temperatures before using any temperature-dependent equipment, kits, or supplies. It is not necessary to record low and high temperatures on days when the laboratory is in operation if daily temperatures are recorded. 
  
  Temperature-dependent equipment and temperature-dependent environments used for procedures at a specified temperature range must be checked on each day of use. Temperature-dependent testing devices with built-in fail-safe technology that will disable utilization if temperatures are out of range are exempted from the daily check. For heat blocks or dry baths, thermocouple probes may be used as an alternative method for checking the temperature. 
  
  Temperatures may be recorded either manually or using a recording device or system by: 1) recording the numerical temperature, or 2) placing a mark on a graph that corresponds to a numerical temperature. If temperatures are recorded manually, the identity of the individual recording temperatures must be recorded (initials of the individual are adequate). 
  
  If an automated (including remote) temperature monitoring system is used instead of manual temperature monitoring, laboratory personnel must have ongoing immediate access to the temperature data so that appropriate corrective action can be taken if a temperature is outside of the acceptable range. System records must demonstrate daily functionality of the automated system in accordance with manufacturer's instructions. This does not require routine daily review of the system records. 
  
  Patient specimens, reagents, and controls may be stored in a frost-free freezer only if protected from thawing. Thermal containers within the freezer may be used. The laboratory must retain records showing that the temperatures stay within the defined range. 
  
  * Repeated freeze-thaw cycles contribute to biomolecular degradation and are detrimental to biospecimen quality. 
  * It is prudent to avoid freeze-thaw altogether by aliquoting specimens before freezing.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a policy (G1013.0_Laboratory_Reagent_Policy.pdf) requiring daily temperature monitoring for storage areas using continuous systems or max/min thermometers, with records maintained in the 'XYZ Lab Temperature and humidity log.' The search summary confirms that acceptable ranges are defined and that annual NIST-traceable calibration is performed. However, while the policy and procedural framework are documented, the actual completed temperature logs (records) were not provided for review to verify consistent daily compliance, documentation of staff initials, or evidence of corrective actions taken for out-of-range events. The document '22_Temperature and Humidity Monitor-CW.docx' indicates staff training on monitoring, but does not serve as evidence of the required daily temperature records.
corrective_actions: 1) Provide representative samples of the 'XYZ Lab Temperature and humidity log' for the past 3 months to verify daily recording and staff initials.
2) Provide documentation of the most recent annual NIST-traceable calibration for all thermometers currently in use.
3) Ensure any out-of-range temperature events are accompanied by documented corrective actions as required by the policy.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30750**: The laboratory monitors and records temperatures for temperature-dependent storage devices, equipment, and environments where reagents and supplies are stored within a specified temperature/humidity range. This policy provides direction for daily temperature and humidity logs and thermometer calibration. Storage area temperatures are monitored daily using a continuous monitoring system or a maximum/minimum thermometer, as applicable, and recorded in the XYZ Lab Temperature and humidity log. All thermometers are calibrated annually against a calibrated NIST traceable thermometer. If a thermometer is found to be out of calibration, action will be taken to recertify analytical accuracy before reuse. The acceptable temperature/humidity range for each monitored item is found at the top of the daily temperature monitoring log, highlighted in green. These ranges are determined by the type of reagents and instruments stored in that area, compared to temperature standards. Supervisors must be immediately notified of any out-of-range readings for prompt resolution.

checks.requirement: The laboratory takes corrective action when acceptable temperature ranges for temperature-dependent storage devices, equipment, and environments are exceeded, including evaluation for adverse effects.
checks.subject: Temperature Corrective Action
checks.note: NOTE: If acceptable temperature ranges are exceeded, stored reagents, controls, calibrators, or other materials must be checked to confirm the accuracy or quality of the material before use, with records retained.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of corrective action for unacceptable temperatures
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory demonstrates awareness of corrective action requirements as evidenced by 'J1002.2_ CA20240508 1201 ULT Freezer Display Discrepancy Report' and the 'J1002.2-CA 250425-TempLog review issue' (referenced in search_summary). These documents confirm that the lab evaluates adverse effects when temperature ranges are exceeded or equipment malfunctions. However, the documentation is inconsistent; while the Fridge 1103 incident includes an assessment of sample integrity, the ULT freezer report indicates an ongoing issue with display drift that remained unresolved as of the June 2024 follow-up. Furthermore, the 'Chest Freezer -80.xlsx' notes physical challenges with thermometer accuracy and ice buildup, which may impede the ability to perform accurate corrective actions. The lab must ensure that all corrective actions include a documented evaluation of the impact on stored materials and that long-term equipment issues are fully resolved rather than just monitored.
corrective_actions: 1) Finalize the transfer of contents from the ULT freezer identified in J1002.2_ CA20240508 and document the final decommissioning of the faulty unit.
2) Implement a formal maintenance schedule to address ice buildup and thermometer accuracy issues identified in Chest Freezer -80.xlsx to ensure reliable temperature monitoring.
cited_documents: J1002.2_ CA20240508 1201 ULT Freezer Display Discrepancy Report.docx
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30800**: The laboratory takes corrective action when acceptable temperature ranges are exceeded. For instance, a corrective action report, J1002.2_ CA20240508 1201 ULT Freezer Display Discrepancy Report, details an ongoing display discrepancy in an ultra-low temperature freezer. Although the freezer remained within the acceptable range of -70 to -80 degrees Celsius, the display drift could lead to degradation of contents over time. Corrective actions included monitoring and recalibrating the display as needed. A follow-up on June 21, 2024, noted continued drifting, leading to a plan to transfer contents to another freezer by July 30th. Another corrective action, J1002.2-CA 250425-TempLog review issue, addressed employees not being properly trained to identify out-of-range temperatures, specifically in Fridge 1103. While temperatures occasionally reached 9-10°C, this short-term exposure was deemed not to compromise sample integrity. Corrective actions included adjusting the fridge's temperature control, reinforcing monitoring protocols, and assigning a monthly review of lab operation documents to the technical supervisor. The acceptable temperature/humidity range for monitored items is found on the daily temperature log. These ranges are determined by the type of reagents and instruments stored and compared to temperature standards.

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Operation/J-Nonconforming Event Management/Corrective Action Report/J1002.2_ CA20240508 1201 ULT Freezer Display Discrepancy Report.docx
policy_evidence.snippet: The unit's low temperature alarm started going off and the unit began cooling again. Since the display was reading around -80, the unit's cooling system was not being turned on frequently enough which caused the rise in temperature. A temperature drift in an ultra-low temperature freezer may not immediately compromise most reagents, but prolonged exposure can lead to degradation, reduced efficacy, and shortened shelf life for more sensitive materials. The lab's current temperature range for the ULT freezers is -70 to -80, and the freezer was never out of range. However, if the freezer’s display continues drifting the constant shift and warmer storage temperatures could cause the contents of the freezers to degrade over time. Main Responsible Person：Brooke Lam Corrective Actions： Implementation beginning on_5/09/2024___ ending on__N/A___ There was a previous CA report about the Freezer’s display discrepancy causing problems (CA20231030 1201 ULT Freezer Display Discrepancy Investigation and Corrective Action Report) The display discrepancy appears to be an ongoing problem with the freezer. Hali and Brooke will keep an eye on the display and recalibrate as needed as soon as excessive temperature drifting is noticed. results.snippet: The unit's low temperature alarm started going off and the unit began cooling again. Since the display was reading around -80, the unit's cooling system was not being turned on frequently enough which caused the rise in temperature. A temperature drift in an ultra-low temperature freezer may not immediately compromise most reagents, but prolonged exposure can lead to degradation, reduced efficacy, and shortened shelf life for more sensitive materials. The lab's current temperature range for the ULT freezers is -70 to -80, and the freezer was never out of range. However, if the freezer’s display continues drifting the constant shift and warmer storage temperatures could cause the contents of the freezers to degrade over time. Main Responsible Person：Brooke Lam Corrective Actions： Implementation beginning on_5/09/2024___ ending on__N/A___ There was a previous CA report about the Freezer’s display discrepancy causing problems (CA20231030 1201 ULT Freezer Display Discrepancy Investigation and Corrective Action Report) The display discrepancy appears to be an ongoing problem with the freezer. Hali and Brooke will keep an eye on the display and recalibrate as needed as soon as excessive temperature drifting is noticed. This will ensure the unit continues to cool properly since the unit's cooling system runs based on the displayed temperature. Main Responsible Person： Brooke Lam

  For Non-Class A pipettes: Pipette checks must be performed following manufacturer's instructions, at minimum and as defined in laboratory procedure. Such checks may be done by gravimetric, colorimetric or other validation procedures. Alternative approaches include spectrophotometry and the use of commercial kits. 
  
  If initial calibration is performed by the manufacturer or other outside facility, sufficient information must be provided to justify acceptance of the pipette's calibration based on the laboratory's written specifications of acceptable bias and imprecision. The outside facility must also provide a record of the technique used to check calibration and ship the pipette in a manner that protects it from damage in transit.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Pipettes and glassware marked Class A OR a NIST certificate OR 
  * Records of initial and ongoing verification of non-Class A pipette and glassware accuracy and reproducibility
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory maintains a robust Equipment Calibration Program (F1002.0V6) that mandates initial and ongoing accuracy/reproducibility verification for non-Class A pipettes. Evidence of compliance is demonstrated through specific verification records, including '2P9-250324 Multi-channel p1200 Pipette Verification' and various certification documents (e.g., CE63095-p200, C142240-p200, S7186711-p200). These records confirm that the laboratory adheres to defined acceptance criteria (99%-101% accuracy and <1% imprecision for specified volumes) and utilizes appropriate validation procedures. The laboratory policy correctly distinguishes between high-precision requirements and applications for less precise measuring devices, ensuring alignment with the requirement for volumetric glassware accuracy.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of performing semi-annual in-house verification and annual external calibration for micropipettes as defined in F1002.0V6 and FS1001.0V2.
cited_documents: 2P9-250324 Multi-channel p1200 Pipette Verification (tested 1ml as maximum).xlsx
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30810**: The Equipment Calibration Program (F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program) and the Micropipette usage, Calibration and Maintenance SOP (FS1001.0V2_Micro Pipette usage Calibration and Maintenance SOP) mandate that new micropipettors undergo accuracy and precision verification before manufacturer calibration expires, while existing units require in-house verification every six months and annual calibration by an accredited laboratory. Pipettes must meet acceptance criteria of 99%-101% accuracy and less than 1% imprecision, with temperature-dependent Z-factors applied to account for water density. If verification fails, the device must be removed from service for repair and calibration. Compliance is documented using the Pipette Verification Template, as evidenced by records including Verification certification_ CE63095-p200, Verification certification_ C142240-p200, Verification certification_ S7186711-p200, 2P9-250324 Multi-channel p1200 Pipette Verification (tested 1ml as maximum), G14224D-250418_ Pipette Verification, and 3_3_25-1P1 Pipette Verification. Less precise measuring devices, such as serological plastic pipettes and graduated cylinders, are restricted to applications where high accuracy is not required and must be specified within relevant SOPs.

2.9 The laboratory should have an appropriate thermometric standard device of known accuracy, which is certified to
meet NIST standards or traceable to NIST standards. 2.9.1 Thermometric standard devices must be recalibrated, recertified, or replaced prior to the date of expiration of the
guarantee of calibration or they are subject to requirements for non-certified thermometers.
2.9.2 All non-certified thermometers should be verified using a certified calibrated thermometer annually. 2.9.3 Thermometers without defined expiration dates must be treated as non-certified thermometers after two years
from the certificate date. 2.9.4 Thermometers should be periodically evaluated for damage (eg, separation of columns). Thermometers with
obvious damage must be rechecked before continued use. 2.10 The temperature for all temperature sensitive instruments/equipment shall be monitored at use and thermometers
be calibrated at least annually. 2.11 For centrifuges used to separate different components, the speed shall be tested and calibrated at least once every
year. 2.12 The calibration and calibration verification procedure for micropipettor is as follows： The accuracy and precision of a newly purchased pipettor shall be verified before the manufacture calibration is due. There is no need for recalibration if verification passes. The accuracy and precision of old pipettors shall be verified once every six months.If the verification passes, there
is no need for re-calibration.

policy_evidence.snippet: XYZ Laboratory Pipette Calibration Verification Certificate Procedure: Use a newly calibrated pipettor from Marshall Scientific as reference to verify the accuracy of the testing pipettor (P200). Make 1:8dilution of the Green fluoresce solution: 1000 ul of the Green Fluorescence solution (Thermo Fisher, Catalog No. Q33237B. Lot No. 2339920) +7000 ul H2O Using the reference pipette and the testing pipette to add 200 ul, 100 ul and 50 ul of the 1:8 dilution of the Green Fluorescence solution to each one of the 5 replicates respectively. Transfer 200 ul of the solution to a 0.5 mL Q4 testing tube, read and record the signal. Read three times for each dilution. Using the same tube for all 5 replicates. Analyze the data to calculate the mean of the 15 data points for each concentration and calculate the percentage difference between the reference pipettor and the testing pipettor. The acceptance criteria: the difference between testing pipettor and the reference pipettor shall be less than 10% (In our laboratory, this pipettor is used for sample processing (50 ul) and reaction mix preparation with volume range from 20 ul to 200 ul.

checks.requirement: Pipettes used for quantitative dispensing (eg, adjustable volume, micropipettes, dilutors, and analytic instruments with integral automatic pipettors) are checked for accuracy and reproducibility initially and according to the manufacturer's recommended interval, or at least annually if not specified, and the results are recorded.
checks.subject: Quantitative Pipette Accuracy and Reproducibility
checks.note:
NOTE: The initial calibration may be performed by the manufacturer or other outside facility, but in such cases the laboratory must have a record from the manufacturer or other facility that includes the technique used to check calibration, the method of shipment to prevent damage in transit, and the accuracy and reproducibility of the pipette(s). The accuracy and reproducibility must meet the specification established by the laboratory. 
  
  If the facility performs pipette checks in house, they must be performed following manufacturer's instructions, at minimum, and as defined in laboratory procedure. Such checks may be done by gravimetric, colorimetric or other validation procedures. Alternative approaches include spectrophotometry and the use of commercial kits. 
  
  For analytic instruments with integral automatic pipettors, this checklist requirement applies, unless such checks are not practical for end-user laboratory. Manufacturers' recommendations must be followed. 
  
  This requirement is not applicable for pre-calibrated inoculation loops that are used in the direct plating of clinical specimens such as urine cultures.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of initial and ongoing verification of pipette accuracy and reproducibility
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a formal policy (FS1001.0V2) and maintains records of pipette verification (e.g., 230717- CP1 Initial Pipette Verification). However, a discrepancy exists between the SOP requirements and the actual practice documented in '221207 special Pipette Verification.xlsx'. The SOP mandates the use of distilled water for gravimetric verification, but the record indicates the use of VTM (Viral Transport Medium) for pipette AP8. Furthermore, the 'Pipette performance verification certification template.docx' lists acceptance criteria (CV% and Accuracy limits) that differ from the 99%-101% accuracy and <1% imprecision criteria defined in the SOP and other templates. The laboratory must reconcile the acceptance criteria across all templates and ensure that verification procedures strictly adhere to the validated SOP methodology.
corrective_actions: 1) Standardize acceptance criteria across all verification templates to match the validated SOP FS1001.0V2.
2) Retrain staff on the requirement to use distilled water for gravimetric verification as specified in the SOP, prohibiting the use of non-standard matrices like VTM.
cited_documents: FS1001.0V2_Micro Pipette usage Calibration and Maintenance SOP.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30820**: XYZ Lab's "Micropipette usage, Calibration and Maintenance SOP" FS1001.0V2 outlines the procedure for pipette calibration verification. Pipettes are sent to an accredited lab annually for calibration and verified in-house every six months. The in-house verification process involves using an analytical balance and distilled water. Three volumes are tested: nominal, 50% of nominal, and 10% of nominal. For each volume, ten replicates are dispensed, and the weight is recorded, with the balance tared between each measurement. The room temperature is recorded, and a Z-factor is used to account for water density at different temperatures. For a pipette to pass, the Imprecision (C.V.) must be less than 1%, and Accuracy must be between 99%-101%. If a pipette fails, it is taken out of use and sent for recalibration or repair. The "Pipette performance verification certification template" and "Pipette Verification Template" are used to record results. Records like "221207 special Pipette Verification" and "230717- CP1 Initial Pipette Verification" demonstrate these checks, showing calculations for mean, standard deviation, imprecision, and accuracy.

checks.requirement: The use of less precise measuring devices such as serological plastic pipettes and graduated cylinders are limited to situations where the accuracy and precision of calibrated glass pipettes are not required.
checks.subject: Measuring Devices
checks.note: NOTE: In contrast with the more stringent accuracy requirements of glass pipettes, ASTM requirements for plastic pipettes are ± 3% of the stated volume. The procedure manual must specify when the use of non-class A measuring devices is permissible.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established policy requirements for measuring devices in 'F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program' and 'FS1001.0V2_Micro Pipette usage Calibration and Maintenance SOP'. These documents correctly identify the need to restrict less precise devices (e.g., plastic pipettes) to applications not requiring high-precision glass pipettes and acknowledge the ASTM ±3% accuracy standard for plastic pipettes. However, while the SOPs define the performance criteria for micropipettes, the current documentation does not explicitly list or define the specific laboratory procedures or test methods where the use of non-class A measuring devices (such as graduated cylinders or serological pipettes) is permissible. The laboratory must explicitly document in the procedure manual which specific assays or steps allow for the use of these less precise devices to ensure compliance with the requirement.
corrective_actions: 1) Update the procedure manual or relevant SOPs to explicitly list the specific laboratory procedures where the use of non-class A measuring devices is permissible.
2) Ensure that all staff are trained on the limitations of plastic pipettes and graduated cylinders as defined in the updated procedure manual.
cited_documents: FS1001.0V2_Micro Pipette usage Calibration and Maintenance SOP.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30830**: The XYZ Lab’s Equipment Calibration Program, F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program, restricts less precise measuring devices like plastic pipettes and graduated cylinders to applications not requiring calibrated glass pipette accuracy, with usage detailed in applicable SOPs and plastic pipettes adhering to ASTM ±3% volume variation standards. Micropipette accuracy and precision are verified before the manufacturer’s due date for new units and every six months for older ones; failed units must be removed from service for repair or calibration. Per FS1001.0V2_Micro Pipette usage Calibration and Maintenance SOP, passing criteria require <1% imprecision and 99%-101% accuracy, consistent with the Pipette performance verification certification template and G14224D-250418_ Pipette Verification, which specify these thresholds for 100-1000 µL volumes. This SOP also mandates daily maintenance, such as setting pipettes to maximum volume to preserve spring integrity. The F1007.1 Instrument Equipment List identifies the "Serological Pipette EP-Pro" (ID SP1) located in the Cell Culture Lab BSC A0022.

checks.requirement: The laboratory evaluates its automatic pipetting systems for carryover.
checks.subject: Pipette Carryover
checks.note:
NOTE: This requirement applies to both stand-alone pipette systems and to sample pipettes integrated with analytic instruments. 
  
  One suggested method to study carryover is to run known high patient samples, followed by known low samples to see if the results of the low-level material are affected. If carryover is detected, the laboratory must determine the analyte concentration above which subsequent samples may be affected, and define this value in the procedure. Results of each analytical run must be reviewed to ensure that no results exceed this level. If results that exceed the defined level are detected, then the appropriate course of action must be defined (repeat analysis of subsequent samples, for example). 
  
  Carryover studies must be performed, as applicable, as part of the initial evaluation of an instrument and be repeated after major maintenance or repair of the pipetting assembly of the instrument. The laboratory may use the data from carryover studies performed by instrument manufacturers, as appropriate. 
  
  In practice, carryover is a problem only for analytes with a wide clinical range of analyte concentration, such that a minute degree of carry-over could have significant clinical implications. Examples include immunoassays such as hCG, certain enzymes (eg, CK), and certain drugs of abuse (eg, benzoylecgonine [cocaine metabolite], which may be present in high concentrations). The laboratory should select representative examples of such analytes for carryover studies. 
  
  Evaluation for carryover is not required for automatic pipettes that use disposable tips.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Record of carryover studies, as applicable
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. While the laboratory maintains policies for pipette calibration and maintenance (FS1001.0V2) and cross-contamination prevention (G1008.0V2), there is no evidence of a formal carryover study for automatic pipetting systems as required by COM.30840. The search summary indicates that while a specific study was performed for the Simplexa™ Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II assay, the laboratory lacks a comprehensive carryover evaluation for other applicable analytical instruments or systems with wide clinical ranges. The current documentation focuses on calibration and aerosol prevention rather than the specific requirement to evaluate and define analyte concentrations where carryover may impact patient results.
corrective_actions: 1) Identify all analytical instruments with automatic pipetting systems that do not use disposable tips and are subject to carryover risks.
2) Perform and document carryover studies for representative high-concentration analytes as defined in the COM.30840 note.
3) Update the Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan (G1001.0) to include defined carryover thresholds and corrective actions for results exceeding these levels.
cited_documents: FS1001.0V2_Micro Pipette usage Calibration and Maintenance SOP.pdf
G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30840**: The Micropipette usage, Calibration and Maintenance SOP (FS1001.0V2) mandates annual external calibration by an accredited lab and in-house verification every six months. Verification requires testing nominal, 50%, and 10% volumes by dispensing distilled water ten times, requiring accuracy between 99%-101% and a coefficient of variation under 1%. Non-compliant pipettes are repaired or retired. The PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program (G1008.0V2) requires regular cleaning and calibration, the use of filtered tips to prevent aerosol contamination, and tip changes between samples. While a carry-over study for the Simplexa™ Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II assay confirmed no contamination in those specific channels, the provided documentation lacks a general record of carry-over studies for automatic pipetting systems.

XYZ Lab Document Name Micropipette usage, Calibration and Maintenance SOP
XYZ Lab Document Number FS1001.0 Version # 2 Author: XYZ Lab Inception Date: 11/12/2020 Date of latest version: 09/26/2023 5.2. Pipette calibration verification using an Analytical Balance
Before calibration collect the following supplies: Pipettes, tips, weight boats, distilled water,
analytical balance. Before using the analytical balance make sure it has been calibrated before use. 5.2. 0. Record the room temperature. 5.2. 1. Place a weigh boat on the balance and tare it. 5.2. 2. Set the pipette to the desired volume. For verification three different volumes
will be used: the nominal volume, 50% of the nominal volume, and the lower
limit of the pipette (10% of the nominal volume). 5.2. 3. Pre-rinse the tip by aspirating and dispensing the distilled water three times. 5.2. 4. Aspirate the desired volume, without bubble formation in the tip, and
dispense the liquid into the weigh boat. 5.2. 5. Record the weight of the liquid and repeat ten times. Make sure to tare
the balance between each measurement. 5.2. 6. Adjust the pipette to the second volume and repeat steps 4-6. 5.2. 7. Adjust the pipette to the third volume and repeat steps 4-6. 5.2.

policy_evidence.snippet:
2.4.6 All pipettes shall be cleaned and calibrated or calibration verified at regular intervals. 2.5 Laboratory Coats
Laboratory coats shall be dedicated to specific use areas and changed when moving between areas. 2.5.1 Gloves
To reduce the possibility of introducing amplified nucleic acid products into the clean areas, disposable gloves shall be
worn and changed when entering or reentering the amplification preparation area. Disposable gloves may be changed
between samples to prevent cross-contamination. 2.6 Biohazard and Amplicon Disposal
All nucleic acids amplification products and remnant patient samples shall be closed and disposed in the biohazard waste
bin. It is critical that all waste shall be removed as soon as possible to reduce the risk of contamination. 2.7 Monitoring
2.7.1No template control shall be run with each test to ensure the testing system is free of contaminants. In cased a system
contamination event is confirmed, investigation experiments shall be performed to identify the source of contamination. Testing environment wipe tests may be performed if necessary. Corrective action shall be taken to eliminate the problem. 2.7.2 Unexpected increase in positive results shall be investigated both experimentally and statically. Experimentally,
investigation involves in control sample, specimen handling, assay process, reagents and consumables. Statistically,
investigation includes population prevalence, specimen characteristics, historic positive distribution/pattern.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30870**: Analytical balances are sensitive precision instruments, and their location significantly impacts the accuracy of weighing results. To ensure accurate and precise measurements, balances should be placed indoors on a stable, vibration-free, and as horizontal as possible surface that can safely support the balance's weight. It is crucial to avoid vibrations, strong drafts, direct sunlight, and excessive temperature fluctuations. If vibrations are present, the weighing location should be protected against them, potentially using vibration absorbers. The balance must be leveled and adjusted each time it is moved to a new location. The "NO STABILITY" error message indicates vibrations at the workplace, and a remedy is to protect the weighing location against vibrations.

checks.requirement: Standard weights of the appropriate American National Standards Institute (ANSI)/ASTM Class are available and used for verifying accuracy of analytical balances at defined intervals, with records retained.
checks.subject: Analytical Balance Accuracy
checks.note:
NOTE: The verification of accuracy of the analytical balance must be performed at a defined interval to ensure accurate creation of analytical calibrators and/or weighed-in controls from standard materials, as well as when gravimetrically checking the accuracy of pipettes. 
  
  Accuracy must be verified at least every six months if used for weighing materials to make standard solutions for method calibration. Accuracy must be verified at the time of installation and whenever a balance is moved. Acceptable ranges must be defined. 
  
  External verification of accuracy requires the appropriate class of ASTM specification weights. ASTM Class 1 weights are appropriate for calibrating high precision analytical balances (0.01 to 0.1 mg limit of precision). ASTM Class 2 weights are appropriate for calibrating precision top-loading balances (0.001 to 0.01 g precision). ASTM Class 3 weights are appropriate for calibrating moderate precision balances, (0.01 to 0.1 g precision). 
  
  Laboratories located outside of the United States may use equivalent certified weights if ANSI/ASTM class standard weights are not available.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established policies for balance calibration verification in 'FS1003.0v3_Analytical Balance Calibration and Use' and 'F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program', which define the use of OIML/ASTM weights and a six-month verification interval. However, while the policy defines the requirements, the current evidence set lacks the actual maintenance and verification logs (records) to demonstrate that these intervals are being met and that accuracy is being documented as required by COM.30880. The search summary confirms the existence of a program, but the specific records of balance accuracy verification were not provided for review. To achieve full compliance, the laboratory must produce the completed verification logs for the analytical balances to prove the defined intervals are being followed.
corrective_actions: 1) Compile and maintain a log of all analytical balance accuracy verifications performed at the defined six-month intervals.
2) Ensure all verification records include the date, the specific ASTM/OIML class weights used, and the measured results compared against the defined acceptable ranges.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30880**: The "Analytical Balance Calibration and Use" SOP, FS1003.0v3_Analytical Balance Calibration and Use, outlines procedures for balance calibration verification. This includes tests for repeatability, eccentricity, linearity, and accuracy. Calibration weights used for the balance are standardized to meet NIST standards. These weights require careful handling, such as using gloves or tweezers, and proper storage in a protective lined case to prevent damage or contamination. External verification of these weights by an ISO 17025 accredited service provider is required every five years. The balance calibration itself must be verified annually following ISO 17025 guidelines. For routine testing, various Precision and Analytical Balances models specify the use of OIML or ASTM CarePac Weights of different classes and gram values. For example, the ME104T model uses 5g (F2)/100g (F2) OIML class weights, while the ME3002 model uses 2000g F2 and 100g F2 OIML CarePac Weights or 2000g 1 and 100g 1 ASTM CarePac Weights. The "Equipment Calibration Program" F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program states that calibration verification must be performed using calibration materials in the same manner as patient samples to confirm instrument stability every six months.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Once a week wipe down the glass panels and
interior surfaces with a damp towel, or a standard cleaning agent. Wipe interior surfaces with
a 70% ethanol solution for decontamination when necessary. 9.2 Maintaining Calibration weights
The weights used for calibrating the balance are standardized to meet NIST standards and are
very sensitive tools. Do not handle with bare hands, the oils from hands can change the value
of the weights to make calibrations inaccurate and can even cause corrosive damage to the
weights, always use the provided gloves or tweezers to handle the weights. Do not drop the
weights or handle them roughly, this could also cause the value of the weights to change and
make calibrations inaccurate. Always store the weights in the protective lined case when not
in use, even small dust and dirt particles can affect the calibration results, if dust and
fingerprints are present clean the weights with a soft brush and make sure not to touch the
bristles with bare hands. Every five years the weights will need to be verified using an external ISO 17025 accredited

checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The search summary confirms that laboratory staff are instructed to wear gloves and avoid touching weights, and that NIST weights are used for weekly calibration per the '2_C1001.2_Laboratory Routine Maintenance Record'. XYZ Lab Document Number FS1001.0 Version # 2 Author: XYZ Lab Inception Date: 11/12/2020 Date of latest version: 09/26/2023 5.2. Pipette calibration verification using an Analytical Balance
Before calibration collect the following supplies: Pipettes, tips, weight boats, distilled water,
analytical balance. Before using the analytical balance make sure it has been calibrated before use. 5.2. 0. Record the room temperature. 5.2. 1. Place a weigh boat on the balance and tare it. 5.2. 2. Set the pipette to the desired volume. For verification three different volumes
will be used: the nominal volume, 50% of the nominal volume, and the lower
limit of the pipette (10% of the nominal volume). 5.2. 3. Pre-rinse the tip by aspirating and dispensing the distilled water three times. 5.2. 4. Aspirate the desired volume, without bubble formation in the tip, and
dispense the liquid into the weigh boat. 5.2. 5. Record the weight of the liquid and repeat ten times. Make sure to tare
the balance between each measurement. 5.2. 6. Adjust the pipette to the second volume and repeat steps 4-6. 5.2. 7. Adjust the pipette to the third volume and repeat steps 4-6. 5.2.

checks.requirement: The laboratory director or designee meeting CAP director qualifications approves the introduction of new waived tests.
checks.subject: Waived Test Implementation and Approval
checks.note:
NOTE: After initial approval, the introduction of additional identical waived instruments performing identical previously approved waived tests does not require approval by the director or designee, providing manufacturer instructions for instrument verification are followed and recorded. 
  
  Waived testing must be performed following the manufacturer's instructions. If the laboratory modifies a waived test, the checklist requirements for high complexity testing apply, including the requirements for validation of the method performance specifications. 
  
  The laboratory director's signature on the written test procedure may be used to show approval of the test for use in patient testing. 
  
  This requirement also applies to tests with FDA emergency use authorization (EUA) specifically designated by the FDA or other entities as designated by the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary for use in patient care settings in the EUA Letter of Authorization. Such tests are deemed to be CLIA waived tests.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of test approval
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a formal 'Test Validation and Verification Program' (G1004.0V3) and a 'Change Request Form' process (G1007.1_Change Request Form for KPI 250324.pdf) that require Laboratory Director approval for test implementation. While these policies align with the requirement for director oversight, the laboratory failed to provide specific 'Records of test approval' for the waived tests currently in use (e.g., COVID/FLU/RSV molecular testing). The documentation confirms the existence of a process, but the actual evidence of director-signed approval for the introduction of these specific waived tests was not verified in the provided document set.
corrective_actions: 1) Locate and archive signed approval records for all currently implemented waived tests, ensuring the Laboratory Director or qualified designee signature is present.
2) Ensure future waived test implementations include a documented approval record, such as a signed test procedure or a completed Change Request Form (G1007.1), as per COM.30980 requirements.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.30980**: The laboratory director or designee, who meets CAP director qualifications, is responsible for approving the introduction of new waived tests. The director's qualifications include holding an MD, DO, or DPM license with specific board certifications or experience, or a doctoral degree with board certification and relevant experience. While the "Records of test approval" were requested, no such records were found in the provided documents. However, the "Change Request Form for KPI" indicates that the laboratory uses waived tests for direct-to-customer molecular testing of COVID/FLU/RSV, and that all tests have run smoothly. The "Test Validation and Verification Program" outlines a process for test validation, including approval of a validation plan by the lab director before experiments begin. The validation report, which includes method performance summaries, must also be approved by the lab director.

checks.requirement:
Prior to clinical use of each unmodified FDA-cleared or approved test, the laboratory has performed a verification study and prepared a written assessment of each of the following test method performance specifications, as applicable, using a sufficient number of characterized samples: 
  
  1. Analytical accuracy 
  2. Analytical precision 
  3. Reportable range
checks.subject: Verification of Test Performance Specifications - FDA-cleared/approved Tests
checks.note:
NOTE 1: This requirement also applies to tests with FDA emergency use authorization (EUA) in moderate or high complexity testing laboratory settings. 
  
  NOTE 2: Accuracy is verified by comparing results to a definitive or reference method, or an established comparative method. Use of matrix-appropriate reference materials, patient specimens (altered or unaltered), or other commutable materials with known concentrations or activities may be used to verify accuracy. The use of routine quality control materials or calibrators used to calibrate the method is not appropriate. 
  
  NOTE 3: Precision is verified by repeat measurement of samples at varying concentrations/activities within run and between run over a period of time. 
  
  NOTE 4: The reportable range of an assay is the range of test result values over which the laboratory has verified accuracy of the instrument or test system measurement response. 
  
  NOTE 5: If multiple identical instruments or devices are in use, there must be records (data and written assessment) showing that the method performance specifications have been separately verified for each test and instrument or device. 
  
  NOTE 6: If a method is verified by someone other than the laboratory's personnel (eg, manufacturer's representative), the laboratory must have records to show that the verification correlates with its in-house test performance by showing confirmation of performance specifications by the laboratory personnel testing known specimens. 
  
  NOTE 7: The requirement for a written assessment applies to all tests implemented after June 15, 2009; however, all nonwaived tests must have records of completed analytical verification, regardless of the implementation date. The written assessment must include an evaluation of each component of the verification study, including the acceptability of the data. If data include discordant results, there must be a record of the discordance and investigation of any impact on the approval of the test for clinical use. 
  
  Templates for analytical verification written assessment can be found on cap.org in e-LAB Solutions Suite - Accreditation Resources - Templates. 
  
  NOTE 8: For contract research organization (CRO) laboratories: For tests performed strictly for research purposes, the laboratory may accept verification studies performed by the sponsor or manufacturer contracting with the laboratory. The laboratory must retain records showing: 1) attestation by the manufacturer (or contractor) that the test was verified; and 2) how the test is used, and attestation that the test is used for research only and will not be accessible for clinical purposes. 
  
  If a test result is used to render any decision that may affect the study subject, even if only to determine enrollment, continued participation of an individual in a study, or as an outcome measure in a clinical trial, the testing is considered patient testing, and the laboratory is responsible for performing on-site analytic verification of the test.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of verification and written assessment of each component of the test method performance specifications for each test
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a framework for verification through 'G1005.0-Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025.pdf' and 'Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft.docx'. However, the current evidence is insufficient to demonstrate full compliance. While the laboratory has a plan for analytical measurement range verification, there is no documented evidence of completed verification studies (data and written assessments) for accuracy, precision, and reportable range for each specific FDA-cleared test currently in use. Per Note 7, the laboratory must provide a written assessment for each test, including an evaluation of data acceptability and any investigations into discordant results. The provided documents are procedural or draft templates and do not constitute the required records of completed performance specification verification for clinical implementation.
corrective_actions: 1) Perform and document verification studies for accuracy, precision, and reportable range for all FDA-cleared tests, ensuring each study includes a written assessment of data acceptability.
2) Ensure all verification reports are reviewed and signed by the laboratory director prior to clinical use, as required by the search summary.
3) Maintain individual verification records for each instrument if multiple identical devices are in use, per Note 5.
cited_documents: G1005.0-Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.40300**: The laboratory must verify or establish analytical and clinical performance characteristics for each test. For unmodified FDA-cleared/approved tests, the verification scope typically includes accuracy, precision, and reportable range. Accuracy is assessed using well-characterized reference material or by comparison to another valid test method, such as through specimen exchange, and expressed as a percentage of concordance. For quantitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples with analyte concentrations across the analytical measurement range should be used. Precision studies verify that expected results are obtained reproducibly from the same sample. The reportable range is the span of all test results considered valid, and its establishment requires a sufficient number of samples. All test systems must be validated/verified to ensure performance specifications meet QC requirements prior to patient sample testing. The validation reports must be reviewed and approved by the laboratory director before using the system for patient samples.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan Document Name
Document Number G1005.0 Version # 1 Author： Wenli Zhou Date of Composition: 04/02/2021 Date of Execution：04/05/2021 Page 1 of 3 Approved by Laboratory Director_____ __, Date _______04/02/2021____ Objective
Provide guidelines on laboratory Analytical Measurement Range (AMR) calibration and calibration verification to
maintain on-going analytical continuity and accuracy for both quantitative and qualitative test systems. Definition:
1.1 AMR: AMR is the range of analyte values that a method can directly measure on the specimen without any dilution,
concentration, or other pretreatment not part of the usual assay process. 1.2 Linearity and the AMR: A plot of measured values from test samples vs. their actual (or expected) concentration or
relative concentrations must be linear within defined acceptance criteria over the AMR. Verifying linearity using such a
plot verifies the AMR. Beyond the limits of the AMR, there may not be a linear relationship between measured and actual
analyte concentrations, and test results may therefore be unreliable. Plans
2.1 For patient samples, only measured values that fall within the AMR (or can be brought into the AMR by sample
dilution or concentration) should be reported. Values that fall outside the AMR may be reported as "less than" or "greater
than" the limits of the AMR.
policy_evidence.title: G1005.0-Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025

checks.requirement:
For laboratories not subject to US regulations, prior to clinical use of each test approved by an internationally recognized regulatory authority (eg, the European Union's Conformité Européenne (CE) Marking), the laboratory has performed a verification study and prepared a written assessment of each of the following test method performance specifications, as applicable, using a sufficient number of characterized samples: 
  
  1. Analytical accuracy 
  2. Analytical precision 
  3. Reportable range 
  4. Any other performance characteristic required to ensure analytical test performance
checks.subject: Verification of Test Performance Specifications - Tests Approved by an Internationally Recognized Regulatory Authority - Laboratories not Subject to US Regulations
checks.note:
NOTE 1: Accuracy is verified by comparing results to a definitive or reference method, or an established comparative method. Use of matrix-appropriate reference materials, patient specimens (altered or unaltered), or other commutable materials with known concentrations or activities may be used to verify accuracy. The use of routine quality control materials or calibrators used to calibrate the method is not appropriate. 
  
  NOTE 2: Precision is verified by repeat measurement of samples at varying concentrations or activities within run and between run over a period of time. 
  
  NOTE 3: The reportable range of an assay is the range of test result values over which the laboratory has verified accuracy of the instrument or test system measurement response. 
  
  NOTE 4: The laboratory must also validate analytic sensitivity (lower detection limit) and analytic specificity (interferences) if the test manufacturer has not documented these test characteristics. Data on interferences may be obtained from manufacturers or published literature, as applicable. The laboratory must validate other relevant analytic characteristics not documented by the test manufacturer, as appropriate. 
  
  NOTE 5: If multiple identical instruments or devices are in use, there must be records (data and written assessment) showing that the method performance specifications have been separately verified for each test and instrument or device. 
  
  NOTE 6: If a method is verified by someone other than the laboratory's personnel (eg, manufacturer's representative), the laboratory must have records to show that the verification correlates with in-house test performance by showing confirmation of performance specifications by the laboratory personnel testing known specimens. 
  
  NOTE 7: The requirement for a written assessment applies to all tests implemented after June 15, 2009; however, all nonwaived tests must have records of completed analytical verification, regardless of the implementation date. The written assessment must include an evaluation of each component of the verification study, including the acceptability of the data; If data include discordant results, there must be a record of the discordance and investigation of any impact on the approval of the test for clinical use. 
  
  Templates for analytical verification written assessment can be found on cap.org in e-LAB Solutions Suite - Accreditation Resources - Templates. 
  
  NOTE 8: For contract research organization (CRO) laboratories: For tests performed strictly for research purposes, the laboratory may accept verification studies performed by the sponsor or manufacturer contracting with the laboratory. The laboratory must retain records showing: 1) attestation by the manufacturer (or contractor) that the test was verified; and 2) how the test is used, and attestation that the test is used for research only and will not be accessible for clinical purposes. 
  
  If a test result is used to render any decision that may affect the study subject, even if only to determine enrollment, continued participation of an individual in a study, or as an outcome measure in a clinical trial, the testing is considered patient testing, and the laboratory is responsible for performing on-site analytic verification of the test.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of the test method performance specifications for each test
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a formal policy for test verification (G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program) and has produced at least one completed verification report (XYZG1004.2501_TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic Assay Verification test report-final signed.pdf). However, the current documentation is insufficient to demonstrate compliance for all tests implemented. While the TaqPath report provides evidence of accuracy and precision, the laboratory must ensure that a written assessment—including evaluation of data acceptability and investigation of any discordant results—is present for every test implemented after June 15, 2009. The 'Liaison MDx Verification Guide' remains in draft status, and there is no evidence provided that all other non-waived tests have completed verification records as required by Note 7. The laboratory must perform a comprehensive audit of all test files to ensure the required performance specifications (accuracy, precision, reportable range) are documented for each assay.
corrective_actions: 1) Conduct a comprehensive audit of all non-waived test files to ensure a written verification assessment exists for every test implemented after June 15, 2009.
2) Finalize the 'Liaison MDx Verification Guide' and implement a standardized template for written assessments that includes data acceptability and discordance investigation as per Note 7.
3) Ensure that for any test with multiple instruments, separate verification records are maintained for each device per Note 5.

checks.ai_evidence_summary:
**COM.40325**: The Test Validation and Verification Program (G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program) outlines the objective to establish and validate/verify lab assay method performance specifications. For unmodified FDA-cleared/approved tests, the scope of validation typically requires verification of accuracy, precision, and reportable range. The Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft also states that the performance of all FDA-cleared, non-modified, moderate- and high-complexity diagnostic tests must be verified for accuracy, precision, reference range, and reportable range, aligning with CMS and CLSI guidelines.

Analytical accuracy can be assessed using well-characterized reference material or by comparison to another valid test method. For quantitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples with analyte concentrations distributed across the analytical measurement range should be used, while qualitative tests require a minimum of 20 samples, including positive, negative, and low-positive samples. Precision studies aim to verify that expected results are obtained reproducibly from the same sample. The TaqPath™ COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Assay Performance Verification Report provides an example of a verification study that includes analytical accuracy and precision verification, using known positive and negative patient samples and contrived samples. This report also details data transfer accuracy validation.

TaqPath™ COVID-19 RNase P Combo Kit 2.0 Verification study report
Date: 01/17/2025 Background
After January 15th, 2025, the reagent of TaqPath™ COVID-19 RNase P Combo Kit 2.0 EUA
assay will be terminated by the manufacturer. XYZ Lab will use the TaqPathTM COVID-19 Diagnostic
PCR Kit Assay, an IVD assay, to replace the EUA assay. This study aims to verify the key performance
specifications of the assay including the analytical accuracy, precision and reportable range in our
laboratory. In addition, we will also validate the data analysis, transfer and reporting process to ensure the
accuracy
Experimental Design 1. Analytical accuracy verification: test 10 known positive and 10 known negative patient samples and
compare their testing results with that of the previous assay, Taqpath COVID-19 RNAse P Combo
Kit 2.0 assay (Taqpath Combo 2.0). In addition, 8 contrived samples with concentration at the level of
LoD were included. The contrived samples were made using a gamma-irradiated quantitative SARS
CoV2 reference sample (BEI resource. NR-52287) at a concentration of 50 copies/mL (see section
Methods 1 for details)
Acceptance criteria: All positive and negative should be tested as expected.

results.snippet:
TaqPath™ COVID-19 RNase P Combo Kit 2.0 Verification study report
Date: 01/17/2025 Background
After January 15th, 2025, the reagent of TaqPath™ COVID-19 RNase P Combo Kit 2.0 EUA
assay will be terminated by the manufacturer. XYZ Lab will use the TaqPathTM COVID-19 Diagnostic
PCR Kit Assay, an IVD assay, to replace the EUA assay. This study aims to verify the key performance
specifications of the assay including the analytical accuracy, precision and reportable range in our
laboratory. In addition, we will also validate the data analysis, transfer and reporting process to ensure the
accuracy
Experimental Design 1. Analytical accuracy verification: test 10 known positive and 10 known negative patient samples and
compare their testing results with that of the previous assay, Taqpath COVID-19 RNAse P Combo
Kit 2.0 assay (Taqpath Combo 2.0). In addition, 8 contrived samples with concentration at the level of
LoD were included. The contrived samples were made using a gamma-irradiated quantitative SARS
CoV2 reference sample (BEI resource. NR-52287) at a concentration of 50 copies/mL (see section
Methods 1 for details)
Acceptance criteria: All positive and negative should be tested as expected.
