checks.requirement:
Prior to clinical use of each modified FDA-cleared or approved test and laboratory-developed tests (LDTs), the laboratory has performed a validation study and prepared a written assessment of each of the following test method performance specifications, as applicable, using a sufficient number of characterized samples: 
  
  * Analytical accuracy 
  * Analytical precision 
  * Reportable range 
  * Analytical sensitivity (lower detection limit) 
  * Analytical specificity 
  * Any other performance characteristic required to ensure analytical test performance
checks.subject: Validation of Test Performance Specifications - Modified FDA-cleared/approved Tests and LDTs
checks.note:
NOTE 1: For laboratories not subject to US regulations, this requirement also applies to: 
  
  * Tests that are not approved by an internationally recognized regulatory authority 
  * Approved tests that have been modified by the laboratory 
  
  NOTE 2: Accuracy is validated by comparing results to a definitive or reference method, or an established comparative method. Use of matrix-appropriate reference materials, patient specimens (altered or unaltered), or other commutable materials with known concentrations or activities may be used to validate accuracy. The use of routine quality control materials or calibrators used to calibrate the method is not appropriate. 
  
  For laboratory-developed tests, an appropriate number of samples to demonstrate analytical accuracy is defined as the following: 
  
  * For quantitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples with analyte concentrations distributed across the analytical measurement range should be used. Proportionate mixtures of samples may be used to supplement the study population. 
  * For qualitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples, including positive, negative, and low-positive samples with concentrations near the lower level of detection should be used; equivocal samples should not be used. 
  * For certain methods that test multiple analytes (eg, next-generation sequencing, HPLC, GC-MS, MALDI-TOF, etc.), analytic accuracy may be established for each method (not necessarily each analyte), as appropriate. 
  
  If the laboratory uses fewer samples, the laboratory director must record the criteria used to determine the appropriateness of the sample size. In many cases, a validation study with more samples is desirable. 
  
  For LDTs in use prior to July 31, 2016, for which limited validation studies are recorded, ongoing data supporting acceptable test performance may be used to meet the above minimum sample requirement, unless the laboratory director has recorded the criteria used to determine the acceptability of a smaller sample size. Examples of such ongoing data include records of proficiency testing, alternative performance assessment, quality control, and correlation with clinical data. 
  
  NOTE 3: Precision is validated by repeat measurement of samples at varying concentrations or activities within-run and between-run over a period of time. 
  
  NOTE 4: The reportable range of an assay is the range of test result values over which the laboratory has established accuracy of the instrument or test system measurement response 
  
  NOTE 5: Analytical sensitivity is the lowest concentration or amount of the analyte or substance that can be measured or distinguished from a blank (lower limit of detection). 
  
  NOTE 6: Analytical specificity refers to the ability of a test or procedure to correctly identify or quantify an entity in the presence of interfering or cross-reactive substances that might be expected to be present. Laboratories are encouraged to review the published literature for guidance on analytical specificity. 
  
  NOTE 7: Examples of other performance characteristics required for analytical test performance include specimen stability, reagent stability, linearity, carryover, and cross-contamination, as appropriate and applicable. 
  
  NOTE 8: If multiple identical instruments or devices are in use, there must be records (data and written assessment) showing that the method performance specifications have been separately validated for each test and instrument or device. 
  
  NOTE 9: The requirement for a written assessment applies to all tests implemented after June 15, 2009; however, all nonwaived tests must have records of completed analytical validation, regardless of the implementation date. The written assessment must include an evaluation of each component of the validation study, including the acceptability of the data. If data include discordant results, there must be a record of the discordance and investigation of any impact on the approval of the test for clinical use. 
  
  Templates for analytical verification written assessment can be found on cap.org in e-LAB Solutions Suite - Accreditation Resources - Templates. 
  
  NOTE 10: For contract research organization (CRO) laboratories: For tests performed strictly for research purposes, the laboratory may accept validation studies performed by the sponsor or manufacturer contracting with the laboratory. The laboratory must retain records showing: 1) attestation by the manufacturer (or contractor) that the test was validated, and 2) how the test is used, and attestation that the test is used for research only and will not be accessible for clinical purposes. 
  
  If a test result is used to render any decision that may affect the study subject, even if only to determine enrollment, continued participation of an individual in a study, or as an outcome measure in a clinical trial, the testing is considered patient testing, and the laboratory is responsible for performing on-site analytic validation of the test. 
  
  NOTE 11: This checklist requirement does not apply to LDTs that employ the following methods: 
  
  * Manual microscopy (eg, histopathologic and cytologic interpretation, microscopic examination of blood or body fluids, Gram stains) 
  * Conventional microbiologic cultures
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of validation and written assessment of each component of the test method performance specifications
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a formal framework for test validation via 'G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program.pdf', which outlines the requirements for accuracy, precision, reportable range, and sensitivity. However, while the policy is present, the laboratory has not provided the specific, completed validation records (written assessments) for individual LDTs or modified FDA-cleared tests to demonstrate compliance with the minimum sample requirements (e.g., 20 samples for quantitative tests) or the laboratory director's approval of these studies. The retrieved documents include alternative proficiency assessment records (K1002.2V2), but these do not constitute the initial analytical validation studies required by COM.40350. Evidence of completed validation data and the corresponding written assessments for current clinical assays remains not verified.
corrective_actions: 1) Compile and finalize written validation assessment reports for all LDTs and modified FDA-cleared tests, ensuring all performance specifications listed in COM.40350 are addressed.
2) Ensure the laboratory director reviews and signs off on all validation data, including documentation of sample size justification if fewer than 20 samples were used.
3) Maintain these records in a centralized validation file for each assay to ensure audit readiness.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.40350**: The "Test Validation and Verification Program" (G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program) outlines plans for establishing and validating laboratory assay method performance specifications. For unmodified FDA-cleared/approved tests, the scope of validation typically verifies accuracy, precision, and reportable range. However, if an FDA-cleared or approved test is modified, a validation plan must be in place to confirm all specifications as for a laboratory-developed test (LDT). Analytical performance parameters for LDTs include accuracy, precision, reportable range, reference interval, analytical sensitivity, limit of detection, analytical specificity, and robustness. Accuracy can be assessed using well-characterized reference material or by comparison to another valid test method, with quantitative tests requiring a minimum of 20 samples with analyte concentrations across the analytical measurement range. Precision studies verify that expected results are obtained reproducibly from the same sample. The laboratory must verify or establish analytical and clinical performance characteristics for each test. Validation reports must be reviewed and approved by the laboratory director before using the system for patient samples.

policy_evidence.snippet: Introduction & Intended Use This example verification guide is intended to serve as an educational resource to assist laboratories in the verification of FDA-cleared tests within their laboratory. Ultimately, the Laboratory and Laboratory Director (or equivalent) are responsible for designing, reviewing, and approving their verification study and determining whether it aligns with federal, state, and local guidelines. Per the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines, the performance of all FDA-cleared, non-modified, moderate- and high-complexity diagnostic tests must be verified for accuracy, precision reference range, and reportable range.1,2 Accuracy Accuracy is typically verified by testing a collection of known clinical/contrived samples and commercially available controls. The number of positive and negative samples needed for each target is determined by the laboratory. When using samples previously categorized by another method, discrepancies can occur due to several factors (e.g., primer design, limit of detection). In the example verification that follows, we chose to incorporate a collection of contrived samples and third-party controls for the accuracy study. Precision Precision studies are intended to verify that expected results are obtained reproducibly from the same sample.
policy_evidence.title: Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft

Collection and Storage of Waste:
(a) Chemical waste should be accumulated at or near the point of generation, under the control of laboratory
workers. (b) Each waste type should be stored in a compatible container pending transfer or disposal. Waste containers
should be clearly labeled and kept sealed when not in use. (c) Incompatible waste types should be kept separate to ensure that heat generation, gas evolution, or another
reaction does not occur. (d) Waste containers should be segregated by how they will be managed. Waste containers should be stored in a
designated location that does not interfere with normal laboratory operations. Ventilated storage and secondary
containment may be appropriate for certain waste types. (e) Waste containers should be clearly labeled and kept sealed when not in use. Labels should include the
accumulation start date and hazard warnings as appropriate. (f) Non-explosive electrical systems, grounding and bonding between floors and containers, and non-sparking
conductive floors and containers should be used in the central waste accumulation area to minimize fire and
explosion hazards. Fire suppression systems, specialized ventilation systems, and dikes should be installed in the
central waste accumulation area. Waste management workers should be trained in proper waste handling 29 CFR 1910.1450 (up to date as of 6/13/2022)

If the laboratory uses more than one nonwaived instrument/method to test for a given

checks.requirement: The laboratory understands the analytical interferences for each test, and has an appropriate plan of action when they are present.
checks.subject: Analytical Interferences
checks.note: NOTE: Interfering substances may pose a significant problem to the clinical laboratory and healthcare providers who may be misled by laboratory results that do not reflect patient clinical status. The laboratory must be aware of common interferences by performing studies or referencing studies performed elsewhere (such as by the instrument-reagent manufacturer).
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Document listing known interferences for each test and plan of action when they are present
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has successfully identified analytical interferences for several assays by referencing manufacturer package inserts, including the TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit, Xpert Xpress SARS-CoV-2/Flu/RSV Assay, and Multi-Drug Test Cup (Urine) package inserts. These documents provide specific data on potential interfering substances (e.g., nasal sprays, blood, adulterants). However, the laboratory lacks a centralized, consolidated document or 'plan of action' that explicitly instructs staff on the specific steps to take when these interferences are suspected or identified in a clinical sample. While the Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan and Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan mention verification of consumables and specimen containers, there is no documented procedure detailing the clinical workflow for handling samples flagged for interference to ensure results do not mislead healthcare providers, as required by the CAP note.
corrective_actions: 1) Develop a centralized 'Analytical Interference Action Plan' that outlines specific troubleshooting steps, reflex testing, or reporting comments for each assay when interference is suspected.
2) Ensure the plan is integrated into the existing Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan and accessible to all testing personnel.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.40500**: Turbidity interferes with PathCheck technology by elevating 900 nm measurements more than 1000 nm, causing low pathlength estimates, while highly colored samples like hemoglobins or porphyrins also cause interference [1]. The TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit identifies various nasal sprays, corticosteroids, and medications as potential interferents, noting that Triamcinolone or Oxymetazoline concentrations exceeding 5% (v/v) may cause false results [2]. The Xpert Xpress SARS-CoV-2 Flu RSV Assay notes competitive interference from co-infections and nasopharyngeal substances like blood or nasal secretions [3]. The Multi-Drug Test Cup (Urine) indicates that technical errors, adulterants like bleach or alum, and interfering substances can produce erroneous results [4]. To mitigate these risks, the Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan requires validation of specimen container changes to prevent analytic interference [5], and the Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan mandates that consumables affecting examination quality be verified with control samples [6].

SpectraMax iD3 Multi-Mode Microplate Reader User Guide 82 5054747 H Note: It is important that you put water in the wells and do not read a dry plate for the
Plate Background OD. A dry plate has a slightly higher OD value than a water filled plate
because of differences in refractive indices. Use of a dry plate results in PathCheck
technology normalized values that are lower than 1 cm cuvette values. Interfering Substances
Material that absorbs in the 900 nm to 1000 nm spectral region could interfere with PathCheck
technology measurements. Fortunately, there are few materials that do interfere at the
concentrations generally used. Turbidity is the most common interference. If you can detect turbidity in your sample, you
should not use the PathCheck technology. Turbidity elevates the 900 nm measurement more
than the 1000 nm measurement and causes an erroneously low estimate of pathlength. Use of
the Cuvette Reference does not reliably correct for turbidity. Samples that are highly colored in the upper-visible spectrum might have absorbance that
extends into the near-infrared (NIR) spectrum and can interfere with the PathCheck technology. Examples include Lowry assays, molybdate-based assays, and samples that contain
hemoglobins or porphyrins. In general, if the sample is distinctly red or purple, you should check
for interference before you use the PathCheck technology.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Xpert® Xpress SARS-CoV-2/Flu/RSV Xpert® Xpress SARS-CoV-2/Flu/RSV 41 302-4419, Rev. C January 2021 22.5 Competitive Interference
Competitive interference of the Xpert Xpress SARS-CoV-2/Flu/RSV caused by co-infections were evaluated by testing
individual SARS-CoV-2, Flu A, Flu B or RSV strains at 1X LoD in the presence of different target strains at a higher
concentration in a simulated background matrix. The concentration at LoD was 131 copies/mL for SARS-CoV-2 and ranged
from 0.004 TCID50/mL to 0.43 TCID50/mL for the Flu and RSV strains; the competitive strains were evaluated at 104 titer units
(copies/mL, TCID50/mL, CEID50/mL or PFU/mL). The corresponding concentration of RNA (copies/mL) for the Flu and RSV
strains was determined by ddPCR. Analytical competitive interference was assessed using a strain of SARS-CoV-2 (inactivated USA-WA1/2020), Flu A H3 (H3/
Victoria/361/2011), Flu B (B/Mass/02/2012), RSV A (RSV-A/2/Australia/61), and RSV B (RSV-B/Wash/18537/62).

checks.requirement: The laboratory verifies or establishes its reference intervals.
checks.subject: Reference Intervals
checks.note:
NOTE: Reference intervals are important to allow a clinician to assess patient results against an appropriate population. The reference intervals must be established or verified for each analyte and specimen source (eg, blood, urine, cerebrospinal fluid), when appropriate. For example, a reference interval can be verified by testing samples from 20 healthy representative individuals; if no more than two results fall outside the proposed reference interval, that interval can be considered verified for the population studied. 
  
  If a formal reference interval study is not possible or practical, then the laboratory should carefully evaluate the use of published data for its own reference intervals, and retain records of this evaluation. For many analytes (eg, therapeutic drugs, cholesterol, and CSF total protein), literature references or a manufacturer's package insert information may be appropriate.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Record of reference interval study OR records of verification of manufacturer's stated interval when reference interval study is not practical (eg, unavailable normal population) OR other methods approved by the laboratory/section director
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established robust policies for reference interval verification, as evidenced by G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program, which outlines the 20-sample verification method, and G1002.0V2-Laboratory Test Standard Operating Procedure Guide, which mandates the inclusion of reference intervals in SOPs. Additionally, 0XYZ0001.0Rev3-Quality Manual2025 confirms that biological reference intervals are required documentation for each method. However, while the policy framework is compliant, the laboratory has not provided specific, completed records of reference interval studies or documented evaluations of published data for current assays. The 'Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft' remains in draft status and does not constitute final evidence of a completed verification study. To achieve full compliance, the laboratory must produce the final, director-approved verification or establishment records for all active analytes.
corrective_actions: 1) Finalize and approve the Liaison MDx Verification Guide and all pending validation/verification reports.
2) Compile a central repository of reference interval verification records or literature-based evaluations for all current laboratory assays.
3) Ensure all records are signed/dated by the laboratory director as required by the Quality Manual.
cited_documents: G1002.0V2-Laboratory Test Standard Operating Procedure Guide.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.40605**: The laboratory's Test Validation and Verification Program (G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program) defines the reference interval as the expected range of results in the normal population. This program specifies that validation studies must include enough samples to verify or establish the test's reference interval. For instance, a reference interval can be verified by testing samples from 20 healthy individuals, and if no more than two results fall outside the proposed range, it is considered verified. If a formal study is not feasible, published data should be carefully evaluated and records of this evaluation retained. The Quality Manual (0XYZ0001.0Rev3-Quality Manual2025) states that biological reference intervals are included in the documentation for each examination method as appropriate. The Laboratory Test Standard Operating Procedure Guide (G1002.0V2-Laboratory Test Standard Operating Procedure Guide) also requires that testing SOPs include reference intervals (normal values). The Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft notes that reference ranges are required to be established during assay verification. The validation or verification process and results must be documented and approved by the lab director before a method can be used for patient samples.

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Operation/F-Instruments/Instrument/Liaison MDX/Simplex FluAB&RSV assay verification/Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft.docx
policy_evidence.snippet: For precision studies, positive or negative samples for a given target are often tested by multiple technologists over multiple days during a verification study. In the example verification that follows, we chose to test third-party controls repeatedly over two days by multiple technologists for the precision study. IQCP An Individualized Quality Control Plan (IQCP) is a framework for laboratories to design their own quality control plans.3 By default, positive and negative controls must be run for moderate- and high-complexity tests daily. In many cases, laboratories conduct an IQCP study to reduce the frequency of running positive and negative controls. The frequency at which the laboratory plans to run controls is determined by the laboratory. This example IQCP verification procedure assumes that the laboratory wishes to perform QC every 14 days, which would require the laboratory to run one positive control and one negative control daily for 14 days. Reference and Reportable Range Reference and reportable ranges are also required to be established during the process of assay verification. checks.requirement: The laboratory evaluates the appropriateness of its reference intervals and takes corrective action if necessary.
checks.subject: Reference Interval Evaluation
checks.note:
NOTE: Criteria for evaluation of reference intervals include: 
  
  1. Change of analytic methodology 
  2. Change in patient population 
  
  If it is determined that the range is no longer appropriate for the patient population, corrective action must be taken.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of evaluation and corrective action, if indicated
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. While G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program outlines the initial establishment of reference intervals during assay validation, the laboratory lacks a documented policy or procedure for the ongoing evaluation of reference intervals following changes in analytic methodology or patient population, as required by COM.40615. Furthermore, no records of periodic evaluation or corrective actions were provided. The laboratory must establish a formal process to trigger and document these evaluations to ensure reference intervals remain appropriate for the current patient population.
corrective_actions: 1) Develop and implement a formal policy for the periodic review and evaluation of reference intervals triggered by methodology changes or shifts in patient demographics.
2) Create a standardized template for documenting reference interval evaluations and any subsequent corrective actions taken.
3) Conduct a retrospective review of current reference intervals to ensure they remain appropriate for existing methodologies and patient populations.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.40615**: The laboratory's "Test Validation and Verification Program" (G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program) defines reference intervals as the expected range of results in a normal population. This program requires that validation studies include enough samples to verify or establish the test's reference interval. For instance, testing samples from 20 healthy individuals can verify a reference interval if no more than two results fall outside the proposed range. If a formal reference interval study is not feasible, published data can be used, provided the evaluation records are retained. The "Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft" also states that reference ranges are required to be established during assay verification. For qualitative tests, the "reference range" refers to the possible calls the test can make, such as "positive" or "negative". No specific policy or procedure document detailing the evaluation of reference intervals due to changes in analytic methodology or patient population, or records of such evaluations and corrective actions, were found in the provided sources.

checks.subject: Body Fluid Analysis
checks.note:
NOTE: This requirement applies directly to body fluid testing that the laboratory offers as a routine, orderable test. If the test is routinely performed on the fluid, there must be a written procedure. The requirement COM.40475 for a method validation or verification approval applies. Method performance specifications for blood specimens may be used for body fluids if the laboratory can reasonably exclude the existence of matrix interferences affecting the latter either by reference in the procedure manual to published literature or by evaluation for interferences due to matrix effects by performing an appropriate study (eg, a dilution study using admixtures of samples, spiking samples, further dilution). 
  
  The reference intervals must be defined and reported with the results, unless the concentration of the analyte is reported in comparison to its concentration in a contemporaneously collected blood specimen. If the result is to be interpreted by comparison to the patient's blood, serum, or plasma, such results must be accompanied by an appropriate comment such as,

checks.requirement: For FDA-cleared/approved tests, the laboratory validates clinical claims not included in the manufacturer's instructions.
checks.subject: Clinical Claims Validation - FDA-cleared/approved Tests
checks.note:
NOTE: For laboratories not subject to US regulations, this requirement also applies to tests that are approved by an internationally recognized regulatory authority. 
  
  A clinical claim is a communication from the laboratory to its users (including but not limited to clinicians and patients) regarding a test's sensitivity and specificity, predictive values for a disease or condition, clinical usefulness, cost-effectiveness or clinical utility. 
  
  To adequately support a clinical claim, the laboratory must perform a clinical validation study, unless the clinical validity of the test is documented in peer-reviewed literature or textbooks. The clinical validation study must include at least 20 samples and must include both positive and negative samples. If the laboratory uses fewer samples, the laboratory director or designee meeting CAP director qualifications must record the criteria used to determine the appropriateness of the sample size.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of clinical studies performed by the laboratory OR peer-reviewed literature that reasonably substantiates all claims made by the laboratory about a test
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a policy framework for test validation in 'G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program', which correctly identifies the need to evaluate clinical performance parameters (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values) when FDA-cleared tests are modified or when clinical claims are made. However, the current evidence is limited to policy and a draft verification guide ('Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft.docx'). There is no record of completed clinical validation studies or documented peer-reviewed literature substantiating specific clinical claims made by the laboratory for any FDA-cleared/approved tests. To meet the requirement, the laboratory must provide specific records of clinical validation studies (minimum 20 samples, including positive and negative) or the specific peer-reviewed literature used to support current clinical claims.
corrective_actions: 1) Conduct and document clinical validation studies for all tests where clinical claims are made outside of manufacturer instructions, ensuring a minimum of 20 samples (positive and negative) are included.
2) Compile a reference library of peer-reviewed literature or textbooks that substantiate existing clinical claims for FDA-cleared tests.
3) Ensure the Laboratory Director reviews and signs off on the clinical validation study or the justification for sample sizes if fewer than 20 samples are used.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.40625**: The Test Validation and Verification Program, G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program, outlines the laboratory's approach to establishing and validating assay method performance specifications. For unmodified FDA-cleared/approved tests, the validation scope involves verifying accuracy, precision, and reportable range with objective evidence. If an FDA-cleared or approved test is modified, including changes to patient population, instrument model, software, specimen types, sample preparation, or cutoff values, a validation plan must be implemented to confirm all specifications, similar to a laboratory-developed test (LDT). This includes evaluating clinical performance parameters such as clinical validity (clinical sensitivity, specificity, predictive values) and clinical utility. The laboratory must verify or establish analytical and clinical performance characteristics for each test, and while manufacturer information or published literature can be used, it should be verified whenever practical. The Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft provides an example for verifying FDA-cleared tests, emphasizing that the Laboratory Director is responsible for designing, reviewing, and approving the verification study.

checks.ai_evidence_summary:
**COM.40700**: The laboratory's Test Validation and Verification Program, G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program, outlines plans for establishing and validating/verifying lab assay method performance specifications. This program requires the laboratory to verify or establish analytical and clinical performance characteristics for each test. Analytical performance parameters include accuracy, precision, reportable range, reference interval, analytical sensitivity, limit of detection, analytical specificity, and robustness. Clinical performance parameters include clinical validity and clinical utility, encompassing clinical sensitivity, clinical specificity, positive and negative predictive value, and likelihood ratios.

For unmodified FDA-cleared/approved tests, the validation scope typically verifies accuracy, precision, and reportable range. If an FDA-cleared/approved test is modified, a validation plan is required to confirm all specifications as for a laboratory-developed test. The validation or verification process and results must be documented and approved by the lab director before the method is used for patient samples. The XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa and Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft documents provide examples of verification studies and IQCP development. A literature review, such as the one detailed in "Direct test for Syphilis", can be used to assess performance characteristics.

To address these questions, a literature review of
papers published between January 1964 and June 2017 was con
ducted by searching OVID Medline, OVID Embase, Cumulated
Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), the
Cochrane Library, and Scopus with a combination of agreed
upon “keywords” as listed in Supplementary Table 1. The search
strategy was executed by expert librarians at the CDC and initial
results were screened to remove duplicates. All unique titles and
abstracts (as available) were assessed by the authors for relevance
to the key questions, and the full text for all applicable articles was
retrieved (as available) and reviewed. Inclusion criteria for this re
view included primary literature assessing the performance char
acteristics of direct detection techniques for T. pallidum, including
DFM, DFA, IHC, NAATs, and molecular strain typing studies. Article exclusion criteria for this literature review included the
following: nonhuman studies, surveillance- or epidemiology
focused studies, editorials, photo quizzes, basic research studies,
studies without direct detection or molecular methods, non
English articles, articles without available abstracts, conference
abstracts, procedures, nonprimary literature, studies focused on
non–T. pallidum subsp. pallidum, and case reports. A summary of
the literature review is presented in Figure 1. Data Extraction

checks.requirement: If the laboratory changes its analytical methodology so that test results or their interpretations may be significantly different, the change is explained to clients.
checks.subject: Analytical Methodology Changes
checks.note:
NOTE: This requirement can be accomplished in any of several different ways, depending on local circumstances. Some methods include directed mailings, laboratory newsletters or part of the test report itself. 
  
  Common examples of assays where changes to the method may significantly affect results include tumor markers and high-sensitivity troponin assays.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records such as directed mailings, laboratory newsletters or comment on the patient report advising of the change
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a process for notifying clients of test report corrections (G1006.0V4-Test Report Correction Process.pdf) and requires client approval for changes to analysis plans (SKG006 Patient Specimen Testing Plan -Nb24 protein level in human humors-final-clean (2) (1).pdf). However, the laboratory lacks documented evidence of a formal communication process specifically for notifying clients when analytical methodology changes result in significantly different test results or interpretations, as required by COM.40800. While the Quality Manual (0XYZ0001.0Rev3-Quality Manual2025.pdf) addresses validation of changed processes, it does not explicitly mandate the notification of clients regarding the clinical impact of methodology shifts. No records of newsletters, directed mailings, or report comments regarding methodology changes were provided for review.
corrective_actions: 1) Develop and implement a formal policy for notifying clients of analytical methodology changes that may significantly impact results or interpretations.
2) Create a template or standard operating procedure for documenting client notifications (e.g., newsletters, report comments, or directed mailings) to ensure compliance with COM.40800.
cited_documents: SKG006 Patient Specimen Testing Plan -Nb24 protein level in human humors-final-clean (2) (1).pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.40800**: Modifications to an effective analysis plan require written, signed approval from the project lead, quality assurance manager, institutional head, and client, with the change filed alongside the original plan [1]. While clients may provide initial consent via fax or email, a formal written amendment is mandatory, and significant procedural changes require laboratory director approval prior to implementation [1]. Upon discovering errors, inaccuracies, or necessary updates in patient test results, the laboratory must promptly notify the ordering physician or customer via phone or email [2]. These notifications, including the content, personnel involved, and timestamp, must be documented in the test report problem log [2]. Subsequently, the laboratory must issue an amended report featuring a new report number, clearly identifying the corrected information and providing a detailed explanation of the original error, the notification process, and the timing of the correction [2].

checks.requirement:
For tests taken out of production for a period of time (eg, seasonal testing for influenza), the laboratory meets the following requirements prior to resuming patient testing, as applicable: 
  
  1. PT or alternative assessment performed within 30 days prior to restarting patient testing 
  2. Method performance specifications verified, as applicable, within 30 days prior to restarting patient testing 
  3. Competency assessed for analysts within 12 months prior to restarting patient testing
checks.subject: Intermittent or Seasonal Testing
checks.note:
NOTE: A test is considered to be taken out of production when (1) patient testing is not offered AND (2) PT or alternative assessment, as applicable, is suspended. It does not apply to situations where a proficiency testing challenge is not performed due to a temporary, short-term situation, such as a reagent back order or an instrument breakdown. In those situations, the laboratory must perform alternative assessment for that testing event. 
  
  For tests for which PT is required by CAP, if a PT challenge is not offered during the 30-day period prior to restarting patient testing, the laboratory may perform an alternative assessment of the test. The laboratory must participate in the next scheduled PT event, if the Laboratory Accreditation Program requires external PT for that analyte.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established policies for Alternative Proficiency Assessment (K1002.2V2_APA NAB 2025-A, K1002.2V2_APA PT qPCR 2025-A) and general analytical quality control (G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan). However, the current documentation does not provide specific records demonstrating that these assessments were performed within the 30-day window prior to restarting patient testing for intermittent or seasonal assays. While competency assessment requirements are defined in the Proficiency Testing Program (K1002.0V2) and general competency standards (Accreditation2020Top10Deficiencies.pdf), specific records confirming that analysts met the 12-month competency requirement immediately prior to resuming testing for these specific assays were not verified. The laboratory must bridge the gap between policy and documented execution for the restart process.
corrective_actions: 1) Create a 'Restart Checklist' for intermittent/seasonal tests to document the date of PT/alternative assessment, method verification, and competency review within 30 days of resumption.
2) Audit and attach existing competency records for all analysts to the restart documentation for any assays currently out of production.
3) Ensure the Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan (G1003.0V5) is updated to explicitly reference the 30-day pre-restart verification requirement.
cited_documents: G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.40805**: The Proficiency Testing Program (K1002.0V2-Proficiency Testing Program) mandates that for tests lacking CAP-PT programs, such as the Cell-based Neutralization Antibody Assay and SKG0106 qPCR Vector Shedding assays, the laboratory must perform alternative performance assessments twice annually by testing certified reference samples, previously examined samples, or split samples. These alternative samples must be processed as customer samples following established testing requirements. Per the Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan (G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan), controls must be run before resuming patient testing after changes to critical reagents, major maintenance, or instrument components, with all SOPs clearly defining quality control types, frequencies, acceptance parameters, and corrective actions. Furthermore, competency assessments for personnel performing nonwaived testing must include six elements per test system, conducted semi-annually during the first year and annually thereafter.

checks.requirement: The laboratory maintains a list of laboratory-developed tests (LDTs) and modified FDA-cleared/approved tests implemented by the laboratory.
checks.subject: Test List - Modified FDA-cleared/approved Tests and LDTs
checks.note:
NOTE: For laboratories not subject to US regulations, the list must also include tests approved by an internationally recognized regulatory authority that have been modified by the laboratory. 
  
  A form is available on the CAP website that may be used for maintaining this list and can be downloaded from the CAP website (cap.org) through e-LAB Solutions Suite.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. While the laboratory has a documented 'Test Validation and Verification Program' (G1004.0V3) and evidence of LDT usage in clinical genetic testing (2-wz- cv2025.pdf) and proficiency testing (ID3A2025_PSR.pdf), the laboratory failed to provide the required master list of all LDTs and modified FDA-cleared/approved tests. The existing documentation outlines the validation process but does not satisfy the requirement to maintain a consolidated, current list of these specific test methodologies as mandated by COM.40830.
corrective_actions: 1) Compile a comprehensive list of all currently implemented LDTs and modified FDA-cleared/approved tests.
2) Ensure the list includes all required elements and is maintained in a central location accessible for inspection.
3) Establish a periodic review process to ensure the list remains current as new tests are implemented or existing ones are modified.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.40830**: The laboratory's Test Validation and Verification Program, G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program, outlines plans for establishing and validating/verifying lab assay method performance specifications. If a test is modified from an FDA-cleared or approved test, including changes to patient population, instrument model, software, specimen types, sample preparation method, or cutoff values, a validation plan must be in place to confirm all specifications as for a laboratory-developed test (LDT). This validation includes clinical performance parameters like clinical validity and utility, and analytical performance parameters such as accuracy, precision, and reportable range. The Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft also provides an example for verifying FDA-cleared tests, emphasizing the laboratory's responsibility for designing and approving verification studies. While the laboratory has established a quality management system with CLIA/CAP/ISO15189 standards and developed LDTs for clinical genetic testing, a specific list of laboratory-developed tests (LDTs) and modified FDA-cleared/approved tests implemented by the laboratory was not found in the provided documents. However, proficiency testing results for RSV and Influenza B indicate the use of "Laboratory-developed test" as a manufacturer for some tests.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Test Validation and Verification Program Document Name
Document Number G1004.0 Version 3 Author： Keqin Gregg Date of Composition: 11/02/2020 Date of Execution：05/16/2025 Page 1 of 5 Objective
Provide plans for establishing and validating/verifying lab assay method performance specifications. For some assays
with special requirements by accreditation or regulatory agents or other national or international standards, the specific
requirements should be noted in its specific policy
Programs
1. Testing Method
1.1 The laboratory must verify or establish analytical and clinical performance characteristics for each test. Laboratories
may use information from manufacturers, published literature, or studies performed in other laboratories, but should
verify such outside information, whenever practical. 1.2 For unmodified FDA-cleared/approved test, the scope of validation is to confirm or verify with objective evidence that
the stated analytical and clinical performance characteristics are met in the particular laboratory setting, this usually need
only verify accuracy, precision, and reportable range. Manufacturer recommended method shall be followed if there is
any.

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Operation/F-Instruments/Instrument/Liaison MDX/Simplex FluAB&RSV assay verification/Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft.docx
policy_evidence.snippet: Introduction & Intended Use This example verification guide is intended to serve as an educational resource to assist laboratories in the verification of FDA-cleared tests within their laboratory. Ultimately, the Laboratory and Laboratory Director (or equivalent) are responsible for designing, reviewing, and approving their verification study and determining whether it aligns with federal, state, and local guidelines. Per the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines, the performance of all FDA-cleared, non-modified, moderate- and high-complexity diagnostic tests must be verified for accuracy, precision reference range, and reportable range.1,2 Accuracy Accuracy is typically verified by testing a collection of known clinical/contrived samples and commercially available controls. The number of positive and negative samples needed for each target is determined by the laboratory. When using samples previously categorized by another method, discrepancies can occur due to several factors (e.g., primer design, limit of detection). In the example verification that follows, we chose to incorporate a collection of contrived samples and third-party controls for the accuracy study. Precision Precision studies are intended to verify that expected results are obtained reproducibly from the same sample.
policy_evidence.title: Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft

checks.requirement: For laboratory-developed tests and modified FDA-cleared/approved tests, the laboratory defines written procedures for calibration and quality control based on the studies performed to evaluate the method performance specifications.
checks.subject: Calibration and Quality Control Procedures - Modified FDA-cleared/approved Tests and LDTs
checks.note:
NOTE: The procedures must define the frequency, number, and concentration of calibrators and controls to be used. 
  
  For laboratories not subject to US regulations, this requirement also applies to tests that are not approved by an internationally recognized regulatory authority and to approved tests that have been modified by the laboratory.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established foundational policies for calibration and quality control, specifically G1003.0V5 (Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan) and G1005.0 (Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025). These documents outline general requirements for AMR verification and QC planning. However, the current evidence set lacks specific documentation demonstrating that the frequency, number, and concentration of calibrators and controls for LDTs and modified FDA-cleared tests were explicitly derived from the method performance specification studies. While 'Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft' mentions precision studies, it is a draft document and does not confirm the finalization of calibration/QC protocols based on those specific study results. Records of the actual implementation of these defined procedures for specific LDTs were not verified.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.40840**: The laboratory maintains a documented Quality Control (QC) plan for each examination method, specifying control materials, schedules, and actions for out-of-range controls. All laboratory standard operating procedures (SOPs) must clearly state the type and frequency of quality control samples, acceptable parameters, and corrective actions based on QC data. For non-waived tests, controls for molecular-based quantitative and qualitative tests are performed daily or more frequently if specified by the manufacturer or CAP Checklist, and when changes occur that may impact patient results. Controls must also be run before resuming patient testing after changes to analytically critical reagents, major preventive maintenance, critical instrument components, or software changes. The Analytical Measurement Range (AMR) must be verified at least every six months after a method is initially placed in service. Calibration verification is performed using calibration materials in the same manner as patient samples to confirm instrument stability within the reportable range every six months. If a test system has been recalibrated, calibration verification is not necessary sooner than six months following recalibration. The laboratory also performs AMR verification whenever specific events occur.

policy_evidence.snippet: For precision studies, positive or negative samples for a given target are often tested by multiple technologists over multiple days during a verification study. In the example verification that follows, we chose to test third-party controls repeatedly over two days by multiple technologists for the precision study. IQCP An Individualized Quality Control Plan (IQCP) is a framework for laboratories to design their own quality control plans.3 By default, positive and negative controls must be run for moderate- and high-complexity tests daily. In many cases, laboratories conduct an IQCP study to reduce the frequency of running positive and negative controls. The frequency at which the laboratory plans to run controls is determined by the laboratory. This example IQCP verification procedure assumes that the laboratory wishes to perform QC every 14 days, which would require the laboratory to run one positive control and one negative control daily for 14 days. Reference and Reportable Range Reference and reportable ranges are also required to be established during the process of assay verification. However, for qualitative tests, the reportable range does not apply. “Reference range” simply refers to the possible calls the test can make for each analyte (e.g., for a qualitative test, values of “positive” or “negative,” or an equivalent).

Reports for laboratory-developed tests (LDTs) contain the following: 
  
  * A statement that the assay was developed by the laboratory AND 
  * A brief description of the method and performance characteristics needed for clinical use, unless the information is readily available to the clinician in another format (eg, test catalog, policy to provide upon request).
checks.subject: LDT Reporting
checks.note: NOTE: For laboratories subject to US regulations, the following disclaimer statement must be included on the patient report:
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a policy for LDT reporting within 'G1001.0V3-Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan_2025', which acknowledges the requirement for LDT report content. However, the current evidence set contains only the process control plan (policy). There is no objective evidence (e.g., redacted patient report samples) to verify that the required FDA disclaimer and the statement of laboratory development are actually being applied to issued patient reports. Furthermore, while the policy mentions the availability of performance characteristics, the actual mechanism for providing this to clinicians upon request has not been verified through record review.
corrective_actions: 1) Perform a retrospective audit of at least 5-10 recent LDT patient reports to verify the presence of the required FDA disclaimer and the laboratory development statement.
2) Document the process for providing method descriptions and performance characteristics to clinicians upon request, ensuring this is accessible via the test catalog or a formal policy document.
3) Update the 'Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan' (G1001.0V3) to include a periodic review schedule for report templates to ensure ongoing compliance.

2025 ID3-A
PARTICIPANT SUMMARY Evaluation Criteria
The CAP is required to submit proficiency testing (PT) results to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
(CMS) for all laboratories that have provided a CLIA identification number. If your laboratory is beginning or
discontinuing testing on any CMS-regulated analyte you must check your CMS Analyte Reporting Selections to
ensure if changes are needed. For information on how to manage your CMS reporting selections, go to cap.org
and search CMS Analyte Reporting Selections. If new products are ordered and/or canceled, this may affect your
reporting selections, so it is recommended that you periodically check this report on e-LAB Solutions Suite, which
will always reflect the most up-to-date information. This information can also be obtained by calling the Customer
Contact Center at 800-323-4040, Option 1 or +1-847-832-7000, Option 1 (for customers outside the US). As stated in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), Title 42, Part 493, Subpart I (Proficiency Testing Programs
for Nonwaived Testing), PT providers are required to grade all analytes regulated for PT at 80% participant or
referee consensus, except for Transfusion Medicine. For information on criteria for non-CMS regulated analytes,
review your participant summary.

checks.requirement:
The IQCP for a test/device/instrument includes a risk assessment to evaluate potential sources of error to include all of the following: 
  
  * Pre-analytic, analytic, and post-analytic phases of the testing process 
  * Intended medical uses of the test and impact if inaccurate results are reported (clinical risk) 
  * Components of the tests including reagents, environment, specimen, testing personnel, and test system 
  * Variations in the components based on use of the tests (eg, use in different environments, by different personnel, or multiple identical devices) 
  * Data from the laboratory's own environment, instrument/equipment performance, and testing personnel demonstrating acceptable performance over the maximum time interval between external quality control runs defined in the IQCP 
  * Manufacturer's instructions and recommendations
checks.subject: Risk Assessment
checks.note:
NOTE: The risk assessment must include a process to identify the sources of potential failures and errors for a testing process, and evaluate frequency and impact of those failures and sources of error. 
  
  The laboratory director must consider the laboratory's clinical and legal responsibilities for providing accurate and reliable patient test results. Published data and information may be used to supplement the risk assessment but are not substitutes for the laboratory's own studies and evaluation. The laboratory must involve a representative sample of testing personnel in the process of conducting the risk assessment. It is not necessary for all personnel to be involved. 
  
  The risk assessment for laboratories with multiple identical devices must show that an evaluation was performed if there are differences in testing personnel or environments where testing is performed, with customization of the quality control plan, as needed. 
  
  The QC study to assess the performance and stability of the tests must support the QC frequency and elements defined in the laboratory's quality control plan. At a minimum, the study must include laboratory data representing the maximum interval between runs of external quality control. Consecutive days of data collection are not specifically required if testing is done sporadically, or is not performed seven days a week. Laboratories may use historical data for tests already in place, and may supplement the study with data from published literature. For new tests, devices, and instruments introduced into the laboratory, the laboratory must collect in-house data and may need to define a more frequent QC interval until sufficient data is available to support a longer time interval between runs of external QC. For susceptibility testing guidance, refer to MIC.21910. 
  
  For affiliated laboratories (eg, systems) with integrated procedures, each accredited laboratory must have its own IQCP approved by the laboratory director. There must be records demonstrating that risks specific to the site were evaluated involving a representative sample of local testing personnel to conduct the risk assessment and that laboratory-specific QC data were used in the study to support the defined frequency of quality control. Laboratories may use data from other sites to supplement risk assessments and to support their findings.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory has demonstrated compliance with COM.50300 through the 'XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa.docx' risk assessment, which evaluates pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical phases, including reagents, environment, specimen, personnel, and test systems. The assessment utilizes a risk acceptability matrix to evaluate frequency and severity of harm. Per the search summary, the laboratory incorporated internal data from November 2022 to March 2023, including instrument QC records, corrected reports, and physician complaints, to support the defined QC frequency. The laboratory director has approved the IQCP, and ongoing monitoring is established via SOP #130G.0. Evidence confirms that the risk assessment considers clinical risk and manufacturer recommendations, and the laboratory has a process for updating the assessment based on quality assessment findings as documented in 'IQCP Quality Assessment_202402.docx'.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of monitoring QCP effectiveness through review of QC failures, PT performance, and patient result reporting errors as defined in SOP #130G.0.
Maintain documentation of periodic risk assessment reviews to ensure alignment with any changes in testing personnel, environment, or manufacturer instructions.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.50300**: The IQCP for Simplexa Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II Assay includes a risk assessment that evaluates potential sources of error across pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical phases. This assessment considers components such as reagents, environment, specimen, testing personnel, and the test system. The risk assessment also incorporates data from the laboratory's own environment, including instrument QC records from November 2022 to March 2023, which showed no performance problems. Corrected reports and physician complaints for the same period also indicated no issues related to instrument or assay malfunction, or unsatisfactory test performance. The risk assessment uses a matrix to assign risk levels based on the frequency of error occurrence and the severity of harm to the patient. Any risk factor deemed "Not Acceptable" must be addressed in the IQCP. The final Quality Control Plan (QCP) for the Simplexa system is based on this risk assessment and quality assessment, detailing instructions in SOP #130G.0. Ongoing monitoring for QCP effectiveness, performed by a supervisor or section head, includes examining reasons for QC failures, PT failures, and patient result reporting errors, and updating the risk assessment as needed.

checks.note:
NOTE: The quality control plan may be part of a test procedure or be a separate written plan. As an efficiency, a single plan may address multiple tests performed on one device. A separate, quality control plan approved by the laboratory director must be in place for each laboratory with a separate CAP and CLIA number. 
  
  The approval of the IQCP may not be delegated in laboratories subject to the CLIA regulations.

policy_evidence.snippet: For precision studies, positive or negative samples for a given target are often tested by multiple technologists over multiple days during a verification study. In the example verification that follows, we chose to test third-party controls repeatedly over two days by multiple technologists for the precision study. IQCP An Individualized Quality Control Plan (IQCP) is a framework for laboratories to design their own quality control plans.3 By default, positive and negative controls must be run for moderate- and high-complexity tests daily. In many cases, laboratories conduct an IQCP study to reduce the frequency of running positive and negative controls. The frequency at which the laboratory plans to run controls is determined by the laboratory. This example IQCP verification procedure assumes that the laboratory wishes to perform QC every 14 days, which would require the laboratory to run one positive control and one negative control daily for 14 days. Reference and Reportable Range Reference and reportable ranges are also required to be established during the process of assay verification. However, for qualitative tests, the reportable range does not apply. “Reference range” simply refers to the possible calls the test can make for each analyte (e.g., for a qualitative test, values of “positive” or “negative,” or an equivalent).
policy_evidence.title: Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft

policy_evidence.snippet: If an internal quality control process (e.g., electronic/procedural/built-in) is used instead of external control material to meet daily quality control requirements, the laboratory must have an individualized quality control plan (IQCP) approved by the laboratory director. This laboratory has been using the Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II molecular test system to detect influenza A, influenza B and RSV viruses from 11/10/2022 to 2/28/2023. Although the assay was verified in June 2022, it was not performed for clinical sample testing until 6 months later. The Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II is an integrated molecular analysis system with nucleic acid extraction and analysis all on the same well/space which is carried in an 8 sample disc. Users will just load individual specimen and reagent to the disc and the test will take care of itself. There is a built-in internal control for each sample to check the assay performance. Therefore, the external controls are not required by the  manufacturer. We started the assay by running one external positive (recommended by and separately purchased from the assay manufacturer) and one negative control (confirmed negative swab sample from past) for CLIA/CAP requirement daily when there is a test and for each new shipment of the reagent.

The individualized quality control plan must define all aspects monitored based on the potential errors identified during the risk assessment, including the following parameters as applicable: 
  
  * The number, type (external and internal quality control systems), and frequency of quality control 
  * Criteria for acceptable performance 
  * Monitoring of the testing environment and reagents 
  * Specimen quality 
  * Instrument calibration, maintenance, and function checks 
  * Training and competency of testing personnel 
  * Provisions for multiple identical devices and variation for uses covered under one IQCP
checks.subject: Quality Control Plan Elements
checks.note:
NOTE: The components of the quality control plan must meet regulatory and CAP accreditation requirements and be in compliance with the manufacturer instructions, at minimum. The quality control plan must control the quality of the test process and ensure accurate and reliable test results. 
  
  External control material samples must be analyzed with new lots and shipments of reagents or more frequently if indicated in the manufacturer's instructions.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory has established an IQCP for the LIAISON® MDX and Simplexa™ Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II Assay, as documented in 'XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa.docx'. The plan addresses the required parameters, including frequency of QC, criteria for acceptable performance, and reagent monitoring. Per the search summary, the IQCP includes a risk assessment covering specimen handling and cross-contamination, and mandates external control analysis with each new reagent lot or shipment. The laboratory's policy aligns with the requirement for concurrent testing of positive and negative controls upon implementation of new lots. Ongoing quality assessment processes are in place to monitor plan effectiveness and investigate QC failures.

checks.requirement:
Ongoing quality assessment monitoring is performed by the laboratory to ensure that the quality control plan is effective in mitigating the identified risks for the IQCP and includes records of the following: 
  
  * Review of quality control and instrument/equipment maintenance and function check data at least monthly 
  * Evaluation of errors relating to preanalytic, analytic and post analytic phases of the testing process 
  * Review of complaints from clinicians and other healthcare providers regarding the quality of testing to confirm the clinical efficacy of testing 
  * Evaluation of corrective actions taken when problems are identified 
  * Re-evaluation of the quality control plan if changes to the reagents, environment, specimen, testing personnel, or test system elements of the risk assessment occur 
  * Reapproval of the quality control plan by the laboratory director or designee at least biennially.
checks.subject: Ongoing Quality Assessment Monitoring
checks.note:
NOTE: If ongoing assessments identify failures in one or more components of the quality control plan, the laboratory must investigate the cause and consider if modifications are needed to the quality control plan to mitigate potential risk. Common examples of failures include unacceptable proficiency testing results, recurrent out-of-range reagent storage or room temperatures, unacceptable quality control results, use of unvalidated specimen types, and the IQCP not being followed as written. 
  
  An example form is available on cap.org through e-LAB Solutions Suite under Accreditation Resources, IQCP Toolbox that may be used for recording ongoing assessments of the IQCP.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory demonstrates ongoing quality assessment monitoring for its IQCP as required. Evidence includes 'IQCP Quality Assessment_202402.docx' and 'IQCP Quality Assessment_202503.docx', which document the periodic review of the IQCP and confirm the Laboratory Director's oversight (Wenli Zhou, 03/20/2025). The '0XYZ0001.0Rev3-Quality Manual2025' establishes the framework for monitoring pre-analytic, analytic, and post-analytic phases, as well as the process for addressing clinician complaints and corrective actions. The laboratory maintains a structured approach to re-evaluating the QCP when changes occur, as supported by the Quality Planning Process document 'A1002.0V2-Quality Planning Process.pdf'. The documentation provided satisfies the requirement for monthly reviews and biennial reapproval.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of performing and documenting monthly IQCP quality assessments.
Ensure biennial reapproval of the IQCP is maintained in accordance with the schedule established in IQCP Quality Assessment_202503.docx.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **COM.50600**: The laboratory performs ongoing quality assessment monitoring to ensure the effectiveness of its quality control plan (QCP) in mitigating identified risks. This monitoring includes a monthly review of quality control, temperature, and maintenance logs to identify problems. The Quality Manual 0XYZ0001.0Rev3-Quality Manual2025 outlines internal assessments such as quality indicators to monitor performance across pre-examination, examination, post-examination, and quality processes, with action taken for unacceptable performance or trends. The laboratory also evaluates errors related to pre-analytic, analytic, and post-analytic phases of testing. checks.requirement: The laboratory director satisfies the personnel requirements of the College of American Pathologists.
checks.subject: Laboratory Director Qualifications
checks.note:
NOTE: The qualifications required by the CAP for the position of laboratory director depend on the testing performed in the laboratory. The qualifications are also dependent upon whether the laboratory is subject to US regulations. 
  
  The following table contains the laboratory director qualifications based on complexity of testing and US regulatory status: 
  
  Laboratories Subject to US Regulation 
  
  Complexity of Testing 
  
  Qualifications 
  
  1. High complexity testing 
  
  a. MD, DO, or DPM licensed to practice in the jurisdiction where the laboratory is located (if required), and: 
  
  i. Certification in anatomic or clinical pathology, or both, by the American Board of Pathology or American Osteopathic Board of Pathology, or 
  ii. Have at least two years of experience supervising high complexity testing 
  
  OR 
  
  b. Doctoral degree (PhD or DPH) in a chemical, biological, or clinical laboratory science from an accredited institution, and: 
  
  i. Have current certification by a board approved by HHS*, and 
  ii. Have at least two years of laboratory training or experience or both, and laboratory experience directing or supervising high complexity testing 
  
  2. Moderate complexity testing 
  
  a. Qualified as in (1) above 
  
  OR 
  
  b. MD, DO, or DPM, licensed to practice in the jurisdiction where the laboratory is located (if required), and: 
  
  i. At least one year of experience supervising nonwaived laboratory testing, or 
  ii. Have at least 20 CE credit hours in laboratory practice that cover director responsibilities as defined in the DRA checklist 
  
  OR 
  
  c. Doctoral degree (PhD or DPH) in a chemical, biological, or clinical laboratory science from an accredited institution, and: 
  
  i. Have current certification by a board approved by HHS*, and 
  ii. Have at least one year of experience directing or supervising nonwaived testing 
  
  3. Provider-performed microscopy (PPM) 
  
  a. MD, DO, or DPM, licensed to practice in the jurisdiction in which the laboratory is located (if required) 
  
  4. Waived tests 
  
  a. MD, DO, or DPM, licensed to practice in the jurisdiction in which the laboratory is located (if required) OR 
  
  b. Doctoral degree (PhD or DPH) in a chemical, biological, or clinical laboratory science from an accredited institution 
  
  Laboratories not subject to US regulations 
  
  All Complexity Levels 
  
  a. MD or DO licensed to practice in the jurisdiction where the laboratory is located (if required) and have one of the following: 
  
  i. Certification in anatomic or clinical pathology; or 
  ii. At least one year of laboratory training during medical residency/fellowship; or 
  iii. At least two years of experience supervising high complexity testing 
  
  OR 
  
  b. Doctoral degree (PhD, DPH, or equivalent) in a chemical, biological, or clinical laboratory science and have both of the following: 
  
  i. At least two years of clinical laboratory training or experience and 
  ii. Two years of laboratory experience directing or supervising high complexity testing 
  
  *A list of boards approved by CMS for doctoral scientists may be found at https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Legislation/CLIA/Certification_Boards_Laboratory_Directors.html 
  
  Detailed information on qualifications for laboratory directors subject to US regulations may be found in the CAP Personnel Guidance Document located in e-LAB Solutions Suite on cap.org (log-in required) under Accreditation Resources - Accreditation Checklists. 
  
  Training and experience must relate to testing of human specimens for the purpose of diagnosing, treating, and monitoring an individual's condition. 
  
  For laboratories subject to US regulations, credentials for all personnel trained outside of the US must be reviewed to ensure that their training and qualifications are equivalent to CLIA requirements, with records of the review available on site. The equivalency evaluations should be performed by a nationally recognized organization. The following types of records may also be used to show equivalency: 1) license to practice medicine issued by the state in which the laboratory is located; or 2) laboratory personnel license in states where laboratory personnel licensure is required and qualifications are at least as stringent as CLIA. Department of Defense laboratories must evaluate equivalency using a process approved by the Center for Laboratory Medicine Services. 
  
  A single individual may direct no more than five laboratories (not including laboratories that perform only waived testing) and may not direct more laboratories than permitted by national, federal, state (or provincial), or local law. 
  
  If more stringent state or local regulations are in place for laboratory director qualifications, including requirements for licensure, they must be followed. 
  
  Additional qualifications for laboratory directors are included for the following types of testing or services: 
  
  * For the subspecialty of dermatopathology, the director may qualify as defined in the CLIA regulation 42CFR493.1449(f). 
  * For the subspecialty of oral pathology, the director must be certified by the American Board of Oral Pathology, American Board of Pathology, or the American Osteopathic Board of Pathology. 
  * Qualifications for histocompatibility section directors/technical supervisors, including continuing clinical laboratory education requirements, can be found in the Histocompatibility Checklist. 
  * For laboratories participating in the Reproductive Laboratory Accreditation Program, directors of laboratories performing andrology testing must meet the requirements described above for high complexity testing and have at least two years of experience in a laboratory performing andrology procedures. This experience must include quality management, quality control, inspection, accreditation, and licensing procedures, as well as andrology procedures. Requirements for embryology laboratory directors are found in the Reproductive Laboratory Medicine Checklist in RLM.10166. 
  * For laboratories participating in the Forensic Drug Testing Accreditation Program, specific requirements for laboratory director/scientific director are in the Forensic Drug Testing Checklist.

The CAP Lab-personnel-Evaluation roster-XYZ2025 identifies Wenli Zhou as the Laboratory Director. While the policy documents outline the required credentials (PhD, HHS-approved certification, and experience), the actual personnel file containing the primary source evidence—such as the specific board certification certificate, transcripts, and documented proof of two years of experience directing/supervising high complexity testing—was not provided for review. The current documentation confirms the policy framework but lacks the specific verification records required by the Evidence of Compliance criteria to confirm the director meets the regulatory standards for high complexity testing.

2) Ensure the personnel file includes a formal equivalency evaluation if the doctoral degree was obtained outside of the US, as required by the checklist note.

These documents state that the director must possess either an MD, DO, or DPM license with certification in anatomic or clinical pathology, or two years of experience supervising high complexity testing. Alternatively, a doctoral degree (PhD or DPH) in a relevant science from an accredited institution, current HHS-approved certification, and at least two years of laboratory training or experience in directing or supervising high complexity testing are acceptable. The 7-D1001.1V2-Lab Director Job Description and Responsibility also specifies an additional requirement of at least 20 CE credit hours in laboratory practice for doctoral degree holders, unless continuously employed in their current role since December 28, 2024. The CAP Lab-personnel-Evaluation roster-XYZ2025 identifies Wenli Zhou as the Laboratory Director, holding a PhD. This roster also indicates that Wenli Zhou fulfills other roles including Clinical Consultant, Technical Consultant, Technical Supervisor, and Testing Personnel.

checks.requirement: Anatomic pathology services are provided by a pathologist certified in anatomic pathology. Exceptions for other qualified individuals for specific subspecialties are described in the NOTE.
checks.subject: Provision of Anatomic Pathology (AP) Services
checks.note:
NOTE: In facilities where anatomic pathology services are provided, a pathologist certified in anatomic pathology must perform such services. Pathologists who qualified to provide these services prior to December 28, 2024, may continue to provide these services if they have done so continuously in a CLIA-certified laboratory. The CMS considers those individuals who have completed their training and are waiting to obtain their board certification to qualify under the regulation for the position of technical supervisors of histopathology, dermatopathology, ophthalmic pathology, oral pathology, and cytopathology. The services of a consulting anatomic pathologist shall be retained if necessary. 
  
  The following are exceptions for specific types of tissue diagnosis for non-pathologist individuals: 
  
  * Neuromuscular pathology specimens may be interpreted by an MD or DO who is licensed to practice in the jurisdiction where the laboratory is located (if required) and has completed a training program in neuromuscular pathology approved by HHS (ie, the American Academy of Neurology Committee for Neuromuscular Pathology Training Program and the United Council for Neurologic Specialties). 
  * Other exceptions for dermatopathology, ophthalmic pathology and oral pathology as defined in the CLIA regulation 42CFR493.1449(f) and (g). 
  
  For laboratories not subject to US regulations, individuals must meet national, state or provincial, or local laws and regulations, and education must be equivalent to US qualifications.

checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory has established clear authority and responsibility for the Laboratory Director as evidenced by D1001.1V3-Lab Director Job Description and Responsibility. This document explicitly outlines the director's oversight of laboratory operations, personnel, and quality systems, meeting the requirements of DRA.10430. Furthermore, K1001.0-External Accreditation Management Process confirms the director's active role in the CAP accreditation process, including self-inspections and corrective action monitoring.
