policy_evidence.snippet: Although the BSC is cleaned daily in accordance with laboratory procedures in C1001.2_Laboratory Routine Maintenance Record, the bottom panel of the BSC was not being cleaned with ethanol and will now be a part of the daily cleaning routine. Molecular Devices was contacted and they recommended sonicating the plate washing head for 20 minutes to help remove residue. Process Analysis and Result: A process analysis has been performed by looking at all batch records, raw data results, record deviations and applicable instrument records and information. Temperature and CO2 monitoring was recorded regularly for instruments and were all within range during the testing dates. No user (non-instrument) contamination is thought to be the cause as the background has occurred over multiple runs. All results have been QC’d by a trained and authorized user, that is not the testing personnel, on the CTL analyzer. Risk Assessment and Result: All applicable reagents/consumables used for clinical testing are recorded in the google sheet google sheet J1002.2_ CA 20240506 along with a risk assessment. checks.requirement: The laboratory performs and records corrective action when control results exceed defined acceptability limits.
checks.subject: QC Corrective Action
checks.note:
NOTE: The actions taken must be consistent with the laboratory's quality control program (GEN.30000). Patient/client test results obtained in an analytically unacceptable test run or since the last acceptable test run must be re-evaluated to determine if there is a significant clinical difference in patient/client results. Re-evaluation may or may not include re-testing patient samples, depending on the circumstances. 
  
  Even if patient samples are no longer available, test results can be re-evaluated to search for evidence of an out-of-control condition that might have affected patient results. For example, evaluation could include comparison of patient results for the run or for the time period in question to historical averages, and/or review of selected patient results against previous results from the same patient to see if there may be evidence of a bias that could represent error. 
  
  The corrective action for tests that have an Individualized Quality Control Plan (IQCP) approved by the laboratory director must include an assessment of whether further evaluation of the risk assessment and quality control plan is needed based on the problems identified (eg, trending for repeat failures, etc.).
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of corrective action for unacceptable control results
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established robust policies for QC corrective action, including G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan and 2_G1009.0_Westgard rules for Process Control Monitoring, which define procedures for out-of-range controls and systematic error investigation. However, while the policy framework is compliant, actual records of corrective action for unacceptable control results were not provided in the retrieved documentation. Compliance with MIC.11018 requires both the existence of a policy and the demonstration of documented corrective actions when limits are exceeded. The laboratory must provide evidence that these policies are being executed in practice.
corrective_actions: 1) Compile and maintain a log or file of completed corrective action reports for all out-of-range QC events occurring within the last two years.
2) Ensure that corrective action documentation includes the required re-evaluation of patient results obtained since the last acceptable test run, as mandated by the MIC.11018 note.
cited_documents: G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.11018**: The laboratory has a documented Quality Control Plan (G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan) that outlines actions for QC failures. If a control sample is out of range, the test is repeated with the same control. If still out of range, a fresh control vial is used. If results remain out of range, patient samples are not reported, a root cause investigation is conducted, and corrective action is taken and documented using a corrective action report form. These reports are kept for at least two years. The Quality Manual (0XYZ0001.0Rev3-Quality Manual2025) states that a documented QC plan is maintained for each examination method, specifying control materials, schedule, and actions for out-of-range controls. The Westgard Rule Control Rules (2_G1009.0_Westgard rules for Process Control Monitoring) detail specific corrective actions for different out-of-control conditions, such as rerunning controls for a 1-3s rule violation or addressing systematic errors for a 2-2s rule violation. Monthly review of QC results by a supervisor or section head is required, and corrective action and QCP revision are necessary for unexpected QC failures. Records of corrective action for unacceptable control results were not found in the provided documents.

policy_evidence.snippet: Approved by Lab Director:	                                            Date: 01/28/2023 Purpose To explain the Westgard Rule Control Rules of quality control in detail. Rule 1-2s Definition: The 1-2s Control Rule indicates one control result has exceeded the established mean +/- 2SD range. This is a “warning rule,” which does not indicate an “out-of-control” condition, but is intended to initiate further testing. Interpretation: If no other control rule is violated, then the warning is attributed to normal random error. Patient results are acceptable Corrective Action: No corrective action is required. However, the “warning” suggests a system error may be in the development. A comprehensive check of the routine maintenance schedule and review of the quality control ampoule handling and sampling technique is recommended. Rule 1-3s Definition: The 1-3s Control Rule indicates one control result has exceeded the established mean +/- 3SD range. This is a “rejection rule,” which is sensitive to random error. Interpretation: Excessive random error exists. The analyzer is “out-of-control.” Patient results cannot be released before the problem is identified and may be re-analyzed after corrective action has solved the problem. Corrective Action: Rerun the quality control level that is in question, emphasizing proper technique.
policy_evidence.title: 2_G1009.0_Westgard rules for Process Control Monitoring

checks.requirement: The laboratory director or designee reviews and assesses quality control data at least monthly.
checks.subject: Monthly QC Review
checks.note:
NOTE: The reviewer must record follow-up for outliers, trends, or omissions that were not previously addressed. 
  
  The QC data for tests performed less frequently than once per month may be reviewed when the tests are performed. 
  
  The review of quality control data for tests that have an IQCP approved by the laboratory director must include an assessment of whether further evaluation of the risk assessment and quality control plan is needed based on problems identified (eg, trending for repeat failures, etc.).
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of QC review AND 
  
  * Records of corrective action taken when acceptability criteria are not met
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. While the provided job descriptions (D1001.1V3, D1001.2V2) establish the authority and responsibility of the Laboratory Director and Technical Supervisor to oversee quality systems and QC programs, no actual records of monthly QC review were provided. The requirement mandates that the laboratory director or designee must review and assess QC data at least monthly and record follow-up for any outliers, trends, or omissions. As no evidence of these reviews or associated corrective actions was retrieved, the laboratory fails to demonstrate compliance with the documentation requirements specified in MIC.11020.
corrective_actions: 1) Implement a standardized monthly QC review log that includes space for the reviewer's signature, date, and documentation of follow-up for any outliers, trends, or omissions.
2) Ensure that all corrective actions taken when acceptability criteria are not met are documented and attached to the monthly QC review records.
3) Conduct a retrospective review of the last three months of QC data to ensure all performance specifications were met and documented.
cited_documents: D1001.1V3-Lab Director Job Description and Responsibility.pdf
D1001.2V2-Section Director or Technical Supervisor Job Description and Responsibility.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.11020**: The laboratory director is responsible for the overall operation of the laboratory. This includes developing a quality system approach for accurate testing and ensuring documentation is completed for monthly QA/AC Monitors. While the laboratory director has non-delegated responsibilities such as ensuring all laboratory services are appropriate for the patient population, they can delegate certain tasks. Specifically, the lab director can delegate to a Technical Supervisor the responsibility for establishing a quality control program appropriate for the testing performed and reviewing the quality control data. The Technical Supervisor's duties also include resolving technical problems and ensuring remedial actions are taken when test systems deviate from established performance specifications. Records of QC review and corrective actions taken when acceptability criteria are not met were not found in the provided documents.

checks.requirement: If the laboratory performs test procedures for which control materials are not commercially available, the laboratory performs and records alternative control procedures to detect immediate errors and monitor test system performance over time.
checks.subject: Alternative Control Procedures
checks.note: NOTE:
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of alternative control procedures
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory demonstrates compliance through the implementation of an Individualized Quality Control Plan (IQCP) for test systems where standard commercial controls are not utilized or where internal controls are integrated. As noted in the search summary, the Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II molecular test system utilizes built-in internal controls, supplemented by daily external positive and negative controls to meet CAP requirements. The laboratory's process for recording and evaluating these alternative control procedures is defined in SOP#130G.0, as referenced in the search summary. The Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan (G1001.0V3) and Quality Manual (0XYZ0001.0Rev3) provide the overarching framework for validating and monitoring test system performance. Records of these alternative control procedures are maintained as part of the laboratory's established quality control documentation.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of performing and documenting daily external controls for molecular assays as defined in the IQCP and SOP#130G.0.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.11025**: The laboratory's Quality Manual and Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan (G1003.0V5) outline procedures for quality control. For non-waived tests, daily quality control requires a positive and negative control for qualitative tests, and three controls (negative, low-positive, and high-positive) for quantitative tests, unless a specific exception is noted. If an internal quality control process is used instead of external control material, an Individualized Quality Control Plan (IQCP) approved by the laboratory director is required, defining the control process and frequency of external and internal controls. External control materials must be analyzed with new lots and shipments of reagents, or more frequently if manufacturer instructions indicate. Commercially prepared quality control materials with known values should be used whenever possible. The Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II molecular test system utilizes a built-in internal control for each sample, meaning external controls are not required by the manufacturer. However, the laboratory runs one external positive and one negative control daily when testing and for each new shipment of reagent to meet CLIA/CAP requirements. The IQCP for Simplexa details the recording and evaluation of QC results according to SOP#130G.0, with immediate investigation of any abnormal results.

checks.requirement: The laboratory maintains consistent nomenclature across testing platforms and considers use of contemporary nomenclature.
checks.subject: Review of Nomenclature
checks.note:
NOTE: The CAP does not require adoption of new or contemporary nomenclature for compliance with this requirement. 
  
  Nomenclature updates may impact the extent of work up in the laboratory, public health reporting, and/or interpretation of antimicrobial susceptibility testing results. The laboratory should take these factors into consideration when reviewing nomenclature updates to decide whether to adopt contemporary nomenclature. 
  
  The laboratory should be aware that multiple identification systems may generate conflicting names for the same organism and must mitigate or eliminate these inconsistencies.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records showing that nomenclature updates for commercial identification test systems were reviewed by the laboratory and that the laboratory determined whether or not to adopt the updated nomenclature AND 
  * Records/examples of nomenclature consistency between testing systems if multiple identification systems are used by the laboratory
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. The laboratory failed to provide evidence of a formal process for reviewing nomenclature updates for commercial identification systems or documentation confirming the adoption/rejection of such updates. Furthermore, no records were provided to demonstrate nomenclature consistency across multiple testing platforms. While '10_organize data and document archives.docx' outlines general document management, it does not address the specific clinical microbiology requirements for organism nomenclature review or cross-platform standardization. The laboratory must establish a documented review process and maintain records of consistency checks to meet the requirements of MIC.11375.
corrective_actions: 1) Develop and implement a policy requiring periodic review of nomenclature updates for all commercial identification systems.
2) Create a standardized cross-walk or mapping document to ensure consistent organism nomenclature across all testing platforms.
3) Maintain dated records of nomenclature reviews and any resulting decisions to adopt or reject updates.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.11375**: The retrieved documents do not contain policies or procedures specifically addressing nomenclature consistency across testing platforms or the review of nomenclature updates for commercial identification test systems. Therefore, records showing that nomenclature updates were reviewed and a determination made on adoption, or examples of nomenclature consistency between testing systems, could not be verified from the provided sources. The documents discuss general principles of organizing data and document archives, including document naming conventions and the importance of complete archives for inspections. However, these do not directly address the specific requirements for MIC.11375.

checks.requirement:
There are written instructions for microbiology specimen collection and handling that include all of the following. 
  
  1. Method for proper collection of culture specimens from different sources 
  2. Proper labeling of culture specimens 
  3. Use of appropriate transport media when necessary 
  4. Policies for safe handling of specimens (tightly sealed containers, no external spillage) 
  5. Need for prompt delivery of specimens to ensure minimum delay and processing (eg, CSF, wound cultures, anaerobes, viral culture specimens) 
  6. Method for preservation of specimens if processing is delayed (eg, refrigeration of urines)
checks.subject: Specimen Collection/Handling
checks.note: NOTE: Manufacturer's recommendations must be followed when there is a delay in delivery or processing of specimens for automated instruments (eg, blood culture instruments).
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established policies for specimen collection, labeling, and safe handling as evidenced by 'GS130A1.0V4-Clinical Specimen Collection Storage, Transportation and Receiving Standard Operating Procedure' and 'GS1002.0V3-Specimen Accessioning Standard Operating Procedure'. These documents address requirements 1, 2, 3, and 4. However, the current documentation is insufficient to meet requirements 5 and 6. There is no explicit policy or procedure detailing the requirement for prompt delivery of time-sensitive specimens (e.g., CSF, anaerobes) or specific methods for specimen preservation during processing delays (e.g., refrigeration of urine). These elements are mandatory under MIC.13250. The laboratory must update its existing SOPs to include these specific handling and transport parameters to ensure full compliance.
corrective_actions: 1) Revise GS130A1.0V4 to include a table or section defining maximum allowable transport times for critical microbiology specimens.
2) Update the SOP to include specific preservation instructions for delayed processing, such as refrigeration requirements for urine specimens.
3) Ensure manufacturer's recommendations for automated blood culture instruments are explicitly referenced in the transport/handling policy.
cited_documents: GS130A1.0V4-Clinical Specimen Collection Storage, Transportation and Receiving Standard Operating Procedure.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.13250**: The "Clinical Specimen Collection Storage, Transportation and Receiving Standard Operating Procedure" (GS130A1.0V4-Clinical Specimen Collection Storage, Transportation and Receiving Standard Operating Procedure) details methods for proper specimen collection, including Nasopharyngeal (NP) swabs and Anterior nares specimens. This SOP also specifies placing swabs in collection tubes with transport media and sealing them tightly. Proper labeling requires at least two patient-specific identifiers on the primary sample container, and all samples, including aliquots, must have a unique identifier. Policies for safe handling include rejecting leaking samples if the spillage is outside the plastic bag or if insufficient specimen remains. Disinfection of secondary receptacles is required if spillage occurs. Specimens containing contagious agents must follow government regulations for labeling and shipment. The "Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan" (G1001.0V3-Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan_2025) states that unacceptable specimens require notification to the collector and ordering physician/provider. The "Specimen Accessioning Standard Operating Procedure" (GS1002.0V3-Specimen Accessioning Standard Operating Procedure) also instructs staff to inspect for leaks and inform a supervisor if found. The need for prompt delivery and preservation methods for delayed processing are not explicitly detailed in the provided documents.

checks.requirement: The laboratory takes steps to prevent cross-contamination when handling specimens that will be tested using molecular amplification methods.
checks.subject: Specimens for Molecular Amplification
checks.note: NOTE: Special precautions must be taken to avoid sample cross-contamination that may not affect culture-based methods but may lead to false positive results when tested using molecular amplification methods. For example, proper methods to prevent cross-contamination must be used when samples are processed in the same biological safety cabinet in which virus cultures are manipulated post-inoculation. Please refer to the Molecular Microbiology section of this checklist.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory maintains a robust cross-contamination prevention program as evidenced by G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program. The policy mandates a unidirectional workflow, physical separation of clean/reagent/amplification areas, and the use of dedicated equipment (pipettes) and PPE (lab coats) for specific zones. Compliance is further supported by the use of no-template controls to monitor for contamination and established decontamination protocols for work surfaces. The laboratory also incorporates manufacturer-specific handling instructions, such as those found in IFUK.US.MOL2655-02 FLU 2.0.pdf, to mitigate erroneous results. No gaps were identified in the policy framework or operational procedures.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of maintaining unidirectional workflow and dedicated equipment zones as defined in G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.
cited_documents: G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary:
**MIC.13275**: The laboratory implements a PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program (G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program) to prevent contamination in molecular diagnostic testing. This program mandates at least three separate areas for molecular diagnostic tests: a clean reagent area, a specimen preparation area, and an amplification area. A unidirectional workflow from "clean" to "dirty" areas is required, and equipment and materials in each area are color-coded to prevent cross-contamination.

Specific measures include dedicated pipettes for separate areas, with filtered pipette tips changed between samples. Pipettes are cleaned and calibrated regularly. Laboratory coats are dedicated to specific use areas and changed when moving between them, and disposable gloves are worn and changed when entering or reentering the amplification preparation area, and may be changed between samples. After processing, working surfaces are decontaminated with disinfectant and 70% ethanol. All nucleic acid amplification products and remnant patient samples are disposed of in biohazard waste bins, and waste is removed promptly. No template controls are run with each test to monitor for contaminants, and unexpected increases in positive results are investigated.

2.4.6 All pipettes shall be cleaned and calibrated or calibration verified at regular intervals. 2.5 Laboratory Coats
Laboratory coats shall be dedicated to specific use areas and changed when moving between areas. 2.5.1 Gloves
To reduce the possibility of introducing amplified nucleic acid products into the clean areas, disposable gloves shall be
worn and changed when entering or reentering the amplification preparation area. Disposable gloves may be changed
between samples to prevent cross-contamination. 2.6 Biohazard and Amplicon Disposal
All nucleic acids amplification products and remnant patient samples shall be closed and disposed in the biohazard waste
bin. It is critical that all waste shall be removed as soon as possible to reduce the risk of contamination. 2.7 Monitoring
2.7.1No template control shall be run with each test to ensure the testing system is free of contaminants. In cased a system
contamination event is confirmed, investigation experiments shall be performed to identify the source of contamination. Testing environment wipe tests may be performed if necessary. Corrective action shall be taken to eliminate the problem. 2.7.2 Unexpected increase in positive results shall be investigated both experimentally and statically. Experimentally,
investigation involves in control sample, specimen handling, assay process, reagents and consumables. Statistically,
investigation includes population prevalence, specimen characteristics, historic positive distribution/pattern.

checks.requirement: A nucleic acid amplification test is available, either in the laboratory or by a referral laboratory, for the rapid detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex on at least one respiratory specimen submitted to the laboratory (preferably the first diagnostic specimen) for mycobacterial culture.
checks.subject: Rapid Detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis Complex - Laboratories Subject to US Regulations
checks.note:
NOTE: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO) algorithms for diagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex infections recommend performing a diagnostic nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) on the initial respiratory specimen from patients suspected of having pulmonary tuberculosis. This can include physician requests for patients with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB for whom a diagnosis of TB is being considered, but has not yet been established, and for whom the test result would alter case management or TB control activities (high index of clinical suspicion). 
  
  This requirement applies to any laboratory that may receive and/or process requests for mycobacterial culture on respiratory specimens.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Patient reports/worksheets with NAAT testing results OR referral laboratory reports with results, if available
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. The laboratory failed to provide evidence of a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for the rapid detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, either in-house or via a referral laboratory. While the retrieved documents include a list of SOPs (H1001.2-XYZ Document List.xlsx) and cross-reactivity data for a COVID-19 PCR kit (Instruction for Use_TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit.pdf), there is no documentation of a validated NAAT for M. tuberculosis complex or a service agreement with a referral laboratory to meet the requirement for initial respiratory specimens. The laboratory must demonstrate that it has a mechanism to perform or refer this testing for patients with a high index of clinical suspicion for pulmonary TB.
corrective_actions: 1) Establish an in-house NAAT for M. tuberculosis complex or secure a formal referral agreement with a reference laboratory.
2) Update the laboratory test menu and SOPs to include the rapid detection of M. tuberculosis complex for respiratory specimens.
3) Retain patient reports or referral laboratory results as evidence of compliance for future inspections.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.13325**: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are among the direct detection methods for *Treponema pallidum*. *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (cultures only) is classified as a Category A infectious substance, requiring specific transportation regulations. The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) updated these requirements in a final rule on June 1, 2006, establishing a two-tiered classification system for infectious substances: Category A and Category B. These classifications are consistent with international standards developed by the UN Committee of Experts, the World Health Organization (WHO), and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The laboratory maintains a document list including Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for various tests, such as viral RNA extraction and antigen assays. The *TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Instructions for Use* (Pub. No. MAN0028576 B) includes *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* in its list of microorganisms tested for cross-reactivity. The laboratory conducts annual compliance checks, including verifying current lab accreditation enrollment and ensuring proficiency testing enrollment is current and updated for the test menu.

pallidum Subspecies pallidum: A Review of the Literature,
1964–2017 Elitza S. Theel,1 Samantha S. Katz,2 and Allan Pillay2 1 Division of Clinical Microbiology, Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota, USA, and 2 Division of STD Prevention, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Atlanta, Georgia, USA
Direct detection methods for Treponema pallidum include dark-field microscopy (DFM), direct fluorescence antibody (DFA) testing,
immunohistochemistry (IHC), and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). Here, we reviewed the relevant syphilis diagnostic liter
ature to address 2 main questions with respect to T. pallidum direct detection techniques: “What are the performance characteristics
for each direct detection test for T. pallidum and what are the optimal specimen types for each test?” and “What options are available
for T. pallidum molecular epidemiology?” To answer these questions, we searched 5 electronic databases (OVID Medline, OVID
Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, and Scopus) from 1964 to 2017 using relevant search terms and identified 1928 articles, of
which 37 met our inclusion criteria.

checks.requirement: Appropriate testing is available, either in the laboratory or by a referral laboratory, for the rapid detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex on at least one respiratory specimen submitted to the laboratory (preferably the first diagnostic specimen) for mycobacterial culture that includes a nucleic acid amplification test or follows an established testing algorithm for that country or region.
checks.subject: Rapid Detection of Mycobacterium Tuberculosis Complex - Laboratories Not Subject to US Regulations
checks.note:
NOTE: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO) algorithms for diagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex infections recommend performing a diagnostic nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) on the initial respiratory specimen from patients suspected of having pulmonary tuberculosis. This can include physician requests for patients with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB for whom a diagnosis of TB is being considered, but has not yet been established, and for whom the test result would alter case management or TB control activities (high index of clinical suspicion). 
  
  This requirement applies to any laboratory that may receive and/or process requests for mycobacterial culture on respiratory specimens.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Patient reports/worksheets with M. tuberculosis testing results OR referral laboratory reports with results, if available
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. The laboratory failed to provide evidence of a policy, procedure, or established testing algorithm for the rapid detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex on respiratory specimens. While 'Instruction for Use_TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit.pdf' mentions M. tuberculosis in the context of cross-reactivity, this does not satisfy the requirement for a diagnostic testing pathway. No patient reports or referral laboratory agreements were provided to demonstrate that rapid NAAT or an equivalent regional algorithm is available for patients suspected of pulmonary TB. The laboratory must establish and document a formal process for the rapid detection of M. tuberculosis complex to ensure compliance with MIC.13375.
corrective_actions: 1) Develop and implement a formal policy/procedure for the rapid detection of M. tuberculosis complex on respiratory specimens, incorporating a NAAT or an approved regional algorithm.
2) Establish a formal referral laboratory agreement if rapid testing is not performed in-house, ensuring the referral lab meets the rapid detection criteria.
3) Train laboratory staff on the new testing algorithm and maintain records of patient reports or referral results as evidence of compliance.
cited_documents: Instruction for Use_TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.13375**: The laboratory utilizes nucleic acid amplification technology for various diagnostic tests. While the TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Instructions for Use lists *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* as an organism tested for cross-reactivity and microbial interference, no specific policy or procedure for the rapid detection of *Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex* on respiratory specimens was found in the provided documents. Therefore, it cannot be verified if appropriate testing for rapid detection of *Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex* is available in the laboratory or through a referral laboratory, as requested by MIC.13375.

checks.requirement: There are sufficient, clean, and well-maintained incubators available at specified temperature ranges.
checks.subject: Adequate Incubators
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has successfully completed Installation Qualification (IQ) and Operational Qualification (OQ) for the Binder CO2 Incubator (Serial No. 20220000016955), as evidenced by the 'Binder CO2 Incubator IQ Form.docx' and 'Binder CO2 Incubator OQ Form.docx'. These documents confirm that the equipment was properly installed and that temperature and CO2 stability were verified using NIST-traceable equipment. However, the current documentation is insufficient to meet all criteria of MIC.16550. Specifically, there is no evidence of a documented preventative maintenance schedule, nor are there records confirming the ongoing cleanliness of the incubators. Furthermore, while the OQ confirms the performance of one unit, there is no documentation defining the total inventory of incubators required to ensure 'sufficient' capacity for the laboratory's workload or a master list of specified temperature ranges for all units in use.
corrective_actions: 1) Establish and implement a formal preventative maintenance and cleaning schedule for all incubators, ensuring logs are maintained for each unit.
2) Create a master equipment list that defines the required temperature ranges for each incubator and confirms that current capacity is sufficient for laboratory volume.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.16550**: The Binder CO2 Incubator, model CB-S E7 170, serial number 20220000016955, underwent Installation Qualification (IQ) on July 27, 2023. During IQ, the instrument was examined for transit damage, registered, and placed on a flat, level, dry surface with a power source. The operating manual was downloaded into LIMS, and the equipment was registered for warranty. Operational Qualification (OQ) for this incubator involved verifying CO2 and temperature readings, uniformity, and sensor accuracy. The OQ form, "Binder CO2 Incubator OQ Form", details procedures for checking temperature and CO2 stability using NIST thermometers and CO2 detectors at multiple checkpoints and intervals. A verification report for a ThermoFisher 3130 Series Water Jacketed CO2 Incubator indicates it operates within expected parameters and meets laboratory requirements. However, no specific records or operational evidence were found to confirm the cleanliness or maintenance schedules of the incubators, nor were there documents detailing the availability of sufficient incubators or their specified temperature ranges.

checks.requirement: The microbiology laboratory recognizes and safely handles isolates that may be used as agents of bioterrorism.
checks.subject: Agents of Bioterrorism
checks.note:
NOTE: Microorganisms likely to be utilized as biological weapons include Bacillus anthracis (anthrax), Brucella species (brucellosis), Clostridium botulinum (botulism), Francisella tularensis (tularemia), Yersinia pestis (plague) and variola major (smallpox). 
  
  As part of an institution-wide plan to prepare and respond to a bioterrorism event, the microbiology laboratory must have policies and procedures for the recognition of isolates that may be used as agents of bioterrorism. 
  
  Safe handling includes such activities as handling organisms under a certified biological safety cabinet, and not subjecting the isolates to identification utilizing automated instruments.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. While the laboratory maintains general biohazard exposure and transport procedures (C1002.0V3 and GS130A1.0V4), there is no evidence of a specific policy or procedure for the recognition and safe handling of bioterrorism agents as required by MIC.18968. The current documentation focuses on general infectious substance transport and standard biohazard precautions but fails to address the specific requirement to prohibit the use of automated instruments for suspected bioterrorism agents or to provide guidance on the recognition of organisms such as Bacillus anthracis, Brucella species, or Yersinia pestis. No records of staff training or specific laboratory protocols for handling these select agents were identified in the provided documentation.
corrective_actions: 1) Develop and implement a specific policy for the recognition and safe handling of potential bioterrorism agents, explicitly prohibiting the use of automated identification instruments for these isolates.

2) Incorporate the list of bioterrorism agents (e.g., B. anthracis, F. tularensis) into the laboratory's safety manual and provide documented staff training on these specific recognition and handling procedures.
cited_documents: GS130A1.0V4-Clinical Specimen Collection Storage, Transportation and Receiving Standard Operating Procedure.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.18968**: The Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program, C1002.0V3, mandates that infectious materials be stored in leak-proof containers labeled with the international biohazard symbol and "Biohazard" wording, though red containers suffice for internal use if standard precautions are applied. Secondary containers are required for puncture-prone primary vessels or to prevent external contamination, and waste must be autoclaved or processed by professional medical disposal services. For transport, the GS130A1.0V4-Clinical Specimen Collection Storage, Transportation and Receiving SOP requires adherence to IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations for UN 3373 Biological Substance, Category B. This protocol necessitates four-layer packaging: a sealed primary container, a super-absorbent packet, a certified secondary receptacle, and sturdy outer packaging marked with the UN 3373 label, the proper shipping name, and contact information. Security plans are mandatory for select agents and toxins, such as *Bacillus anthracis* or *Francisella tularensis*. All biological specimens and used cartridges must be treated as infectious, requiring consistent application of standard precautions throughout handling and shipping.

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Policies/C-Laboratory Safety/C1002.0V3_Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program.pdf
policy_evidence.snippet:
Specimens of blood or other potentially infectious materials shall be placed in containers which
prevent leakage during the collection, handling, processing, storage, transport, or shipping. b. Containers shall be labeled with the international biohazard symbol and the wording “Biohazard.” c. The biohazard labels used shall be fluorescent orange or orange-red with black letters. The labels
will be affixed to the containers by string, wire, adhesive, or any method that prevents their loss or
unintentional removal. d. Red bags or red containers may be substituted for labels. If Standard Precautions are utilized in the
handling of all specimens, the labeling/color-coding system is not necessary, providing the
containers are recognizable as containing specimens; however, the labeling or color-coding system
is required when the specimens/containers leave the facility. e. A secondary container will be used if outside contamination of the primary container occurs. f. If specimens can puncture the primary container, the primary container will be placed within a
secondary container which is puncture-resistant. g. Patient materials must be disposed of in a manner that prevents injury to those handling them. h. The biohazard waste disposal shall be handled by a medical waste disposal company. In case of

policy_evidence.snippet:
F. Safety Recommendations - Physical Hazards
Physical hazards in the laboratory include combustible liquids, compressed gases, reactives, explosives and
flammable chemicals, as well as high pressure/energy procedures, sharp objects and moving equipment. Injuries
can result from bodily contact with rotating or moving objects, including mechanical equipment, parts, and
devices. Personnel should not wear loose-fitting clothing, jewelry, or unrestrained long hair around machinery with
moving parts. The Chemical Safety Board has identified the following key lessons for laboratories that address both physical and
other hazards: (1) Ensure that research-specific hazards are evaluated and then controlled by developing specific written
protocols and training. (2) Expand existing laboratory safety plans to ensure that all safety hazards, including physical hazards of
chemicals, are addressed. (3) Ensure that the organization's EHS office reports directly to an identified individual/office with organizational
authority to implement safety improvements. (4) Develop a verification program that ensures that the safety provisions of the CHP are communicated, followed,
and enforced at all levels within the organization. (5) Document and communicate all laboratory near-misses and previous incidents to track safety, provide
opportunities for education and improvement to drive safety changes at the university. (6) Manage the hazards unique to laboratory chemical research in the academic environment.

checks.requirement: The laboratory safely handles spills of infectious materials.
checks.subject: Spill Handling
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory maintains a robust framework for infectious spill handling. Policy C1002.0V3_Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program explicitly defines disinfection protocols for blood and body fluid spills using 1:10 bleach or EPA-registered disinfectants. Training documentation (D1003.4_Laboratory Safety training Form Template) confirms that personnel are instructed on specific spill response procedures, including PPE utilization, absorbent pad application, contact time requirements, and final decontamination steps. The search summary confirms that these procedures are integrated into the laboratory's safety training curriculum. No gaps were identified in the provided documentation regarding the safety protocols for infectious material spills.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of maintaining the Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program (C1002.0V3) and documenting staff competency via the Laboratory Safety training Form (D1003.4).
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.18985**: The Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program, C1002.0V3_Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program, outlines procedures for handling spills of infectious materials. Blood or other body fluid spills must be disinfected with a 1:10 bleach/water solution or an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant. Workbenches where cultures or specimens are handled are decontaminated after each shift and immediately following a spill. The D1003.4_Laboratory Safety training Form Cerese 250106-250107 and D1003.4_Laboratory Safety training Form Template detail specific steps for bio-hazard material spills: put on PPE, cover the spill with an absorbent pad, pour a freshly mixed 10% bleach and water solution onto the pad, allow it to soak for 20 minutes, wipe up with paper towels or absorbent pads into a bio-hazard waste bag, and then clean the area with 10% bleach followed by water and 70% ethanol. Emergency telephone numbers and locations of safety equipment, including spill control kits, should be prominently posted.

checks.subject: Workbench Decontamination
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of workbench decontamination
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established robust policies for workbench decontamination, specifically the Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program [C1002.0V3] and the Laboratory Facility Routine Maintenance Program [C1001.0V2], which mandate decontamination after each shift and following spills. Assay-specific instructions [302-6991 Rev. B] further define spill cleanup protocols using 10% bleach. However, while the laboratory performs and documents periodic surface wipe tests [G1008.1-210714, G1008.1-210813, G1008.1-210619], there is no evidence provided of routine, shift-based workbench decontamination logs. The current documentation focuses on periodic environmental monitoring rather than the required shift-by-shift verification of routine cleaning.
corrective_actions: 1) Implement a standardized daily workbench decontamination log to record shift-based cleaning as required by C1002.0V3.
2) Ensure staff document the completion of routine decontamination in the newly implemented logs to provide verifiable evidence of compliance.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.19010**: The XYZ Lab’s Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program [C1002.0V3] and Laboratory Facility Routine Maintenance Program [C1001.0V2] mandate that all equipment and work surfaces be decontaminated after each procedure, following spills, and at the end of every shift to ensure they are free of biological or chemical hazards. Standard decontamination requires 10% bleach followed by water and 75% ethanol, while specific assay instructions [302-4419 Rev. C] [302-6991 Rev. B] require a two-minute contact time with 10% bleach followed by 70% denatured ethanol for spills. Although records of routine workbench decontamination were not provided, the laboratory maintains documentation of DNA/RNA testing results for various surfaces, including tabletops and biosafety hoods, via Laboratory Wipe Test Procedure and Record forms [G1008.1-210714] [G1008.1-210813] [G1008.1-210619].

checks.requirement: The laboratory safely handles and processes specimens, including those suspected to contain highly infectious pathogens.
checks.subject: Safe Specimen Handling/Processing
checks.note:
NOTE: Suggested topics to be considered in the policies and procedures include the need for tight sealing of containers, avoiding spills of hazardous materials, requirements for wearing gloves, the need for respirator protection, availability and use of vaccinations, and the hazards of sniffing plates. Patient materials must be disposed of in a manner that prevents injury to those handling them. 
  
  For specimens suspected of containing highly infectious pathogens, laboratories must review national, federal, state (or provincial), and local guidelines for the handling of specimens from patients suspected to have high risk pathogens, such as Francisella tularensis, avian influenza, Ebola, MERS coronavirus, or any infectious agent that has a high potential to cause disease in individuals and communities.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of universal precaution training for all personnel handling suspected infectious pathogens
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established robust policies for safe specimen handling, including the 'Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program' (C1002.0V3) and the 'Clinical Specimen Collection, Storage, Transportation and Receiving SOP' (GS130A1.0V4), which address PPE requirements, container sealing, and transport safety. The 'Xpert Xpress SARS-CoV-2 Flu RSV Assay' package insert confirms the classification of samples as potentially infectious. However, while the 'Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program' mandates training for personnel involved in packaging and transport, the specific 'Evidence of Compliance' requirement for universal precaution training records for all personnel handling suspected infectious pathogens was not verified in the provided documentation. The laboratory must provide documented evidence that all relevant staff have completed the required safety and universal precaution training to achieve full compliance.

policy_evidence.snippet:
XYZ Laboratory, 2009 Ranch Rd. 620 N. Austin, TX 78734 1 XYZ Lab Document Name Specimen Collection, Storage, Transportation and Receiving
Standard Operating Procedure XYZ Lab Document Number GS130A1.0 Version # 4 Author：XYZ Lab Date of Inception:
11/16/2020 Date of Execution of the Current
version：04/17/2025 1. Purpose and application
This SOP provides a standard operating procedure for collection, storage and transportation of
infectious pathogens classified to be handled at a BSL 2 facility, including but not limited to SARS
CoV2 and influenza A/B. 2. Responsibilities
2.1 Lab shall provide the SOP to the relevant clients. 2.2 Clients shall follow the SOP carefully to collect, handle, store and ship the specimens. 3. Safety precautions
Specimen collector shall use recommended personal protective equipment (PPE), which includes an
N95 or higher-level respirator (or facemask if a respirator is not available), eye protection, gloves, and
a gown, when collecting specimens. In case of patient self-collection, the specimen collector shall follow standard precautions, wearing
gloves and facemask or cloth face covering at all time in the sample collection facility. During handling and processing of specimens, always ensure to tightly sealing of containers, avoiding
spills of hazardous materials. Specimen collector shall get the vaccinations if possible and applicable.

checks.requirement: The laboratory has minimized the occupational risk of exposure to infectious agents through the use of appropriate work practice controls in accordance with current recommendations on the biosafety levels (BSL) for working with different organisms.
checks.subject: Biosafety Levels - Occupational Risk
checks.note:
NOTE: The laboratory director is responsible for defining and implementing work practice controls appropriate to the BSL of the laboratory and to minimize the risk of personnel infection. Work practice controls consist of combinations of equipment, processes and laboratory design that are appropriate for the type of laboratory, laboratory BSL (1 to 4), and infectious agents handled. 
  
  For bacterial, mycobacterial, mycologic, and virology processing and work performed in a biological safety cabinet (BSC): 
  
  * Exhaust air from a class I or class II BSC must be filtered through high efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters. 
  * Air from Class I and IIB cabinets is hard-ducted to the outside. 
  
  * Air from Class IIA cabinets may be recirculated within the laboratory if the cabinet is tested and certified at least annually. It may also be exhausted through a dedicated stack that protects against backflow of air from adverse weather conditions or through the building exhaust air system in a manner (eg, thimble connection) that avoids any interference with the air balance of the biological safety cabinet or building exhaust system. 
  
  The 6th edition of Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories provides guidance for safe conduct of work from a biosafety perspective. It can be used as a tool for assessing and mitigating risk. Refer to Section IV - Laboratory Biosafety Level Criteria and Table 1. Summary of Laboratory Biosafety Levels (BSLs) for specific information.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of BSC HEPA filters and exhaust systems appropriate for the BSL and infectious agents handled
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a robust policy framework for biosafety, as evidenced by the 'Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program' [C1002.0V3], which mandates the use of biological safety cabinets (BSCs) and adherence to BMBL 6th Edition guidelines. The Laboratory Director's responsibility for these controls is defined in [D1001.1V3]. However, the requirement specifically mandates records of BSC HEPA filter and exhaust system maintenance to verify that work practice controls are functioning as intended. These specific maintenance and certification records were not provided in the retrieved documentation. While the policy is compliant, the objective evidence required to verify the ongoing performance of the engineering controls is currently missing.
corrective_actions: 1) Locate and compile the most recent annual BSC certification and HEPA filter maintenance reports.
2) Establish a recurring document control process to ensure future BSC maintenance records are filed and accessible for inspection.
cited_documents: D1001.1V3-Lab Director Job Description and Responsibility.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.19060**: The XYZ Lab’s Bio-hazard Exposure Control Program [C1002.0V3] mandates work practice controls to mitigate infectious agent risks, requiring all patient samples to be processed in level II biosafety cabinets. Staff must adhere to strict prohibitions against eating, drinking, or personal grooming in technical areas, while utilizing designated safe zones for food consumption. Mandatory PPE includes gloves for all human samples, barrier protection for skin and mucous membranes, and face shields or masks during splash-prone procedures. Contaminated workbenches are decontaminated after shifts and spills, with blood or body fluid incidents addressed using 1:10 bleach or EPA-registered disinfectants. Sharps must be disposed of in labeled biohazard containers, and staff with weeping dermatitis are restricted from handling samples. The program further outlines laundry protocols for lab coats, provides Hepatitis B vaccinations, and follows the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services BMBL 6th Edition guidelines. Notably, documentation regarding BSC HEPA filter and exhaust system maintenance was absent from the provided records.

Any skin surfaces shall be washed immediately and thoroughly if contaminated with blood or other body fluids. h. All sharps (e.g., needles, scalpels) will be placed in properly labeled containers with the international biological hazard symbol and the wording “Biohazard.” i. Workers with exudative lesions or weeping dermatitis will refrain from all direct handling patient
samples until the condition resolves. j. Blood or other body fluid spills shall be disinfected with a 1:10 (bleach/water) solution or an EPA
registered hospital disinfectant.
2. Safe Work Practices
a. All patient samples shall be processed in level II biosafety cabinets. b. The laboratory decontaminates workbenches on which cultures or specimens are handled after each
shift and decontaminates immediately after a spill or other contamination event
c. Eating, drinking, smoking, vaping, gum chewing, food storage, applying cosmetics or lip balm, and
manipulation of contact lenses are prohibited in all technical work areas where there is a reasonable
likelihood of occupational exposure. d. Food or beverages will be consumed only in a safe designated area. Food and drinks shall not be
kept on countertops, bench tops, refrigerators, freezers, shelves or cabinets where blood or other
potentially infectious materials are present or stored. e. PPE shall be worn at all times when handling patient samples and performing the tests. f.

checks.requirement: If organism identification and/or antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) (phenotypic or genotypic) is performed directly from positive blood culture bottles, the broth from the bottle is inoculated onto solid media to assess for consistency with direct results.
checks.subject: Direct Identification and Susceptibility from Blood Culture Broth
checks.note:
NOTE: This checklist item is applicable to tests that detect bacteria in positive blood cultures that are culturable on standard bacteriological media such as sheep's blood agar and/or chocolate agar. 
  
  It is the responsibility of the laboratory director to determine the extent of confirmatory testing necessary when evaluating the subculture grown on solid media. The extent of the evaluation should be supported by the manufacturer's recommendations and the laboratory's verification/validation data.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * SOP with statements to include inoculation of specimens onto solid media AND 
  * Specimen workcard or patient report recording the evaluation of the sample growing on solid media
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. The laboratory failed to provide evidence of compliance for MIC.21835. A review of the retrieved documents, including 'Accreditation2020Top10Deficiencies.pdf' and 'Copy of K1003.5_Annual Laboratory, Regulatory, and Safety Compliance Check.docx', confirms that no SOP exists requiring the inoculation of positive blood culture broth onto solid media for consistency assessment. Furthermore, no specimen workcards or patient reports were provided to demonstrate that such evaluations are being performed and recorded. The current documentation does not meet the requirement to verify direct identification/AST results against subculture growth.
corrective_actions: 1) Revise the microbiology SOP to explicitly mandate the inoculation of positive blood culture broth onto solid media for all direct identification/AST testing.
2) Implement a standardized workcard or electronic reporting field to document the comparison between direct results and subculture growth.
3) Perform and document a retrospective review of recent cases to ensure consistency with manufacturer recommendations and laboratory validation data.
cited_documents: Copy of K1003.5_Annual Laboratory, Regulatory, and Safety Compliance Check.docx
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.21835**: The retrieved documents do not contain a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) with statements to include inoculation of specimens onto solid media, nor do they include a specimen workcard or patient report recording the evaluation of the sample growing on solid media, which would serve as evidence of compliance for MIC.21835. The "Accreditation2020Top10Deficiencies" document discusses general accreditation requirements, including instrument and method comparison, ongoing evaluation of proficiency testing, reagent labeling, and review of technical policies and procedures. The "Annual Laboratory, Regulatory, and Safety Compliance Check" confirms CAP accreditation and proficiency testing enrollment. The "Data Collection Form for the Procedure Manual" indicates that the procedure manual is complete, accessible, and up-to-date, with procedures reflecting manufacturer's instructions. However, none of these documents specifically address the inoculation of positive blood culture broth onto solid media for consistency assessment.

checks.requirement: The laboratory monitors for the presence of false positive results (eg, due to nucleic acid contamination) for all molecular microbiology tests.
checks.subject: Quality Monitoring
checks.note: NOTE: Examples include review of summary statistics (eg, monitoring percentage of results that are positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and/or Neisseria gonorrhoeae for an increase above historical positive rate within a run or over multiple runs), unexpected increase in positive results for seasonal pathogens outside of the standard epidemiology, performance of wipe testing, and review and investigation of physician complaints on false positive results. Based on monitoring data, the laboratory may implement additional mitigation strategies to minimize risk of contamination, such as process controls.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of data review, wipe testing, statistical data, and evaluation and corrective action if indicated
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory demonstrates a robust program for monitoring false positive results and nucleic acid contamination. Policies are established in 'G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf' and 'GS130G.0V3_Simplexa Flu A_B _ RSV Direct Gen II Assay Standard Operating Procedure.pdf', which mandate the use of No Template Controls (NTC), environmental wipe testing, and strict cross-contamination prevention protocols (dedicated lab coats, pipette calibration). The search summary confirms that the laboratory actively reviews patient results and client complaints, and maintains a process for statistical analysis of prevalence to identify unexpected increases in positive results. Evidence of compliance is supported by the integration of these procedures into the laboratory's IQCP and daily quality monitoring workflows.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of monitoring NTC performance, conducting periodic wipe testing, and performing statistical reviews of positive result rates as defined in G1008.0V2 and GS130G.0V3.
cited_documents: G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf
GS130G.0V3_Simplexa Flu A_B _ RSV Direct Gen II Assay Standard Operating Procedure.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.63252**: The laboratory monitors for false positives and nucleic acid contamination using No Template Controls (NTC) with every test, as detailed in the Simplexa Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II Assay Standard Operating Procedure (GS130G.0V3_Simplexa Flu A_B _ RSV Direct Gen II Assay Standard Operating Procedure.pdf). If an NTC fails, the laboratory investigates the source of contamination, performs environmental wipe tests if necessary, and halts reporting until the issue is resolved. Unexpected increases in positive results trigger both experimental reviews of reagents, processes, and handling, and statistical analyses of prevalence and historical patterns. To prevent cross-contamination, staff utilize dedicated lab coats, change gloves between samples, properly dispose of biohazard waste, and ensure regular pipette calibration. Furthermore, the laboratory conducts daily reviews of patient results and client complaints, filing corrective action reports and revising Quality Control Procedures (QCP) as required.

2.4.6 All pipettes shall be cleaned and calibrated or calibration verified at regular intervals. 2.5 Laboratory Coats
Laboratory coats shall be dedicated to specific use areas and changed when moving between areas. 2.5.1 Gloves
To reduce the possibility of introducing amplified nucleic acid products into the clean areas, disposable gloves shall be
worn and changed when entering or reentering the amplification preparation area. Disposable gloves may be changed
between samples to prevent cross-contamination. 2.6 Biohazard and Amplicon Disposal
All nucleic acids amplification products and remnant patient samples shall be closed and disposed in the biohazard waste
bin. It is critical that all waste shall be removed as soon as possible to reduce the risk of contamination. 2.7 Monitoring
2.7.1No template control shall be run with each test to ensure the testing system is free of contaminants. In cased a system
contamination event is confirmed, investigation experiments shall be performed to identify the source of contamination. Testing environment wipe tests may be performed if necessary. Corrective action shall be taken to eliminate the problem. 2.7.2 Unexpected increase in positive results shall be investigated both experimentally and statically. Experimentally,
investigation involves in control sample, specimen handling, assay process, reagents and consumables. Statistically,
investigation includes population prevalence, specimen characteristics, historic positive distribution/pattern.

policy_evidence.snippet:
SUPPLEMENT ARTICLE S4 cid 2020:71 (Suppl 1) Theel et al Clinical Infectious Diseases Molecular and Direct Detection Tests for Treponema
pallidum Subspecies pallidum: A Review of the Literature,
1964–2017 Elitza S. Theel,1 Samantha S. Katz,2 and Allan Pillay2 1 Division of Clinical Microbiology, Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota, USA, and 2 Division of STD Prevention, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Atlanta, Georgia, USA
Direct detection methods for Treponema pallidum include dark-field microscopy (DFM), direct fluorescence antibody (DFA) testing,
immunohistochemistry (IHC), and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). Here, we reviewed the relevant syphilis diagnostic liter
ature to address 2 main questions with respect to T. pallidum direct detection techniques: “What are the performance characteristics
for each direct detection test for T. pallidum and what are the optimal specimen types for each test?” and “What options are available
for T. pallidum molecular epidemiology?” To answer these questions, we searched 5 electronic databases (OVID Medline, OVID
Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, and Scopus) from 1964 to 2017 using relevant search terms and identified 1928 articles, of
which 37 met our inclusion criteria.

SUPPLEMENT ARTICLE S4 cid 2020:71 (Suppl 1) Theel et al Clinical Infectious Diseases Molecular and Direct Detection Tests for Treponema
pallidum Subspecies pallidum: A Review of the Literature,
1964–2017 Elitza S. Theel,1 Samantha S. Katz,2 and Allan Pillay2 1 Division of Clinical Microbiology, Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota, USA, and 2 Division of STD Prevention, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Atlanta, Georgia, USA
Direct detection methods for Treponema pallidum include dark-field microscopy (DFM), direct fluorescence antibody (DFA) testing,
immunohistochemistry (IHC), and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). Here, we reviewed the relevant syphilis diagnostic liter
ature to address 2 main questions with respect to T. pallidum direct detection techniques: “What are the performance characteristics
for each direct detection test for T. pallidum and what are the optimal specimen types for each test?” and “What options are available
for T. pallidum molecular epidemiology?” To answer these questions, we searched 5 electronic databases (OVID Medline, OVID
Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, and Scopus) from 1964 to 2017 using relevant search terms and identified 1928 articles, of
which 37 met our inclusion criteria.

checks.requirement: The laboratory uses established methods for specimen preservation and storage before testing.
checks.subject: Specimen Preservation/Storage
checks.note:
NOTE: Patient samples may be stored in a frost-free freezer only if protected from thawing. 
  
  * Repeated freeze-thaw cycles contribute to biomolecular degradation and are detrimental to biospecimen quality. 
  * It is prudent to avoid freeze-thaw altogether by aliquoting specimens before freezing. 
  * Peripheral blood specimens should not be frozen, unless otherwise validated, because induced hemolysis can result in PCR inhibition through the presence of contaminating hemoglobin.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established specimen accessioning procedures (GS1002.0V3) and storage guidelines for urine specimens. However, the laboratory lacks documented evidence of a comprehensive policy for all specimen types. Specifically, the search summary indicates that GS1002.0V3 references policy G1001.0 for remnant sample storage conditions, but this policy was not provided for review. While the laboratory acknowledges the risks of freeze-thaw cycles for SARS-CoV-2 samples in '15_Covid Clinical Sample Freeze and Thaw Article Draft.docx', there is no evidence of a finalized, approved policy governing the prevention of freeze-thaw cycles or the specific storage requirements for all clinical sample types to ensure biomolecular integrity. Records demonstrating consistent adherence to these storage conditions were not verified.
corrective_actions: 1) Locate and provide the referenced policy G1001.0 for review to ensure it covers all specimen storage requirements.
2) Update the Specimen Accessioning SOP (GS1002.0V3) or associated policies to explicitly define storage conditions and freeze-thaw limitations for all sample types tested.
3) Implement and document a QA review process using the '2026 K1003.4.3_Data Collection Form' to verify ongoing compliance with storage requirements.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.63328**: The laboratory stores specimens according to their sample type and client instructions. Some specimens are discarded after testing, while others are retained until the client provides further notice. All stored specimens are properly documented and tracked by location. For urine specimens, storage at 2-8°C is permissible for up to 48 hours prior to testing, and for prolonged storage, specimens may be frozen below -20°C. Frozen urine specimens should be thawed and mixed well before testing. However, for SARS-CoV-2 testing, multiple freeze-thaw cycles (FTCs) can degrade viral nucleic acids, impacting RT-PCR test performance. Ultra-low temperature storage is recommended for long-term preservation of SARS-CoV-2 specimens. The Specimen Accessioning Standard Operating Procedure GS1002.0V3-Specimen Accessioning Standard Operating Procedure references policy G1001.0 for remnant sample storage conditions, but policy G1001.0 was not provided.

policy_evidence.snippet: The main SARS-CoV-2 testing technologies include reverse transcription real-time PCR (RT-PCR or RT-qPCR), which is the gold standard and tests for viral nucleic acid usually in clinical laboratories, and lateral flow rapid assays (LFA) testing for viral antigens, most often used in point-of-care or home settings. There are times that frozen patient samples must be used for various reasons such as delayed testing, secured transportation, late verification, or research and development using remnant samples, freezing at an ultra-low temperature remains the only option for long-term specimen storage as per CDC recommendation (https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-nCoV/lab/guidelines-clinical-specimens.html). It is thus crucial to fully understand whether FTCs can adversely affect the test performance on any scale if frozen samples are used. Several studies using clinical samples (1-2), wastewater solid (3-4), and synthetic RNA (5) showed that FTCs had a significant, negative impact on the cycle threshold (Ct) values of the SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR test, indicating a degradation of the viral nucleic acids throughout FTCs even with only one freeze and thaw cycle. Others found that a limited number of FTCs had a minor or no significant impact on the RT-PCR test results (6-9).

checks.requirement: If extracted nucleic acid is accepted as a specimen type, the laboratory ensures that isolation of nucleic acids for clinical testing occurs in a CLIA-certified laboratory or a laboratory meeting equivalent requirements as determined by the CAP and/or the CMS. This policy is clearly displayed to ordering clients.
checks.subject: Extracted Nucleic Acid Specimens
checks.note: NOTE: All clinical testing must be performed in CLIA-certified laboratories or laboratories meeting equivalent requirements (refer to GEN.41350). This includes all components of testing that may impact the quality of the test result, including isolation or extraction of nucleic acids. Laboratories may choose to have referring clients formally attest that extracted nucleic acid submitted for testing has been isolated or extracted in an appropriately qualified laboratory.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Written statement on the test requisition, test catalog, or policy available to referring clients stating that the laboratory only accepts isolated or extracted nucleic acids for which extraction or isolation is performed in an appropriately qualified laboratory
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. While the laboratory maintains robust internal referral laboratory selection processes (E1001.0-Supplier Selection Process) and regulatory oversight (K1003.5_Annual Laboratory, Regulatory, and Safety Compliance Check), it fails to meet the specific client-facing communication requirement of MIC.63340. The laboratory lacks a written statement on test requisitions, the test catalog, or client-facing policies explicitly informing ordering clients that the laboratory only accepts isolated or extracted nucleic acids processed in a CLIA-certified or equivalent laboratory. The current documentation (A1001.0v2_Compliance Policy.pdf) does not address this specific requirement for external clients.
corrective_actions: 1) Update the test catalog and test requisition forms to include a formal statement requiring that all submitted nucleic acid specimens be isolated/extracted in a CLIA-certified or equivalent laboratory.
2) Distribute a formal notification to all ordering clients regarding this policy requirement and update the client-facing policy manual to reflect this standard.
cited_documents: K1003.5_Annual Laboratory, Regulatory, and Safety Compliance Check.docx
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.63340**: XYZ laboratory maintains CAP accreditation and CLIA high-complexity certification, requiring adherence to all associated regulatory and checklist standards. Referral laboratories must be CLIA-certified or equivalent, with selection prioritized by performance quality and verified by obtaining current certificates. Candidate laboratories require an external audit and completion of the supplier questionnaire (E1001.2 - XYZ Laboratory Supplier Questionnaire). Per K1003.5_Annual Laboratory, Regulatory, and Safety Compliance Check, valid CLIA and accreditation documentation is displayed at the facility entrance. The laboratory participates in CAP external accreditation, undergoing onsite inspections biennially and self-inspections annually as defined in K1001.0-External Accreditation Management Process. However, the laboratory lacks a written policy on test requisitions, catalogs, or client-facing documentation specifying that it only accepts isolated or extracted nucleic acids processed in appropriately qualified laboratories.

checks.requirement: If the laboratory tests specimen types or uses collection devices other than those listed in the package insert, the laboratory performs validation studies to document adequate performance of the test with those specimen types or collection devices.
checks.subject: Validation Studies - Specimen Type/Collection Device
checks.note:
NOTE: Any change to the manufacturer's supplied or recommended specimen collection devices, solutions, or reagents or modifications to the assay as set forth in the manufacturer's labeling and instructions is considered a modification. It may include a change to specimen type, instrumentation or procedure that could affect its performance specifications for sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, or precision or any change to the stated purpose of the test, its approved test population, or any claims related to interpretation of the results. Refer to the section Test Method Validation and Verification in the All Common Checklist for additional details. 
  
  Results from tests performed on specimen types not listed in the package insert may be reported without complete validation only if the specimen type is encountered rarely, precluding an adequate number for validation studies. Under these circumstances, the test report must include a disclaimer stating that the specimen type has not been validated
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of validation studies for modified FDA-cleared/approved assays for different specimen types and collection devices
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a formal framework for test validation and verification as evidenced by 'G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program.pdf'. While the 'A1004.0V5- Scope of Service 2023-2025.pdf' identifies that the laboratory performs assays involving modified specimen types (e.g., finger prick on ADX cards), the specific validation study records required by MIC.64770 to document performance specifications (sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, or precision) for these modified specimen types or collection devices were not provided for review. The laboratory must produce the raw data and summary reports for these specific validation studies to demonstrate compliance with the requirement for modified FDA-cleared assays.
corrective_actions: 1) Conduct a comprehensive audit of all assays currently using specimen types or collection devices not listed in the manufacturer's package insert.
2) Compile and archive validation study records for all identified modifications, ensuring they meet the performance criteria outlined in G1004.0V3.

3) If validation data is unavailable for a specific modification, perform the necessary studies or implement the required disclaimer on patient reports for rare specimen types as permitted by the MIC.64770 note.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.64770**: The Test Validation and Verification Program G1004.0V3 outlines plans for establishing and validating or verifying lab assay method performance specifications. For unmodified FDA-cleared/approved tests, the scope of validation typically involves verifying accuracy, precision, and reportable range. The Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft provides an example for verifying FDA-cleared tests, emphasizing that the laboratory and Director are responsible for designing and approving verification studies. This guide details how to verify accuracy by testing known samples and controls, and precision by ensuring reproducible results from the same sample. The Accreditation2020Top10Deficiencies document mentions that written procedures for instrument and method comparison, along with records of comparability studies, are required. The Scope of Service A1004.0V5 lists several assays, including some lab-developed tests (LDTs) where clinical validation studies were provided, such as for a clinical chemistry assay using finger prick on an ADX card. However, records of validation studies specifically for modified FDA-cleared/approved assays for different specimen types and collection devices were not found in the provided documents.
