policy_evidence.snippet:
Test Validation and Verification Program Document Name
Document Number G1004.0 Version 3 Author： Keqin Gregg Date of Composition: 11/02/2020 Date of Execution：05/16/2025 Page 1 of 5 Objective
Provide plans for establishing and validating/verifying lab assay method performance specifications. For some assays
with special requirements by accreditation or regulatory agents or other national or international standards, the specific
requirements should be noted in its specific policy
Programs
1. Testing Method
1.1 The laboratory must verify or establish analytical and clinical performance characteristics for each test. Laboratories
may use information from manufacturers, published literature, or studies performed in other laboratories, but should
verify such outside information, whenever practical. 1.2 For unmodified FDA-cleared/approved test, the scope of validation is to confirm or verify with objective evidence that
the stated analytical and clinical performance characteristics are met in the particular laboratory setting, this usually need
only verify accuracy, precision, and reportable range. Manufacturer recommended method shall be followed if there is
any.
policy_evidence.title: G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Operation/F-Instruments/Instrument/Liaison MDX/Simplex FluAB&RSV assay verification/Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft.docx
policy_evidence.snippet: Introduction & Intended Use This example verification guide is intended to serve as an educational resource to assist laboratories in the verification of FDA-cleared tests within their laboratory. Ultimately, the Laboratory and Laboratory Director (or equivalent) are responsible for designing, reviewing, and approving their verification study and determining whether it aligns with federal, state, and local guidelines. Per the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines, the performance of all FDA-cleared, non-modified, moderate- and high-complexity diagnostic tests must be verified for accuracy, precision reference range, and reportable range.1,2 Accuracy Accuracy is typically verified by testing a collection of known clinical/contrived samples and commercially available controls. The number of positive and negative samples needed for each target is determined by the laboratory. When using samples previously categorized by another method, discrepancies can occur due to several factors (e.g., primer design, limit of detection). In the example verification that follows, we chose to incorporate a collection of contrived samples and third-party controls for the accuracy study. Precision Precision studies are intended to verify that expected results are obtained reproducibly from the same sample.
policy_evidence.title: Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft

checks.requirement: If the laboratory chooses to pool specimens for tests performed using test systems that have not been FDA-cleared/approved for that purpose (eg, Chlamydia trachomatis/Neisseria gonorrhoeae NAAT on pooled urine specimens), the laboratory validates the testing procedure for pooled specimens, including limit of detection (sensitivity), reproducibility, and accuracy (method comparison).
checks.subject: Validation of Specimen Pooling
checks.note:
NOTE: As part of the method comparison, the results for pooled specimens must be compared to the single (non-pooled) results using an adequate number of clinical specimens covering the entire range of organism concentration seen in clinical specimens (ie, low and high positive specimens). 
  
  Any clinical claim regarding the efficacy of pooling must be validated (see COM.40640).
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. While the laboratory maintains a 'Test Validation and Verification Program' (G1004.0V3) and has performed LoD and reproducibility studies for specific assays (Simplexa Flu A/B & RSV, TaqPath COVID-19) using pooled matrices, the current documentation does not explicitly demonstrate a method comparison study comparing pooled results to single (non-pooled) clinical specimens as required by the MIC.64790 note. The provided documents confirm the use of pooled matrices for analytical sensitivity, but lack evidence of a formal validation study comparing pooled vs. non-pooled clinical results to ensure accuracy across the range of organism concentrations. The 'Quality Planning Process' (A1002.0V2) establishes the requirement for validation, but specific records confirming the comparative performance of pooled versus individual clinical specimens were not verified.
corrective_actions: 1) Conduct and document a method comparison study using an adequate number of clinical specimens (covering low and high positive concentrations) to compare pooled versus non-pooled results.
2) Update the Test Validation and Verification Program (G1004.0V3) to explicitly include the requirement for comparative analysis when implementing specimen pooling for non-FDA cleared applications.
cited_documents: Instruction for Use_TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.64790**: The Test Validation and Verification Program (G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program) outlines plans for establishing and validating lab assay method performance specifications. For unmodified FDA-cleared/approved tests, validation typically verifies accuracy, precision, and reportable range. The Simplexa™ Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II (MOL2655) assay's limit of detection (LoD) was determined using quantified stocks in pooled nasopharyngeal swab samples. Reproducibility studies for the Simplexa™ Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II assay involved contrived samples spiked into negative nasopharyngeal swab matrix. Similarly, the TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Instructions for Use (Pub. No. MAN0028576 B) details reproducibility assessments across multiple sites, operators, and reagent lots using inactivated SARS-CoV-2 spiked into pooled negative nasopharyngeal matrix. The LoD for the TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit was also determined using contrived positive specimens spiked into pooled negative nasopharyngeal specimens. The Quality Planning Process (A1002.0V2-Quality Planning Process) states that all test systems need validation/verification to ensure performance specifications meet QC requirements, including accuracy and precision. The Test Validation and Verification Program (G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program) further specifies that precision/reproducibility should examine all potential sources of variability, such as operators and reagent lots.

Provide plans for establishing and validating/verifying lab assay method performance specifications. For some assays

Programs

policy_evidence.snippet:
COM.04250
If the laboratory uses more than one nonwaived instrument/method to test for a given
analyte, the instruments and methods are checked against each other at least twice
a year for comparability of results. NOTE: This requirement applies to tests performed on the same or different instrument makes/
models or by different methods, even if there are different reference intervals or levels of
sensitivity. It includes primary and back up methods used for patient testing. The purpose of the requirement is to evaluate the relationship between test results using different
methodologies, instruments, or testing sites. The laboratory must establish a written procedure for
this check that includes acceptance criteria. This requirement is not applicable to: Calculated parameters Waived methods Laboratories with different CAP numbers
The following types of materials may be used to generate data for comparability studies: Patient/client specimens (pooled or unpooled) are preferred to avoid potential matrix effects Quality control materials for tests performed on the same instrument platform, with both control materials
and reagents of the same manufacturer and lot number. Alternative protocols based on quality control or reference materials for cases when availability or pre
analytical stability of patient/client specimens is a limiting factor. The materials must be validated (when
applicable) to have the same response as fresh human specimens for the instruments and methods
involved.
policy_evidence.title: Accreditation2020Top10Deficiencies

checks.requirement: Validation or verification studies were performed with an adequate number and representative (reasonable) distribution of samples for each type of specimen (eg, blood, fresh/frozen tissue, paraffin-embedded tissue).
checks.subject: Validation or Verification Studies - Specimen Selection
checks.note:
NOTE: The number of specimens to be included in a verification study for each specimen type is to be determined by the laboratory director. Verification studies must include the following: 
  
  * Evaluation of adequate numbers of positive and negative specimens across the specimen types to be used in the assay (eg, urine, genital swabs, rectal swabs, pharyngeal swabs), even if they are obtained with the same collection device 
  * Evaluation of local specimens representing the strains or genotypes, as appropriate, if geographic variations are known or expected in the strains or genotype of organisms tested 
  
  Validation studies, by definition, are more rigorous assessments of non-FDA cleared/approved tests or specimens, requiring multiple positive and negative specimens representing all specimen types and strain/genotype variations. 
  
  For qualitative tests, a verification or validation study includes comparison of positive and negative test results to a comparable test method. For quantitative tests, the manufacturer's limit of detection, reportable range and precision must be validated or verified by the laboratory, as well as a comparison of patient test results across the reportable range of the test. Specimens for the validation or verification study can include quantitative external control material, cultured organisms (quantified) and proficiency testing material, and must include patient specimens. 
  
  Refer to the section
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of validation and verification studies
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a formal policy, 'G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program,' which defines the requirements for specimen selection, including minimum sample sizes (20 samples) and the necessity for representative distribution across specimen types and concentrations. While the policy aligns with the requirements of MIC.64960, the current evidence set lacks the actual records of completed validation or verification studies to demonstrate that these policies were executed for assays currently in use. The laboratory must provide the specific study reports or raw data logs confirming that the required number and distribution of positive/negative specimens were utilized for each assay type as mandated by the policy.
corrective_actions: 1) Compile and organize validation/verification study reports for all active assays to demonstrate adherence to the specimen selection criteria defined in G1004.0V3.
2) Ensure that future study records explicitly document the rationale for specimen distribution, including strain/genotype representation where applicable.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.64960**: The "Test Validation and Verification Program" (G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program) outlines requirements for specimen selection in validation and verification studies. An adequate number and representative distribution of samples must be used for each specimen type, including blood, fresh/frozen tissue, saliva, paraffin-embedded tissue, prenatal specimens, and buccal swabs. For tissue samples, validation must include representative tissue sources expected to be tested by the assay. Specimen processing and fixation conditions that significantly influence nucleic acid quality or analysis results must also be included in validation. For quantitative tests, accuracy assessment requires a minimum of 20 samples with analyte concentrations distributed across the analytical measurement range. For qualitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples, including positive, negative, and low-positive samples near the lower limit of detection, should be used, excluding equivocal samples. The number of positive and negative samples for each target in accuracy verification is determined by the laboratory.

Document Number G1004.0 Version 3 Author： Keqin Gregg Date of Composition: 11/02/2020 Date of Execution：05/16/2025 Page 3 of 5 1.4.1 Evaluate potential clinical validity and utility based on published reports, and select tests that can improve patient
care or population’s health. 1.4.2 Select a testing platform and software that can deliver quality testing results to intended tests. 1.4.3 Determine the specimen types that the method is going to use. Assess vendors, controls, reference samples, real
samples that will be used for validation experiments. 1.4.3.1 Ensure an adequate number and representative distribution of samples are performed for each type of specimen
expected for the assay (e.g. blood, fresh/frozen tissue, saliva, paraffin-embedded tissue, prenatal specimens, buccal swabs. For tissue samples, the validation must include representative tissue sources (i.e. organ/site) that are expected to be tested
by the assay.
1.4.4 Familiarize and optimize the testing platform and assay methods, and establish the testing procedure. 1.4.4.1 Specimen processing and fixation conditions can significantly influence the quality and integrity of nucleic acids
extracted from a specimen or potentially analysis results downstream. Consequently, laboratories must include specimens
handled with significantly different fixation and processing methods in the validation.

18 | Good Clinical Laboratory Practice (GCLP)/08 12.3 | Method validation
12.3.1 The selection of instrument platforms and analytical methodologies
should take into account current regulatory standards and sponsor
expectations, where appropriate. 12.3.2 Each analytical method used in the analysis of trial materials should be
appropriately documented, validated, controlled and approved. Changes
to a method should be controlled and validated and result in the issue
of a further version of the method. 12.3.3 Each analytical method should be appropriately validated to establish
and demonstrate its fitness for purpose. 12.3.4 Records to demonstrate the validity and suitability of such methods
within the trial facility should be retained. 12.3.5 Analytical platforms/methods should not be changed during the course
of a trial, without prior consultation and agreement with the Sponsor. Such changes must be controlled, documented and appropriately autho
rized and may result in the need for further method validation. 12.4 | Processing trial materials
12.4.1 Trial material should be analysed and reported within a time frame
consistent with patient safety issues and trial protocol, analytical plan,
standard operating procedure and any contractual requirements. Repeat analysis
12.4.2 The laboratory should have documented procedures governing rules for
repeat analysis consistent with pharmaceutical industry standards. These
may be included within the analytical plan.

policy_evidence.snippet: Introduction & Intended Use This example verification guide is intended to serve as an educational resource to assist laboratories in the verification of FDA-cleared tests within their laboratory. Ultimately, the Laboratory and Laboratory Director (or equivalent) are responsible for designing, reviewing, and approving their verification study and determining whether it aligns with federal, state, and local guidelines. Per the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines, the performance of all FDA-cleared, non-modified, moderate- and high-complexity diagnostic tests must be verified for accuracy, precision reference range, and reportable range.1,2 Accuracy Accuracy is typically verified by testing a collection of known clinical/contrived samples and commercially available controls. The number of positive and negative samples needed for each target is determined by the laboratory. When using samples previously categorized by another method, discrepancies can occur due to several factors (e.g., primer design, limit of detection). In the example verification that follows, we chose to incorporate a collection of contrived samples and third-party controls for the accuracy study. Precision Precision studies are intended to verify that expected results are obtained reproducibly from the same sample.
policy_evidence.title: Liaison MDx Verification Guide - Draft

concentration if applicable, date prepared, person preparing the reagent, storage condition, and expiration date. 4. Reagent Verification and Lot-to-Lot / Shipment-to-Shipment Control
4.1 All new reagents, new reagent lots, and new shipments of reagents that may affect examination quality shall
be verified for performance before use in patient testing. 4.2 Verification may include side-by-side comparison of old lot versus new lot using identical samples, retesting
of previously tested samples using the new reagent, testing of known positive and negative samples, or other
assay-specific performance checks. 4.3 Verification results shall meet acceptance criteria established in the assay-specific SOP or manufacturer QC
instructions before release for use. 4.4 For non-waived qualitative testing, at least one positive and one negative clinical sample shall be used for
verification unless otherwise specified by assay-specific SOP. The new reagent is acceptable only when the
testing results are in 100% agreement with the known results.

checks.evidence_of_compliance:

checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. The laboratory utilizes qualitative assays, such as the TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit and the Multi-Drug Test Cup (Urine), which rely on defined cut-off values for result interpretation. While the laboratory maintains general validation documentation (G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program.pdf), there is no evidence provided to demonstrate that the laboratory has specifically validated a modified cut-off value if one is utilized. The search summary confirms that records of cut-off validation for modified values were not found in the provided documentation. To meet the requirement, the laboratory must provide specific validation data confirming the performance characteristics of any modified cut-off values used in clinical testing.
corrective_actions: 1) Conduct and document a formal validation study for any assay where the manufacturer's cut-off value has been modified.
2) Ensure validation records include sufficient sample numbers and performance metrics to support the new cut-off value before clinical implementation.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.64975**: For qualitative tests, cut-off values must be established during test validation using a sufficient number of samples before the test is put into service. The TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Instructions for Use (Pub. No. MAN0028576 B) specifies that a result is positive when two or more of the three SARS-CoV-2 targets are positive and the internal control is valid. The software uses Ct values to interpret results, as detailed in Appendix A of the instructions. The Multi-Drug Test Cup (Urine) Package Insert AP indicates that a positive result means the drug concentration is above the designated cut-off for a specific drug, and a negative result means it is below the detectable level. Records of cut-off validation when different cut-off values are utilized were not found in the provided documents.

checks.requirement: The laboratory calibrates each test system as defined and reviews the calibration records for acceptability.
checks.subject: Calibration Procedure
checks.note: NOTE: Calibration of FDA-cleared/approved methods must be performed following the manufacturer's instructions, at minimum, including the number, type, and concentration of calibration materials, frequency of calibration, and criteria for acceptable performance. Calibration procedures are typically specified in the manufacturer's instructions but may also be established by the laboratory.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a policy framework for calibration via 'F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program' and 'A1002.0V2-Quality Planning Process', which mandate adherence to manufacturer instructions. However, while the laboratory utilizes 'K1003.3.4_Data Collection Form for Calibration and Calibration Verification' to gather data, the provided documentation explicitly states that these forms are 'NOT your QA review.' No evidence of the completed, signed-off QA reviews for calibration records was provided to verify that the laboratory is performing the required review for acceptability as mandated by MIC.65100. Furthermore, calibration verification for specific systems (ABI Quant DX, ID3, and CTL) is currently on hold, requiring documentation of the justification and impact assessment for these deferred activities.
corrective_actions: 1) Perform and document the required QA review for all calibration data collection forms to ensure acceptability criteria are met.
2) Maintain a formal record of the justification and clinical impact assessment for the deferred calibration verification of the ABI Quant DX, ID3, and CTL systems.
cited_documents: K1003.3.4_Data Collection Form for Calibration and Calibration Verification.docx
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65100**: The laboratory's Equipment Calibration Program, F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program, outlines the objective to ensure instrument calibration, calibration verification, or function checks to maintain analytical continuity and accuracy. Calibration is defined as establishing the relationship between reagent system/instrument response and corresponding concentration/activity values. Calibration verification confirms the validity of current calibration settings for a test system. The laboratory must perform equipment calibration at defined intervals following manufacturer instructions. Calibration can be performed by the manufacturer, a certified third-party, or qualified laboratory staff. A calibration log is required for each equipment/instrument to document schedules and results. The lab general supervisor is responsible for the calibration schedule. Calibration verification must be performed using calibration materials in the same manner as patient samples to confirm stability over a six-month interval. The Analytical Measurement Range (AMR) must also be verified at least every six months. Calibration verification for ABI Quant DX, ID3, and CTL is currently on hold due to clinical trials being on hold. However, the laboratory schedules calibrations in advance to ensure completion.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Equipment Calibration Program XYZ Lab Document Name
XYZ Lab Document Number F1002.0 Version # 6 Author： XYZ Lab Date of Inception: 11/02/2020 Start Date of Current Version：04/26/2026 Page 1 of 3 1. Objective
This document is to ensure laboratory instrument/equipment calibration, calibration verification or function check so as to
maintain on-going analytical continuity and accuracy for both quantitative and qualitative test systems. Definition:
1.1 Calibration: calibration is a set of operations that establish, under specified conditions, the relationship between
reagent system/instrument response and the corresponding concentration/activity values of an analyte. 1.2 Calibration verification/function check: calibration verification denotes the process of confirming that the current
calibration settings for each analyte remain valid for a test system. 2. Process and Requirements
2.1 The laboratory must perform equipment/instrument calibration at a defined interval following the manufacturer's
instruction. 2.2 Calibration can be performed by the equipment manufacturer, a certified third-party provider or trained and qualified
laboratory staff. 2.3 The laboratory shall have a calibration log for each equipment/instrument to document the calibration schedule and
result. 2.4 The lab general supervisor or designee shall be in charge of the calibration schedule to ensure all
equipment/instruments are calibrated when it is first placed in service and thereafter on schedule.
policy_evidence.title: F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program

policy_evidence.snippet:
2.13 Equipment, reagents, and materials:
2.13.1 Equipment: all equipment used for testing shall be calibrated and maintained according to manufacturer's
instruction. The preventive maintenance and function check activities of the testing equipment shall be
documented in specific forms. The documentation shall be reviewed monthly by the lab director or designee.
2.13.2 Reagents and materials: all reagents and materials used for testing shall be tested with control samples
prior to using for patient sample testing. All reagents and materials shall be stored and used as instructed by
their manufacturers. No reagents and materials shall be used when they have exceeded their expiration date,
have deteriorated or are of substandard quality. A reagents and materials QC form will be used to document the
quality control of the reagents and materials from different lots and shipments. The reagents and materials QC
form shall be reviewed monthly by lab director or designee. 2.14 Quality control procedures: each batch of the test shall include control samples to ensure the testing
procedure is correctly performed and the results obtained are accurate. The control sample testing results shall
be documented and reviewed to ensure the test result accuracy prior to releasing the test results for reporting. In case the control samples failed to produce the expected results, investigation shall be performed to identify
the root cause, and the corresponding corrective action shall be taken to fix the problem.

Equipment Calibration Program XYZ Lab Document Name
XYZ Lab Document Number F1002.0 Version # 6 Author： XYZ Lab Date of Inception: 11/02/2020 Start Date of Current Version：04/26/2026 Page 1 of 3 1. Objective
This document is to ensure laboratory instrument/equipment calibration, calibration verification or function check so as to
maintain on-going analytical continuity and accuracy for both quantitative and qualitative test systems. Definition:
1.1 Calibration: calibration is a set of operations that establish, under specified conditions, the relationship between
reagent system/instrument response and the corresponding concentration/activity values of an analyte. 1.2 Calibration verification/function check: calibration verification denotes the process of confirming that the current
calibration settings for each analyte remain valid for a test system. 2. Process and Requirements
2.1 The laboratory must perform equipment/instrument calibration at a defined interval following the manufacturer's
instruction. 2.2 Calibration can be performed by the equipment manufacturer, a certified third-party provider or trained and qualified
laboratory staff. 2.3 The laboratory shall have a calibration log for each equipment/instrument to document the calibration schedule and
result. 2.4 The lab general supervisor or designee shall be in charge of the calibration schedule to ensure all
equipment/instruments are calibrated when it is first placed in service and thereafter on schedule.
results.title: F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program

2.13 Equipment, reagents, and materials:
2.13.1 Equipment: all equipment used for testing shall be calibrated and maintained according to manufacturer's
instruction. The preventive maintenance and function check activities of the testing equipment shall be
documented in specific forms. The documentation shall be reviewed monthly by the lab director or designee.
2.13.2 Reagents and materials: all reagents and materials used for testing shall be tested with control samples
prior to using for patient sample testing. All reagents and materials shall be stored and used as instructed by
their manufacturers. No reagents and materials shall be used when they have exceeded their expiration date,
have deteriorated or are of substandard quality. A reagents and materials QC form will be used to document the
quality control of the reagents and materials from different lots and shipments. The reagents and materials QC
form shall be reviewed monthly by lab director or designee. 2.14 Quality control procedures: each batch of the test shall include control samples to ensure the testing
procedure is correctly performed and the results obtained are accurate. The control sample testing results shall
be documented and reviewed to ensure the test result accuracy prior to releasing the test results for reporting. In case the control samples failed to produce the expected results, investigation shall be performed to identify
the root cause, and the corresponding corrective action shall be taken to fix the problem.

Test Validation and Verification Program Document Name
Document Number G1004.0 Version 3 Author： Keqin Gregg Date of Composition: 11/02/2020 Date of Execution：05/16/2025 Page 1 of 5 Objective
Provide plans for establishing and validating/verifying lab assay method performance specifications. For some assays
with special requirements by accreditation or regulatory agents or other national or international standards, the specific
requirements should be noted in its specific policy
Programs
1. Testing Method
1.1 The laboratory must verify or establish analytical and clinical performance characteristics for each test. Laboratories
may use information from manufacturers, published literature, or studies performed in other laboratories, but should
verify such outside information, whenever practical. 1.2 For unmodified FDA-cleared/approved test, the scope of validation is to confirm or verify with objective evidence that
the stated analytical and clinical performance characteristics are met in the particular laboratory setting, this usually need
only verify accuracy, precision, and reportable range. Manufacturer recommended method shall be followed if there is
any.

policy_evidence.snippet: If an internal quality control process (e.g., electronic/procedural/built-in) is used instead of external control material to meet daily quality control requirements, the laboratory must have an individualized quality control plan (IQCP) approved by the laboratory director. This laboratory has been using the Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II molecular test system to detect influenza A, influenza B and RSV viruses from 11/10/2022 to 2/28/2023. Although the assay was verified in June 2022, it was not performed for clinical sample testing until 6 months later. The Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II is an integrated molecular analysis system with nucleic acid extraction and analysis all on the same well/space which is carried in an 8 sample disc. Users will just load individual specimen and reagent to the disc and the test will take care of itself. There is a built-in internal control for each sample to check the assay performance. Therefore, the external controls are not required by the  manufacturer. We started the assay by running one external positive (recommended by and separately purchased from the assay manufacturer) and one negative control (confirmed negative swab sample from past) for CLIA/CAP requirement daily when there is a test and for each new shipment of the reagent.

The laboratory has established a framework for calibration and calibration verification through G1005.0-Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025 and F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program.pdf, which mandate the use of matrix-appropriate materials. The K1003.3.4_Data Collection Form for Calibration and Calibration Verification provides a mechanism to document these activities. However, while the policy and forms are present, the current evidence set lacks specific, completed calibration verification records for LDTs or modified FDA-cleared tests to confirm that the matrix-equivalence and range requirements (as specified in the MIC.65130 note) are consistently met in practice. The laboratory must demonstrate that these procedures are being executed for all relevant test systems.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65130**: Calibration verification must be performed using calibration materials in the same manner as patient samples. These materials should have matrix characteristics and target values appropriate for the method. Acceptable materials include proficiency testing survey materials, previously tested unaltered patient specimens, primary or secondary standards, reference materials, and calibrators used for the analytic measurement system. Routine control materials are generally not suitable for calibration verification unless specifically designated by the manufacturer, and if used, the lot number for calibration should differ from the QC lot number whenever possible. For Analytical Measurement Range (AMR) verification, materials must be near the upper and lower limits of the AMR. The G1005.0-Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025 document specifies that AMR verification requires matrix-appropriate materials covering the low, mid, and high concentration ranges. The G1013.0_Laboratory_Reagent_Policy outlines requirements for reagent verification, including lot-to-lot comparisons and performance checks for new reagents or lots before use in patient testing. The Data Collection Form for Calibration and Calibration Verification indicates that appropriate materials and methods are used for calibration verification, as advised by the manufacturer, with additional lab alterations recorded in each calibration verification file.

4.1 All new reagents, new reagent lots, and new shipments of reagents that may affect examination quality shall
be verified for performance before use in patient testing. 4.2 Verification may include side-by-side comparison of old lot versus new lot using identical samples, retesting
of previously tested samples using the new reagent, testing of known positive and negative samples, or other
assay-specific performance checks. 4.3 Verification results shall meet acceptance criteria established in the assay-specific SOP or manufacturer QC
instructions before release for use. 4.4 For non-waived qualitative testing, at least one positive and one negative clinical sample shall be used for
verification unless otherwise specified by assay-specific SOP. The new reagent is acceptable only when the
testing results are in 100% agreement with the known results.

checks.requirement: The quality of all calibration materials used for laboratory-developed tests is evaluated and recorded.
checks.subject: Calibration Materials - Laboratory Developed Tests
checks.note: NOTE: Commercial standards used to prepare calibrators require certificates of analysis. The laboratory must evaluate the accuracy of a new lot of calibrators by checking the new lot against the current lot.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has provided evidence of equipment calibration compliance via ISO/IEC 17025:2017 certificates (Calibration_591304, 588926, 591293, 557077) and policy F1002.0V6. However, these documents pertain to instrument calibration (thermometric standards) rather than the specific requirement for Laboratory Developed Test (LDT) calibration materials. The requirement mandates that the laboratory evaluate and record the quality of LDT calibration materials, specifically checking new lots against current lots and maintaining certificates of analysis for commercial standards. While the search summary mentions a 'Data Collection Form for Calibration and Calibration Verification,' this specific record was not provided for review. The laboratory must demonstrate the process for lot-to-lot verification of LDT calibrators to meet the specific criteria of MIC.65140.
corrective_actions: 1) Implement and document a lot-to-lot verification procedure for all LDT calibrators, ensuring new lots are checked against current lots as required by the MIC.65140 note.
2) Maintain and archive Certificates of Analysis for all commercial standards used in LDT calibrator preparation.
3) Ensure the 'Data Collection Form for Calibration and Calibration Verification' is completed and signed for all LDT calibration material lot changes.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65140**: The laboratory evaluates and records the quality of calibration materials for laboratory-developed tests, requiring calibration verification every six months using materials processed like patient samples, such as proficiency testing surveys, unaltered patient specimens, or primary standards [1] [1] [1] [1]. Routine control materials are generally unsuitable unless manufacturer-designated, and when used, should ideally differ in lot number from daily QC. All reagents and materials are stored per manufacturer instructions and tested with controls prior to patient use, with lot-specific quality control documented on forms reviewed monthly by the lab director. Lab-developed controls require five independent, concordant tests before implementation. Compliance with ISO/IEC 17025:2017 is evidenced by Certificates of Calibration, while the Data Collection Form for Calibration and Calibration Verification ensures that all calibration activities are scheduled and completed in a timely manner.

2.9 The laboratory should have an appropriate thermometric standard device of known accuracy, which is certified to
meet NIST standards or traceable to NIST standards. 2.9.1 Thermometric standard devices must be recalibrated, recertified, or replaced prior to the date of expiration of the
guarantee of calibration or they are subject to requirements for non-certified thermometers.
2.9.2 All non-certified thermometers should be verified using a certified calibrated thermometer annually. 2.9.3 Thermometers without defined expiration dates must be treated as non-certified thermometers after two years
from the certificate date. 2.9.4 Thermometers should be periodically evaluated for damage (eg, separation of columns). Thermometers with
obvious damage must be rechecked before continued use. 2.10 The temperature for all temperature sensitive instruments/equipment shall be monitored at use and thermometers
be calibrated at least annually. 2.11 For centrifuges used to separate different components, the speed shall be tested and calibrated at least once every
year. 2.12 The calibration and calibration verification procedure for micropipettor is as follows： The accuracy and precision of a newly purchased pipettor shall be verified before the manufacture calibration is due. There is no need for recalibration if verification passes. The accuracy and precision of old pipettors shall be verified once every six months.If the verification passes, there
is no need for re-calibration.
policy_evidence.title: F1002.0V6-Equipment Calibration Program

checks.requirement: Criteria for the frequency and acceptability of recalibration or calibration verification are defined and followed.
checks.subject: Recalibration/Calibration Verification Criteria
checks.note:
NOTE: Laboratories must either recalibrate or perform calibration verification at least every six months and if any of the following occur: 
  
  1. At changes of reagent lots unless the laboratory can demonstrate that the use of different lots does not affect the accuracy of patient/client results 
  2. If QC shows an unusual trend or shift or is outside acceptable limits and the system cannot be corrected to bring control values into the acceptable range 
  3. After major preventive maintenance or change of a critical instrument component 
  4. When recommended by the manufacturer 
  
  Single use devices, and other test devices that do not allow user calibration, do not require calibration verification.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of calibration verification at defined frequency

Evidence of compliance is present in the form of established procedures and data collection templates, but the actual performance records for all equipment are not fully verified as compliant due to the identified lapse.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Suitable materials
for AMR verification include the following：
2.7.1 Linearity material of appropriate matrix
2.7.2 Previously tested patient specimens，that may be altered by admixture with other specimens, dilution, spiking in
known amounts of an analyte, or other techniques. 2.7.3 Primary or secondary standards or reference materials with matrix characteristics and target values appropriate for
the method. 2.7.4 Control materials, if they adequately span the AMR and have method specific target values. If control material is
used for calibration or calibration verification, the lot number for calibration should be different than the lot number used
for QC, whenever possible. 2.8 When verifying the AMR, it is required that materials used are near the upper and lower limits of the AMR. Factors to
consider in verifying the AMR are the expected analytic imprecision near the limits, the clinical impact of errors near the
limits, and the availability of test specimens near the limits. It may be difficult to obtain specimens with values near the
limits for some analytes. In such cases, reasonable procedures should be adopted based on available specimen materials. The method manufacturer's instructions for verifying the AMR should be followed, when available. The Laboratory
Director must define limits for accepting or rejecting verification tests of the AMR:
2.9 If AMR verification fails, the affected method shall be taken offline.

policy_evidence.snippet:
2.9 The laboratory should have an appropriate thermometric standard device of known accuracy, which is certified to
meet NIST standards or traceable to NIST standards. 2.9.1 Thermometric standard devices must be recalibrated, recertified, or replaced prior to the date of expiration of the
guarantee of calibration or they are subject to requirements for non-certified thermometers.
2.9.2 All non-certified thermometers should be verified using a certified calibrated thermometer annually. 2.9.3 Thermometers without defined expiration dates must be treated as non-certified thermometers after two years
from the certificate date. 2.9.4 Thermometers should be periodically evaluated for damage (eg, separation of columns). Thermometers with
obvious damage must be rechecked before continued use. 2.10 The temperature for all temperature sensitive instruments/equipment shall be monitored at use and thermometers
be calibrated at least annually. 2.11 For centrifuges used to separate different components, the speed shall be tested and calibrated at least once every
year. 2.12 The calibration and calibration verification procedure for micropipettor is as follows： The accuracy and precision of a newly purchased pipettor shall be verified before the manufacture calibration is due. There is no need for recalibration if verification passes. The accuracy and precision of old pipettors shall be verified once every six months.If the verification passes, there
is no need for re-calibration.

checks.requirement: Verification of the analytical measurement range (AMR) is performed at least every six months and following defined criteria. Records are retained.
checks.subject: AMR Verification
checks.note:
NOTE: The AMR must be verified at least every six months after a method is initially placed in service and if any of the following occur: 
  
  1. At changes of reagent lots unless the laboratory can demonstrate that the use of different lots does not affect the accuracy of patient/client results, and the range used to report patient/client test data 
  2. If QC shows an unusual trend or shift or is outside acceptable limits, and the system cannot be corrected to bring control values into the acceptable range 
  3. After major preventive maintenance or change of a critical instrument component 
  4. When recommended by the manufacturer 
  
  It is not necessary to independently verify the AMR if the calibration of an assay includes calibrators that span the full range of the AMR, with low, midpoint and high values represented (ie, three points) and if the system is calibrated at least every six months. A one-point or two-point calibration does not include all of the necessary points to verify the AMR. 
  
  AMR verification is not required for calculated test results as long as the individual results contributing to the calculation have AMR verification.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of AMR verification, as required, at least every six months
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a robust policy framework for AMR verification, specifically through G1005.0-Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025 and G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program. These documents correctly define the requirements for materials and the frequency of verification. However, while the policy and the data collection template (K1003.3.4_Data Collection Form) are present, the actual completed records of AMR verification performed within the last six months were not provided for review. Compliance with MIC.65160 requires both the existence of a policy and the availability of documented evidence that the verification was performed at the required intervals or triggered by the specified events (reagent lots, maintenance, etc.).
corrective_actions: 1) Compile and organize all completed AMR verification records for the past six months for all active methods.
2) Perform a retrospective audit of instrument maintenance and reagent lot change logs to ensure AMR verification was triggered and documented as required by G1005.0.
3) Ensure all future AMR verification data is captured using the K1003.3.4 form and filed for immediate retrieval during inspections.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65160**: The Analytical Measurement Range (AMR) must be verified at least every six months after a method is initially placed in service. This verification is also required following changes in reagent lots (unless the laboratory demonstrates no impact on patient results), if QC shows unusual trends or shifts, after major preventive maintenance or critical instrument component changes, or when recommended by the manufacturer. Records of AMR verification must be available. Suitable materials for AMR verification include linearity material, previously tested patient specimens, primary or secondary standards, or control materials that adequately span the AMR. The materials used must have matrix characteristics appropriate for the method and include specimens near the low, midpoint, and high values of the AMR. If AMR verification fails, the affected method must be taken offline. It is not necessary to independently verify the AMR if calibration includes calibrators spanning the full range (low, midpoint, high values) and the system is calibrated at least every six months. A one-point or two-point calibration is insufficient for AMR verification. The G1005.0-Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025 document outlines these guidelines.

checks.requirement: Verification of the analytical measurement range (AMR) is performed with matrix-appropriate materials, which at a minimum, include low, mid and high range of the AMR, and appropriate acceptance criteria are defined.
checks.subject: AMR Verification Materials
checks.note:
NOTE: The matrix of the sample (ie, the environment in which the sample is suspended or dissolved) may influence the measurement of the analyte. In many cases, the method manufacturer will recommend suitable materials. Other suitable materials for AMR verification include the following: 
  
  1. Linearity material of appropriate matrix, eg, CAP CVL Survey-based or other suitable linearity verification material 
  2. Previously tested patient/client specimens, that may be altered by admixture with other specimens, dilution, spiking in known amounts of an analyte, or other technique 
  3. Primary or secondary standards or reference materials with matrix characteristics and target values appropriate for the method 
  4. Patient samples that have reference method assigned target values. 
  5. Control materials, if they adequately span the AMR and have method specific target values 
  
  Factors to consider in verifying the AMR are the expected analytic imprecision near the limits, the clinical impact of errors near the limits, and the availability of test specimens near the limits. It may be difficult to obtain specimens with values near the limits for some analytes. In such cases, reasonable procedures should be adopted based on available specimen materials. The closeness of sample concentrations and activities to the upper and lower limits of the AMR are defined at the laboratory director's discretion.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of AMR verification
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory has established a formal framework for AMR verification as documented in G1005.0-Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025. This policy explicitly requires the use of matrix-appropriate materials covering the low, mid, and high ranges of the AMR and mandates the definition of acceptance criteria. Evidence of implementation is provided in the XYZG1004.2204_XYZ Liaison MDx Verification Report-Final, which details the methodology, materials, and results of the assay verification process. The laboratory's approach aligns with the requirements of MIC.65170 by utilizing validated materials and maintaining comprehensive records of the verification activities.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice. Ensure all future AMR verifications are documented in accordance with G1005.0 and the established acceptance criteria defined in the XYZ Liaison MDx Verification-Plan.
cited_documents: G1005.0-Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65170**: The G1005.0-Analytical Measurement Range Calibration and Verification Plan 2025, authored by Wenli Zhou on 04/05/2021, mandates that AMR verification for quantitative and qualitative systems utilize matrix-appropriate materials covering low, mid, and high ranges with defined acceptance criteria. Suitable materials include linearity sets, altered patient specimens, reference standards, or control materials, provided they span the AMR and possess method-specific target values. When using controls for calibration, lot numbers should ideally differ from those used for routine QC. The Laboratory Director must establish acceptance limits, and any verification failure requires the affected method to be taken offline. Records of these activities must be maintained, while specific assay verification methods and materials, including positive and negative samples, are detailed in the XYZG1004.2204_XYZ Liaison MDx Verification Report-Final and XYZ Liaison MDx Verification-Plan documents.

checks.requirement: The laboratory performs controls for molecular-based quantitative and qualitative tests each day of testing, or more frequently if specified in manufacturer's instructions or the CAP Checklist, and when changes occur that may impact patient results.
checks.subject: Daily QC - Molecular-based Testing - Nonwaived Tests
checks.note:
NOTE: The laboratory must define the number and type of quality control used and the frequency of testing in its quality control procedures. Control testing is not required on days when patient testing is not performed. 
  
  Controls must be run prior to resuming patient testing when changes occur that may impact patient results, including after a change of analytically critical reagents, major preventive maintenance, change of a critical instrument component, or with software changes, as appropriate. 
  
  Daily quality control must be run as follows: 
  
  * Quantitative tests - three controls at least daily, including a negative control, a low-positive control and a high-positive control, except where a specific exception is given in this checklist 
  * Qualitative tests - a positive and negative control at least daily 
  
  Controls should verify assay performance at relevant decision points. The selection of these points may be based on clinical or analytical criteria. 
  
  If an internal quality control process (eg, electronic/procedural/built-in) is used instead of an external control material to meet daily quality control requirements, the laboratory must have an individualized quality control plan (IQCP) approved by the laboratory director defining the control process, including the frequency and use of external and internal controls. At a minimum, external control materials must be analyzed with new lots and shipments of reagents or more frequently if indicated in the manufacturer's instructions. Please refer to the IQCP section of the All Common Checklist for the eligibility of tests for IQCP and requirements for implementation and ongoing monitoring of an IQCP. 
  
  Controls must assess adequacy of extraction and amplification, eg, positive and negative controls that go through the entire testing process. 
  
  * Laboratories performing tests using an IQCP may define their own quality control procedures to monitor the extraction and amplification phases based on the risk assessment performed by the laboratory and the manufacturer's instructions. 
  * If an IQCP is not in place that monitors the extraction and amplification processes, the following must be followed: 
  
  * An extraction control must be used for each run with the positive control(s). 
  * If the samples from an extraction batch are tested over multiple amplification runs, each amplification run must have its own amplification control. A single extraction control need only be tested in one of the amplification runs. 
  * If samples from multiple extraction batches are tested in a single amplification run, each extraction batch needs an extraction control. All extraction controls must be tested in a single amplification run. A single amplification control is sufficient.

checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory policy (G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan) correctly defines the frequency and type of controls for qualitative and quantitative tests. While the lab currently performs daily external positive and negative controls for the Simplexa Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II Assay (XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa.docx), the lab has proposed a modification to run a negative control only when no negative patient samples are included in the daily batch. This proposed change lacks documentation of a formal risk assessment or an approved IQCP amendment to ensure compliance with the requirement that controls must assess the adequacy of extraction and amplification. Furthermore, while policy is established, specific daily QC logs demonstrating consistent adherence to these requirements across all molecular platforms were not verified during this review.
corrective_actions: 1) Formalize and document the risk assessment for the proposed negative control frequency change, ensuring it meets the extraction and amplification monitoring requirements of MIC.65200.
2) Obtain Laboratory Director approval for any modifications to the existing IQCP.
3) Compile and maintain a continuous log of daily QC results for all molecular-based tests to demonstrate ongoing compliance.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65200**: The XYZ Lab's G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan mandates daily positive and negative controls for qualitative tests and three controls—negative, low-positive, and high-positive—for quantitative tests, unless exceptions apply. Controls are required daily, or more frequently per manufacturer or CAP guidelines, and following changes to reagents, maintenance, or software. When internal quality control processes replace external materials, an Individualized Quality Control Plan (IQCP) approved by the laboratory director is required. The XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa for the Simplexa Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II Assay utilizes built-in internal controls, though the lab currently runs one external positive and one negative control daily to meet CLIA/CAP requirements and verify new reagent shipments. The lab has proposed modifying this protocol to run a negative control only when no negative patient samples are included in the daily batch.

IQCP An Individualized Quality Control Plan (IQCP) is a framework for laboratories to design their own quality control plans.3 By default, positive and negative controls must be run for moderate- and high-complexity tests daily. In many cases, laboratories conduct an IQCP study to reduce the frequency of running positive and negative controls. The frequency at which the laboratory plans to run controls is determined by the laboratory. This example IQCP verification procedure assumes that the laboratory wishes to perform QC every 14 days, which would require the laboratory to run one positive control and one negative control daily for 14 days. Reference and Reportable Range Reference and reportable ranges are also required to be established during the process of assay verification. Xpert® Xpress SARS-CoV-2/Flu/RSV Xpert® Xpress SARS-CoV-2/Flu/RSV 29 302-4419, Rev. C January 2021 Figure 33. Test Result Screen (Example) 17 Quality Control 17.1 Internal Controls
Each cartridge includes a Sample Processing Control (SPC) and Probe Check Control (PCC). Sample Processing Control (SPC) – Ensures that the sample was processed correctly. The SPC verifies that sample processing
is adequate. Additionally, this control detects sample-associated inhibition of the real-time PCR assay, ensures that the PCR
reaction conditions (temperature and time) are appropriate for the amplification reaction, and that the PCR reagents are
functional. The SPC should be positive in a negative sample and can be negative or positive in a positive sample. The SPC
passes if it meets the validated acceptance criteria. Probe Check Control (PCC) – Before the start of the PCR reaction, the GeneXpert System measures the fluorescence signal
from the probes to monitor bead rehydration, reaction tube filling, probe integrity, and dye stability. The PCC passes if it meets
the validated acceptance criteria. 17.2 External Controls
External controls should be used in accordance with local, state, and federal accrediting organizations as applicable.

policy_evidence.snippet:
1.1.3 For non-waived test, daily quality control must be run as follows: Qualitative tests - a positive and negative control
at least daily. Quantitative tests - three controls at least daily, including a negative control, a low-positive control and a
high-positive control, except where a specific exception is given in this checklist.
1.1.4 If an internal quality control process (eg, electronic/procedural/built-in) is used instead of an external control
material to meet daily quality control requirements, the laboratory must have an individualized quality control plan
(IQCP) approved by the laboratory director defining the control process, including the frequency and use of external and
internal controls. At a minimum, external control materials must be analyzed with new lots and shipments of reagents or
more frequently if indicated in the manufacturer's instructions. 1.2 Whenever possible, commercially prepared quality control materials with known values shall be used as quality
control samples. Manufacturer’s instructions for QC sample preparation and storage shall be followed without alteration. 1.3 Quality control samples shall be run in the same manner as patient samples following the manufacturer guidelines and
SOPs. The quality control samples shall meet the following criteria: It reacts to the examining system in a similar manner to patient samples. The concentration of the control is within the same range as the patient samples.

policy_evidence.snippet:
1.3.2.1 Accuracy: Accuracy can be assessed using well-characterized reference material together with appropriate
biological matrix or by comparison to another valid test method, such as through specimen exchange， and expressed as
percentage of concordance. For quantitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples with analyte concentrations distributed across
the analytical measurement range should be used. Proportionate mixtures of samples may be used to supplement the study
population. For qualitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples, including positive, negative, and low-positive samples with
concentrations near the lower level of detection should be used; equivocal samples should not be used. For certain
methods that test multiple analytes (eg, next-generation sequencing, FISH, HPLC, GC-MS, MALDI-TOF, etc.), analytic
accuracy may be established for each method (not necessarily each analyte), as appropriate.

checks.requirement: Acceptability limits are defined for all control procedures, control materials, and standards.
checks.subject: Control and Standard Acceptability Limits
checks.note: NOTE: These controls must be appropriate for the range of sensitivities tested and should, ideally, focus on result ranges that are near clinical decision points.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory has established defined acceptability limits for control procedures and standards as required by MIC.65230. Documentation provided in G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan mandates that all SOPs specify control types, frequencies, and acceptance parameters. Specific quantitative and non-quantitative accuracy and CV limits are defined in SOP.XYZSKG-006.V3 (referenced in search_summary), and process control monitoring is supported by Westgard rules detailed in 2_G1009.0_Westgard rules for Process Control Monitoring.docx. The laboratory also utilizes a Risk Acceptability Matrix for molecular testing as documented in XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa.docx. The current documentation framework satisfies the requirement to focus on clinical decision points and appropriate sensitivity ranges.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of monitoring control performance against defined limits in G1003.0V5 and SOP.XYZSKG-006.V3.
cited_documents: G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65230**: The Laboratory Director must establish acceptance criteria for control procedures, standards, and Analytical Measurement Range (AMR) verification, with failed methods removed from service. Per SOP.XYZSKG-006.V3, non-quantitative curve points require ±20% accuracy and ≤20% CV, while quantitative points require ±25% accuracy and ≤25% CV; additionally, at least two-thirds of quality control samples must maintain ±20% accuracy and ≤20% CV. The G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan mandates that all SOPs specify control types, frequencies, acceptance parameters, and corrective actions. These protocols are further supported by Westgard Rules, such as 1-2s and 1-3s, which trigger corrective actions for out-of-range results. Furthermore, the XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa document utilizes a Risk Acceptability Matrix to define acceptable risk levels based on error frequency and potential patient harm.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Suitable materials
for AMR verification include the following：
2.7.1 Linearity material of appropriate matrix
2.7.2 Previously tested patient specimens，that may be altered by admixture with other specimens, dilution, spiking in
known amounts of an analyte, or other techniques. 2.7.3 Primary or secondary standards or reference materials with matrix characteristics and target values appropriate for
the method. 2.7.4 Control materials, if they adequately span the AMR and have method specific target values. If control material is
used for calibration or calibration verification, the lot number for calibration should be different than the lot number used
for QC, whenever possible. 2.8 When verifying the AMR, it is required that materials used are near the upper and lower limits of the AMR. Factors to
consider in verifying the AMR are the expected analytic imprecision near the limits, the clinical impact of errors near the
limits, and the availability of test specimens near the limits. It may be difficult to obtain specimens with values near the
limits for some analytes. In such cases, reasonable procedures should be adopted based on available specimen materials. The method manufacturer's instructions for verifying the AMR should be followed, when available. The Laboratory
Director must define limits for accepting or rejecting verification tests of the AMR:
2.9 If AMR verification fails, the affected method shall be taken offline.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Laboratory Test Standard Operating Procedure Guide XYZ Lab Document Name
XYZ Lab Document Number G1002.0 Version 2 Author：XYZ Laboratory Date of Composition: 11/10/2020 Date of the Current Version：11/01/2024 Page 1 of 2 1. Objective
Provide a guidance for constructing laboratory pre-analytical, analytical and postanalytical operating procedure. 2. Testing Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) Requirements
The testing SOP should consist of the following sections 1) Principle and clinical significance of the test 2) Requirements for patient preparation; specimen collection, labeling, storage, preservation, transportation, processing, and referral; and criteria for specimen acceptability and rejection 3) Preparation of slides, solutions, calibrators, controls, reagents, stains, and other materials used in testing. 4) Calibration and calibration verification procedures (procedure calibration). 5) Step-by-step performance of the procedure, including test calculations and interpretation of results 6) Analytic measurement range for test results for the test system, if applicable. 7) Control procedures 8) Corrective action to take when calibration or control results fail to meet the laboratory's criteria for acceptability. 9) Limitations in the test methodology, including interfering substances 10) Reference intervals (normal values) 11) Imminently life-threatening (critical) test results 12) Pertinent literature references
policy_evidence.title: G1002.0V2-Laboratory Test Standard Operating Procedure Guide

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Operation/D-Personnel/2_Continue Education Materials/2023-learning materials and quizzes/2_G1009.0_Westgard rules for Process Control Monitoring.docx
policy_evidence.snippet: Approved by Lab Director:	                                            Date: 01/28/2023 Purpose To explain the Westgard Rule Control Rules of quality control in detail. Rule 1-2s Definition: The 1-2s Control Rule indicates one control result has exceeded the established mean +/- 2SD range. This is a “warning rule,” which does not indicate an “out-of-control” condition, but is intended to initiate further testing. Interpretation: If no other control rule is violated, then the warning is attributed to normal random error. Patient results are acceptable Corrective Action: No corrective action is required. However, the “warning” suggests a system error may be in the development. A comprehensive check of the routine maintenance schedule and review of the quality control ampoule handling and sampling technique is recommended. Rule 1-3s Definition: The 1-3s Control Rule indicates one control result has exceeded the established mean +/- 3SD range. This is a “rejection rule,” which is sensitive to random error. Interpretation: Excessive random error exists. The analyzer is “out-of-control.” Patient results cannot be released before the problem is identified and may be re-analyzed after corrective action has solved the problem. Corrective Action: Rerun the quality control level that is in question, emphasizing proper technique.
policy_evidence.title: 2_G1009.0_Westgard rules for Process Control Monitoring

policy_evidence.snippet:
Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan XYZ Lab Document Name
XYZ Lab Document Number G1003.0 Version # 5 Author： XYZ Lab Date of Inception: 11/02/2020 Date of Execution of this version：04/26/2026 Page 1 of 4 Objective
Define the quality control acceptability of the testing system to guarantee accurate testing results, thereby providing high
quality care for the customer. Quality Control Plan
Contents: 1. Control Samples and Utilization 2. Reagent Control (see G1013.0) 3. Consumable Control 1. Control Samples and Utilization
1.1 . All lab standard operating procedures (SOP) should clearly state the type and frequency of quality control samples used, the quality control accepting parameters and corrective actions based on quality control data. 1.1.1 For non-waived test, the laboratory should perform controls for molecular-based quantitative and qualitative tests
each day of testing, or more frequently if specified in manufacturer's instructions or the CAP Checklist, and when changes
occur that may impact patient results. 1.1.2 Controls must be run prior to resuming patient testing when changes occur that may impact patient results, including
after a change of analytically critical reagents, major preventive maintenance, change of a critical instrument component,
or with software changes, as appropriate.
policy_evidence.title: G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan

checks.subject: QC Statistics
checks.note: NOTE: The laboratory must use statistical methods such as calculating SD and CV monthly to evaluate variance in numeric QC data.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory maintains a defined process for monthly statistical analysis of quantitative QC data as required by MIC.65240. Policy G1003.0V5 (Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan) mandates the calculation of SD and CV to evaluate analytic imprecision and monitor trends. The search summary confirms that the Technical Supervisor monitors these metrics for all active assays and that the IQCP Quality Assessment_202503 verifies the timely and effective execution of this monthly review process. While K1003.3.6 provides the data collection form, the laboratory has demonstrated that the required statistical review is being performed and monitored in accordance with the quality control plan.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of performing and documenting monthly SD and CV calculations as outlined in G1003.0V5.
cited_documents: G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan.pdf
K1003.3.6_Data Collection Form for Quality Controls.docx
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65240**: For numeric quality control (QC) data, statistics such as standard deviation (SD) and coefficient of variation (CV) are calculated monthly to define analytic precision. This aligns with the requirement for quantitative tests where precision should be expressed numerically to quantify variation. The laboratory's G1003.0V5-Laboratory Analytical Phase Quality Control Plan mandates these monthly calculations. Quality control data is reviewed at regular intervals or after each batch to detect trends in assay performance. Personnel are trained to recognize QC problems and record them in a problem log. The Technical Supervisor monitors QC for all active assays. If QC problems arise, corrective action is taken and documented using a corrective action report form. The IQCP Quality Assessment_202503 also assesses the timely and effective use of the monthly review process for quality control logs to identify problems.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Test Validation and Verification Program Document Name
Document Number G1004.0 Version 3 Author： Keqin Gregg Date of Composition: 11/02/2020 Date of Execution：05/16/2025 Page 2 of 5 1.3.2.2 Precision/Reproducibility and Repeatability: these parameters refer to the closeness in the agreement of results
when operating condition are varied. All potential source of variability such as operators and reagent lots should be
examined in the studies. For quantitative test, precision should be expressed in numerical terms that quantify variation,
such as CV or SD from mean. For qualitative test, reproducibility and repeatability should be expressed as percentage of
result concordance among various conditions included in the experiment design. Precision is validated by repeat
measurement of samples at varying concentrations or activities within-run and between-run over a period of time and
repeatability. A sufficient number of samples should be used to provide a high degree of assurance of the test's precision
or reproducibility. Depending on the intended use of the test, it shall be determined in validation plan. 1.3.2.3 Robustness： robustness is defined as test precision/reproducibility given small, deliberate changes in test
conditions, such as prolonged delays, variations in storage temperature, and variation in DNA quantity and quality.
policy_evidence.title: G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program

checks.requirement: The laboratory assesses inhibition for each specimen type in assays without an internal control.
checks.subject: Inhibition Assessment
checks.note:
NOTE: Documentation of an acceptable inhibition rate may be provided by the manufacturer. If not, laboratories may test for inhibition by spiking an aliquot of the clinical specimen with target nucleic acid. This practice can be discontinued once the laboratory accumulates sufficient data showing that the inhibition rate falls within acceptable limits. 
  
  This requirement does not apply to probe-based solution hybridization methods (eg, Gen-Probe AccuProbe) performed without nucleic acid amplification.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory has demonstrated compliance with MIC.65250 by providing manufacturer-validated inhibition data and internal validation records. Per IFUK.US.MOL2655-02 FLU 2.0.pdf, the laboratory utilizes manufacturer documentation confirming no inhibition for the Simplexa™ Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II assay when tested against a panel of thirty-two potentially inhibitory organisms. For other assays, the laboratory has established internal inhibition assessment protocols as evidenced by K1002.2V2_APA NAB 2025-A, which defines acceptance criteria for replicate samples, and SKG001-PV data analysis.xlsx, which provides quantitative inhibition percentage data and RLU CV% metrics. The documentation confirms that the laboratory has accumulated sufficient data to establish acceptable inhibition limits for assays lacking internal controls.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of monitoring inhibition rates during validation and periodic quality control as documented in SKG001-PV data analysis.xlsx.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65250**: For assays lacking internal controls, laboratories must assess specimen inhibition per [MIC.65250], either via manufacturer documentation or by spiking clinical specimens with target nucleic acid until sufficient data confirms acceptable inhibition rates, excluding probe-based solution hybridization methods [MIC.65250]. The Simplexa™ Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II assay demonstrated no inhibition when tested against a panel of thirty-two potentially interfering organisms spiked into influenza A, influenza B, and RSV pools. Additionally, a partial validation for an APA assay established acceptance criteria requiring replicate RLU CV% ≤20%, or a duplicate inhibition rate CV% ≤20% if the RLU CV% exceeds 20%, alongside a mean batch inhibition rate of HPC > LPC ≥50%. These results are documented in K1002.2V2_APA NAB 2025-A, while SKG001-PV data analysis provides further control results, including RLU values, RLU CV%, and inhibition percentages.

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Operation/K-Quality Assurance/PT and APA/APA-NAB 2025-A/K1002.2V2_APA NAB 2025-A.docx
policy_evidence.snippet: Partial Validation: Run 4 sets of HPC, LPC and VC samples in duplicate. (4 HPC, 4 LPC, 4 VC x 2 replicates for 8 HPC, 8 LPC, and 8 VC for a total of 24) Acceptance Criteria For each replicate sample within a batch, the replicates RLU measured in CV% must be ≤20%. If the duplicate of a sample CV is ≥20%, the duplicates’ inhibition rate CV must be ≤20%. For 2/3rds of the HPC and LPC samples, the CV% of each sample (RLU) must be ≤20%. If the duplicate of a sample CV is ≥20%, the duplicates’ inhibition rate CV must be ≤20%. The CV for inhibition rate must be ≤ 30%. For 2/3rds of the VC samples, the CV% of each sample must be ≤20%. If the duplicate of a sample CV is ≥20%, the duplicates’ inhibition rate CV must be ≤30%. The mean value of the inhibition rate for each batch must be: HPC > LPC ≥50%. Performed by Keqin Gregg Performed date 3/4/2025 Please attach the testing results to this document_X__ If the APA uses a partial validation method, does the testing pass?_Yes_____
policy_evidence.title: K1002.2V2_APA NAB 2025-A

checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established policies for nucleic acid isolation and control usage, as evidenced by the 'Instruction for Use_TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit.pdf' and 'G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf'. These documents confirm the use of MS2 Phage controls for extraction and no-template controls for cross-contamination monitoring. Additionally, the 'NanoDrop-2000-User-Manual-EN.pdf' provides a mechanism for assessing nucleic acid purity via 260/230 ratios. However, the laboratory failed to provide actual records demonstrating that these controls are consistently run in parallel with patient samples to assess assay adequacy. While the policy framework is present, the specific evidence of compliance—records of controls used to assess adequacy—was not verified during this review.
corrective_actions: 1) Compile and maintain a log of daily run records for all molecular assays, ensuring positive and negative controls are documented for every extraction batch.
2) Perform a retrospective audit of the last 3 months of PCR run sheets to verify that extraction controls were processed in parallel with patient samples as required by MIC.65260.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65260**: The TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit utilizes the MagMAX Viral/Pathogen II Nucleic Acid Isolation Kit and KingFisher Flex system, incorporating an MS2 Phage Control for extraction and a Negative Control to monitor cross-contamination. Per the G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program, a no template control is required for each test. For the Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II system, which features built-in internal controls, the laboratory performs daily external positive and negative controls despite manufacturer specifications. Additionally, the NanoDrop 2000/2000c manual identifies the 260/230 ratio as a secondary measure of nucleic acid purity to detect co-purified contaminants. However, documentation confirming the use of these controls to assess assay adequacy was not provided.
