policy_evidence.snippet:
Summary and explanation of the test The TaqPath™ COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit includes the assays and controls for a multiplex real-time
RT-PCR test for the qualitative detection of RNA from SARS-CoV-2 in nasopharyngeal and anterior
nasal specimens from individuals suspected of COVID-19 by their healthcare provider. Each kit includes the following components: Multiplexed assays that contain three primer/probe sets specific to different SARS-CoV-2 genomic
regions and primers/probes for bacteriophage MS2 MS2 Phage Control as an internal process control for nucleic acid extraction TaqPath™ COVID‑19 Diagnostic PCR Control as a positive RNA control that contains targets
specific to the SARS-CoV-2 genomic regions targeted by the assays
Results are analyzed and interpreted using COVID‑19 Interpretive Software IVD Edition. For more
information, see Chapter 6, “Analysis and results”. The workflow begins with nucleic acid extraction from upper respiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal
and anterior nasal swabs) that arrive at the testing site in transport media. Nucleic acids are isolated
and purified from the specimens using the MagMAX™ Viral/Pathogen II Nucleic Acid Isolation Kit. Nucleic acid isolation is performed via an automated process using the KingFisher™ Flex Purification
System.
policy_evidence.title: TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Instructions for Use (Pub. No. MAN0028576 B)

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Operation/G-Test Process Management/XYZ Simplexa IQCP/XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa.docx
policy_evidence.snippet: If an internal quality control process (e.g., electronic/procedural/built-in) is used instead of external control material to meet daily quality control requirements, the laboratory must have an individualized quality control plan (IQCP) approved by the laboratory director. This laboratory has been using the Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II molecular test system to detect influenza A, influenza B and RSV viruses from 11/10/2022 to 2/28/2023. Although the assay was verified in June 2022, it was not performed for clinical sample testing until 6 months later. The Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II is an integrated molecular analysis system with nucleic acid extraction and analysis all on the same well/space which is carried in an 8 sample disc. Users will just load individual specimen and reagent to the disc and the test will take care of itself. There is a built-in internal control for each sample to check the assay performance. Therefore, the external controls are not required by the  manufacturer. We started the assay by running one external positive (recommended by and separately purchased from the assay manufacturer) and one negative control (confirmed negative swab sample from past) for CLIA/CAP requirement daily when there is a test and for each new shipment of the reagent.
policy_evidence.title: XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa

policy_evidence.snippet:
2.4.6 All pipettes shall be cleaned and calibrated or calibration verified at regular intervals. 2.5 Laboratory Coats
Laboratory coats shall be dedicated to specific use areas and changed when moving between areas. 2.5.1 Gloves
To reduce the possibility of introducing amplified nucleic acid products into the clean areas, disposable gloves shall be
worn and changed when entering or reentering the amplification preparation area. Disposable gloves may be changed
between samples to prevent cross-contamination. 2.6 Biohazard and Amplicon Disposal
All nucleic acids amplification products and remnant patient samples shall be closed and disposed in the biohazard waste
bin. It is critical that all waste shall be removed as soon as possible to reduce the risk of contamination. 2.7 Monitoring
2.7.1No template control shall be run with each test to ensure the testing system is free of contaminants. In cased a system
contamination event is confirmed, investigation experiments shall be performed to identify the source of contamination. Testing environment wipe tests may be performed if necessary. Corrective action shall be taken to eliminate the problem. 2.7.2 Unexpected increase in positive results shall be investigated both experimentally and statically. Experimentally,
investigation involves in control sample, specimen handling, assay process, reagents and consumables. Statistically,
investigation includes population prevalence, specimen characteristics, historic positive distribution/pattern.
policy_evidence.title: G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Policies/G-Test Process Management/G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program.pdf
policy_evidence.snippet:
Test Validation and Verification Program Document Name
Document Number G1004.0 Version 3 Author： Keqin Gregg Date of Composition: 11/02/2020 Date of Execution：05/16/2025 Page 3 of 5 1.4.1 Evaluate potential clinical validity and utility based on published reports, and select tests that can improve patient
care or population’s health. 1.4.2 Select a testing platform and software that can deliver quality testing results to intended tests. 1.4.3 Determine the specimen types that the method is going to use. Assess vendors, controls, reference samples, real
samples that will be used for validation experiments. 1.4.3.1 Ensure an adequate number and representative distribution of samples are performed for each type of specimen
expected for the assay (e.g. blood, fresh/frozen tissue, saliva, paraffin-embedded tissue, prenatal specimens, buccal swabs. For tissue samples, the validation must include representative tissue sources (i.e. organ/site) that are expected to be tested
by the assay.
1.4.4 Familiarize and optimize the testing platform and assay methods, and establish the testing procedure. 1.4.4.1 Specimen processing and fixation conditions can significantly influence the quality and integrity of nucleic acids
extracted from a specimen or potentially analysis results downstream. Consequently, laboratories must include specimens
handled with significantly different fixation and processing methods in the validation.
policy_evidence.title: G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Operation/F-Instruments/Equipment/NanoDrop 2000/Manual/NanoDrop-2000-User-Manual-EN.pdf
policy_evidence.snippet:
Section 3- Applications 260/230 - ratio of absorbance at 260 nm and 230 nm. This is a secondary measure of nucleic acid purity. The 260/230 values for a “pure” nucleic acid are often higher than the respective 260/280 values and are
commonly in the range of 1.8-2. 2. If the ratio is appreciably lower, this may indicate the presence of co
purified contaminants. Baseline correction - if selected, the default wavelength for the bichromatic normalization is 340 nm. The
user can manually enter a different wavelength for the bichromatic normalization of the absorbance data. In
either case, the baseline is automatically set to the absorbance value of the sample at the selected
wavelength. All wavelength data will be referenced off this value. Note: If a baseline correction is not selected, the spectra may be offset from the baseline and the calculated
concentration will change accordingly. Making Nucleic Acid Measurements 1. Select the Nucleic Acid application from the main menu. If the wavelength verification window appears, ensure the arm is down and click OK. 2. Select the type of sample to be measured from the Type drop-down list. The default setting is DNA-50. 3. Choose the concentration units from the drop-down list adjacent to the color coded concentration box. The
default units are ng/µL.
policy_evidence.title: NanoDrop 2000/2000c Spectrophotometers - User Manual

checks.requirement: For qualitative tests that use a quantitative cut-off value to distinguish positive from negative results, the cut-off value is established initially, and verified with every change in lot or at least every six months.
checks.subject: Cut-Off for Qualitative Laboratory-Developed Tests
checks.note: NOTE: The limit of detection that distinguishes a positive from a negative result must be established or verified when the test is initially placed in service, and verified with every change in lot (eg, new master mix), instrument maintenance, or at least every six months thereafter. Note that a low-positive control that is close to the limit of detection can satisfy this checklist requirement, but must be external to the kit (eg, weak-positive patient sample or reference material prepared in appropriate matrix).
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of initial establishment and verification at defined frequency
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established policies for test validation and verification as outlined in 'G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program.pdf', which requires the use of low-positive samples near the limit of detection. Furthermore, the manufacturer package inserts for 'Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus' and 'TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit' provide the necessary analytical sensitivity (LoD) data for initial establishment. However, the current evidence set lacks documentation verifying that the LoD or cut-off values are being re-verified at the required frequency (every six months or with every change in lot). While the policy exists, the specific records demonstrating ongoing compliance with the six-month or lot-change verification requirement were not provided for review.
corrective_actions: 1) Compile and maintain a log of LoD verification studies performed at each reagent lot change or at minimum six-month intervals.
2) Ensure that low-positive controls used for verification are external to the kit, as required by the MIC.65270 note.
cited_documents: Xpert Xpress CoV-2 FLU RSV plus PI 302-6991 Rev. B EUA.pdf
Instruction for Use_TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65270**: For qualitative tests utilizing a quantitative cut-off, the cut-off value must be established during test validation with a sufficient number of samples before the test is put into service. This establishment includes determining analytical sensitivity, also known as the Limit of Detection (LoD). For example, the Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus test estimated LoD values using two reagent lots and verified them with two lots of reagents. Similarly, the TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit determined its LoD using contrived positive specimens and confirmed it by testing replicates at various concentrations. The Multi-Drug Test Cup (Urine) Package Insert AP also details performance characteristics including accuracy and analytical sensitivity, with cut-off levels for various drugs. The Test Validation and Verification Program, G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program, specifies that for qualitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples, including positive, negative, and low-positive samples near the lower level of detection, should be used for accuracy assessment. The analytical measurement range (AMR) must be verified at least every six months after a method is initially placed in service.

policy_evidence.snippet:
1.3.2.1 Accuracy: Accuracy can be assessed using well-characterized reference material together with appropriate
biological matrix or by comparison to another valid test method, such as through specimen exchange， and expressed as
percentage of concordance. For quantitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples with analyte concentrations distributed across
the analytical measurement range should be used. Proportionate mixtures of samples may be used to supplement the study
population. For qualitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples, including positive, negative, and low-positive samples with
concentrations near the lower level of detection should be used; equivocal samples should not be used. For certain
methods that test multiple analytes (eg, next-generation sequencing, FISH, HPLC, GC-MS, MALDI-TOF, etc.), analytic
accuracy may be established for each method (not necessarily each analyte), as appropriate.
policy_evidence.title: G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program

policy_evidence.snippet:
Xpert® Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus 20.2 Analytical Sensitivity (Limit of Detection)
The analytical sensitivity of the Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus test was first estimated using two reagent lots by testing
limiting dilutions of seven respiratory viruses (NATtrol SARS-CoV-2, Flu A H1, Flu A H3, Flu B Victoria lineage, Flu B
Yamagata lineage, RSV A and RSV B) into pooled negative clinical NP swab matrix, following the guidance in Clinical and
Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) document EP17-A2. The estimated LoD values as determined by Probit regression
analysis were verified using two lots of Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus reagents. The verified LoD values for the viruses
tested are summarized in Table 5. Table 5. Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus Limit of Detection Virus/Strain LoD Concentration SARS-CoV-2 (USA-WA1/2020) 138 copies/mL Influenza A/Idaho/07/2018 0.007 TCID50/mL Influenza A/Hong Kong/45/2019 0.44 FFU/mL Influenza B/Washington/2/2019 12.9 CEID50/mL Influenza B/Wisconsin/10/2016 2.4 TCID50/mL RSV A/2/Australia/61 0.33 TCID50/mL RSV B/9320/MA/77
policy_evidence.title: Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus EUA IFU 302-6991 Rev. B

policy_evidence.snippet: The study was performed with two types of specimens, one was various strains of inactivated viral culture fluids, and another was clinical remnant samples. For inactivated viral culture fluids, the limit of detection (LoD) was first determined using the rapid antigen kit (Hotgen Coronavirus (2019-nCoV)-Antigen test- (Beijing Hotgen Biotech Co. Ltd., Beijing, China), or Antigentest) for each viral culture sample. Contrived samples at various low to middle concentrations along with a negative matrix were aliquoted, then subjected to various FTCs. For the clinical remnant samples, no dilutions were performed. The remnant samples had various Ct values representing high and low viral loads; these were directly aliquoted and subjected to various FTCs. Enough aliquot volume for each sample was made so that each aliquoted sample could be used for both the RT-PCR and antigen tests after the designated number of FTCs. checks.requirement: All test reagents and controls are stored properly and in a manner which minimizes target DNA/RNA contamination and degradation.
checks.subject: Reagent Storage
checks.note:
NOTE: Pre- and post-amplification reagents and controls must be stored under appropriate temperature and conditions in designated pre- and post-amplification areas. Temperature-sensitive reagents and/or controls may not be stored in frost-free freezers, unless either of the following conditions are met: 1) Reagent/control materials are kept in thermal containers and the laboratory can demonstrate that the function of these materials is not compromised; or 2) Freezer temperature is monitored by a continuous monitoring system, or a maximum/minimum thermometer. 
  
  Patient samples may be stored in a frost-free freezer only if the temperature is monitored in accordance with (2), above.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory has established a policy for reagent storage and cross-contamination prevention as documented in 'G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf', which mandates the separation of reagent preparation areas. Furthermore, the search summary confirms that specific storage requirements for Simplexa™ Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II (MOL2655) and TaqPath COVID-19 kits are identified. However, the current evidence set lacks verification of the physical storage environment. Specifically, there is no documentation confirming that frost-free freezers (if in use) are equipped with continuous monitoring systems or max/min thermometers as required by the note in MIC.65300. Additionally, while the policy exists, records demonstrating that reagents are consistently stored in designated pre- and post-amplification areas and maintained at required temperatures (e.g., -10 to -30 °C for Simplexa™) were not verified during this review.
corrective_actions: 1) Conduct a physical audit of all freezers used for reagent storage to confirm they are not frost-free or, if they are, verify the presence and calibration of continuous monitoring systems or max/min thermometers.
2) Implement a standardized temperature log or digital monitoring report to document daily compliance with storage temperature requirements for all molecular reagents.
3) Perform a walkthrough to verify that physical signage and storage containers clearly delineate pre- and post-amplification reagent zones.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65300**: Reagents for Simplexa™ Flu A/B & RSV Direct Gen II (MOL2655) must be stored at -10 to -30 °C and not in a frost-free freezer. These reagents should also be stored away from light. The Reaction Mix should not be refrozen. For the TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Instructions for Use (Pub. No. MAN0028576 B), reagents must be stored and handled as specified in the "Contents and storage" section. All reagents used in nucleic acid amplification must be prepared, aliquoted, and stored in a dedicated reagent preparation area separate from sample preparation and amplification areas. Master mixes should be prepared for specific assays and aliquoted to minimize opening stock reagent tubes, thereby reducing contamination risk. Reagents, master mixes, assays, and controls should be kept on ice or cold blocks during use to prevent degradation. The lot number of stock reagents used for master mix preparation should be documented in a reagent preparation form and recorded in the testing batch record for source identification in case of cross-contamination.

REAGENT HANDLING AND STORAGE 1. Store reagents at -10 to -30 °C (do not use a frost-free freezer). 2. Allow reagents to thaw at room temperature (approximate range 18 to 25 °C) before use. 3. Do not use kits or reagents beyond their expiration dates. 4. After removing Reaction Mix from freezer storage, initiate the test within thirty (30) minutes. 5. Do not vortex the Reaction Mix. 6. Do not smoke, drink, eat, handle contact lenses or apply make-up in areas where kit reagents and/or human specimens are being used. 4. Follow your institution’s safety procedures for working with chemicals and handling biological specimens. 5. Do not use reagents beyond their expiration date. 6. Dispose of unused kit reagents and human specimens according to local, state and federal regulations.

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Policies/G-Test Process Management/G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf
policy_evidence.snippet:
2.3 Reagents and Solutions
2.3.1 All reagents used in nucleic acid amplification shall be prepared, aliquoted, and stored in the reagent preparation
area that is separated from the areas used for sample preparation and amplification.
2.3.2 Dedicated equipment and supplies shall be used for reagent preparation. 2.3.3 Master mixes shall be made for specific assays according to a corresponding SOP and if applicable, aliquoted to a
specific volume required for each batch of the test. This practice will minimize the number of times that a single stock
reagent tube is opened so that to reduce the risk for contamination.
2.3.4 The lot number of the stock reagents used for the master mix preparation should be documented in the reagent
preparation form. The lot number will be recorded in the testing batch record that will make easier for source
identification should cross contamination occurs. 2.3.5 When setting up a reaction, reagents (deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs), primers, buffers, and enzymes)
shall always be added prior to adding the sample. When setting up multiple reactions, first make a master mix of reagents
enough for all samples, then aliquot the mix into reaction tubes or wells and add the sample last. It is important to only
open the tube of a reagent or a sample at the point of use and cap it right after.

checks.requirement: For multiplex tests, at least two analytes are individually verified for each new shipment and lot, and the analytes verified are periodically rotated.
checks.subject: New Reagent Lot - Multiplex Tests
checks.note: NOTE: A multiplex test simultaneously detects a defined set of analytes (eg, two or more pathogen-specific nucleic acid sequences) from a single run or cycle of the assay. Although a sample of analytes (at least two) may be used to verify each lot and shipment, the analytes verified must be rotated periodically as defined in laboratory procedure to assess all analytes in the multiplex test over time.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of new lot and shipment verification
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. The laboratory failed to provide documentation demonstrating compliance with MIC.65320. A review of the provided documents, including A1001.0v2_Compliance Policy.pdf and K1003.4-Evaluation and Audit Form for Post-Analytical Phases Activities.docx, confirms that no policy or procedure exists to define the verification of multiplex test analytes. Furthermore, no records of new lot or shipment verification were provided to demonstrate that at least two analytes are individually verified or that a rotation schedule is implemented as required by the checklist note. The laboratory lacks both the governing policy and the objective evidence of performance for multiplex test lot-to-lot verification.
corrective_actions: 1) Develop and implement a written procedure defining the verification process for new multiplex reagent lots and shipments, including the requirement to verify at least two analytes per lot.
2) Establish a rotation schedule within the procedure to ensure all analytes in the multiplex panel are assessed over time.
3) Maintain and archive records of all future lot and shipment verifications to serve as objective evidence of compliance.
cited_documents: K1003.4-Evaluation and Audit Form for Post-Analytical Phases Activities.docx
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65320**: The provided documents do not contain a policy or procedure (X) detailing the verification requirements for multiplex tests, specifically regarding the individual verification of at least two analytes for each new shipment and lot, or the periodic rotation of verified analytes. checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65330**: The Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus test evaluates analytical specificity by bench-testing a panel of 48 microorganisms, including human coronaviruses and common respiratory pathogens. This panel is tested in pools, and individual members are tested if a pool yields a positive result. The analytical specificity was 100%. Microbial interference for the Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus test is also evaluated using a panel of 10 commensal microorganisms, consisting of 7 viral and 3 bacterial strains. For *T. pallidum* detection, well-described gene targets like *tpp47*, *polA*, and *bmp* are used for initial screening. Subsequent subtyping uses *arp/tpr* and strain typing involves additional gene analyses. The performance of this test is validated using the procedures in the package insert, and modifications may alter performance. The laboratory maintains awareness of literature on pathogens and stays informed of manufacturer updates and bulletins regarding assay post-market performance. QC policies are consistently followed, and personnel are trained to recognize and log QC problems. The Technical Supervisor monitors QC for all active assays.

This additional level of discrimination can lead
to improved epidemiologic surveillance of circulating strains
and outbreak events in communities and may be of increasing

specimen sources (eg, lesion exudate, CSF, blood, etc), as de

are first screened for the presence of T. pallidum nucleic acid
using well-described gene targets, including tpp47, polA, and
bmp, with only screen-positive samples undergoing subsequent

as indicated above, with the highest sensitivity reported from

a higher copy number of T.  pallidum genomic DNA since
some (16–50%) NAAT-positive samples were not able to be
fully typed by both arp and tpr.

checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. The laboratory utilizes a TaqMan probe-based RT-PCR assay (LDT) for SARS-CoV-2 detection. Per the search summary, the target genes (ORF1ab, N, and S) are identified; however, the specific oligonucleotide sequences, concentrations, and purity records required by MIC.65340 for LDT troubleshooting and interpretation are not verified in the provided documentation. While the retrieved documents include package inserts for commercial kits (e.g., 'Xpert Xpress SARS-CoV-2 Flu RSV Assay' and 'TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit'), these do not satisfy the requirement for LDT-specific probe/primer characterization records. The laboratory must maintain documentation of these characteristics to ensure the ability to troubleshoot the LDT effectively.
corrective_actions: 1) Compile and maintain a technical file for the LDT containing specific oligonucleotide sequences, concentrations, and purity specifications for all primers and probes.
2) Ensure these records are accessible to laboratory staff for troubleshooting purposes as required by MIC.65340.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65340**: The Xpert Xpress SARS-CoV-2/Flu/RSV assay uses primers and probes for the in vitro qualitative detection and differentiation of RNA from Flu A, Flu B, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 viruses. Specifically, the Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus test primers and probes are designed to amplify and detect unique sequences in the nucleocapsid (N), envelope (E), and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) genes of SARS-CoV-2, as well as various genes for influenza A, influenza B, and RSV A and B nucleocapsid. The TaqPath™ COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit includes multiplexed assays with three primer/probe sets specific to different SARS-CoV-2 genomic regions. These probes anneal to three specific SARS-CoV-2 target sequences located between unique forward and reverse primers for the ORF1ab, N, and S genes. XYZ laboratory utilizes a TaqMan probe-based RT-PCR assay (LDT) to detect SARS-CoV-2 RNA. While the specific oligonucleotide sequences, concentrations, or purity of these probes and primers are not provided in the retrieved documents, the target genes for the probes and primers are identified.

Summary and explanation of the test The TaqPath™ COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit includes the assays and controls for a multiplex real-time
RT-PCR test for the qualitative detection of RNA from SARS-CoV-2 in nasopharyngeal and anterior
nasal specimens from individuals suspected of COVID-19 by their healthcare provider. Each kit includes the following components: Multiplexed assays that contain three primer/probe sets specific to different SARS-CoV-2 genomic
regions and primers/probes for bacteriophage MS2 MS2 Phage Control as an internal process control for nucleic acid extraction TaqPath™ COVID‑19 Diagnostic PCR Control as a positive RNA control that contains targets

information, see Chapter 6, “Analysis and results”. The workflow begins with nucleic acid extraction from upper respiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal
and anterior nasal swabs) that arrive at the testing site in transport media. Nucleic acids are isolated
and purified from the specimens using the MagMAX™ Viral/Pathogen II Nucleic Acid Isolation Kit. Nucleic acid isolation is performed via an automated process using the KingFisher™ Flex Purification

results.snippet:
Summary and explanation of the test The TaqPath™ COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit includes the assays and controls for a multiplex real-time
RT-PCR test for the qualitative detection of RNA from SARS-CoV-2 in nasopharyngeal and anterior
nasal specimens from individuals suspected of COVID-19 by their healthcare provider. Each kit includes the following components: Multiplexed assays that contain three primer/probe sets specific to different SARS-CoV-2 genomic
regions and primers/probes for bacteriophage MS2 MS2 Phage Control as an internal process control for nucleic acid extraction TaqPath™ COVID‑19 Diagnostic PCR Control as a positive RNA control that contains targets
specific to the SARS-CoV-2 genomic regions targeted by the assays
Results are analyzed and interpreted using COVID‑19 Interpretive Software IVD Edition. For more
information, see Chapter 6, “Analysis and results”. The workflow begins with nucleic acid extraction from upper respiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal
and anterior nasal swabs) that arrive at the testing site in transport media. Nucleic acids are isolated
and purified from the specimens using the MagMAX™ Viral/Pathogen II Nucleic Acid Isolation Kit. Nucleic acid isolation is performed via an automated process using the KingFisher™ Flex Purification
System.
results.title: TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Instructions for Use (Pub. No. MAN0028576 B)

results.snippet:
8 Active surveillance programs in conjunction with infection prevention
precautions are important components for preventing transmission of SARS-CoV-2, influenza and RSV. The use of assays
providing rapid results to identify patients infected with these viruses can be an important factor for effective control, proper
choice of treatment, and prevention of widespread outbreaks. 5 Principle of the Procedure The Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus test is an automated in vitro diagnostic test for the simultaneous qualitative detection
and differentiation of RNA from SARS-CoV-2, Flu A, Flu B, and RSV. The Xpert Xpress CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus test is
performed on GeneXpert Instrument Systems (Dx and Infinity Systems). The primers and probes in the Xpert Xpress
CoV-2/Flu/RSV plus test are designed to amplify and detect unique sequences in the following: nucleocapsid (N) and
envelope (E) and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) genes of the SARS-CoV-2 virus genome, influenza A matrix
(M), influenza A basic polymerase (PB2), influenza A acidic protein (PA), influenza B matrix (M), influenza B non
structural protein (NS), and the RSV A and RSV B nucleocapsid.

checks.requirement: Individual wells (or a representative sample thereof) of thermocyclers are checked for temperature accuracy before being placed in service and at least annually thereafter.
checks.subject: Thermocycler Temperature Checks
checks.note: NOTE: A downstream measure of well-temperature accuracy (such as productivity of amplification) may be substituted to functionally meet this requirement. For closed systems, this function should be performed as a component of the manufacturer-provided preventive maintenance.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Records of thermocycler verification
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. While the Quality Manual (0XYZ0001.0Rev3-Quality Manual2025) and the document list (H1001.2-XYZ Document List.xlsx) reference general equipment calibration and PM programs, there is no evidence of thermocycler-specific well temperature accuracy verification or documented downstream functional measures (e.g., amplification productivity) as required by MIC.65400. The provided documentation focuses on incubator temperature stability and general thermometer calibration, which does not satisfy the specific requirement for thermocycler well-temperature accuracy checks before service and annually thereafter.
corrective_actions: 1) Establish a protocol for annual thermocycler well-temperature verification or define a validated downstream functional measure (amplification productivity) to meet the requirement.
2) Perform and document initial verification for all currently active thermocyclers.
3) Update the Equipment Calibration Program (F1002.2) to include specific thermocycler maintenance schedules.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65400**: The Quality Manual, 0XYZ0001.0Rev3-Quality Manual2025, outlines the Equipment Calibration Program (F1002.0) as a supporting process for equipment management. This program includes the calibration of thermometers annually against a calibrated NIST traceable thermometer. If a thermometer is found to be out of calibration, action will be taken to recertify analytical accuracy before it is put back in use. The policy also directs the recording of daily temperature and humidity logs for the lab. Analysts are required to record and reset min/max temperature and humidity readings daily and monitor automatic sensors. If temperatures exceed acceptable levels, corrective action will be taken, and affected supplies, reagents, or samples will be checked for accuracy or quality. The document list, H1001.2-XYZ Document List, includes "Instruments PM or Calibration record and plan" under document F1002.2, which is part of the Equipment Calibration Program. However, specific records of thermocycler verification or temperature accuracy checks for individual wells were not found in the provided documents. The "Verification Report for Binder CO2 Incubator" details a procedure for checking temperature stability in an incubator using a Professional Thermohygrometer (NIST Certified) at multiple checkpoints and replicates, but this document does not pertain to thermocyclers.

policy_evidence.snippet: The absence of supervisor review during this period was due to the neglect of the then-supervisor, Shawn Macha, who was laid off at the end of 2024 for other reasons not related to this responsibility. Lack of Supervisor Review (January – April 2025): The lapse in review during this period resulted from personnel transition challenges. Shawn Macha (Lab Supervisor) departed in December 2024, followed by Hali Weeks (an experienced employee) in January 2025. Three new employees were hired in January 2025 to fill these roles, leading to a chaotic transition period. Training new staff on safety, assay procedures and routine lab maintenance tasks took priority, and the Lab Director, overwhelmed by these demands, inadvertently overlooked the temperature log review, although the temperatures were consistently recorded during this period. The lab Director usually will check tasks delegated to supervisors’ at the time of their competency performance evaluation. However, Shawn Macha left before his evaluation was due. Temperature Monitoring Compliance: Aside from Fridge 1103, all monitored storage units-maintained temperatures within the acceptable range during the review gap. Root Cause for Fridge 1103 Temperature Deviation: Investigation revealed that the temperature control for Fridge 1103 was set too high (not sure how it happened), preventing it from adequately cooling down after door openings.

policy_evidence.snippet: Most of the time a re-test is due to specimen inhibition or a reagent issue. Specifically, we have had a batch of Cepheid Gene Xpert Xpress  Strep-A cartridges that were faulty. We had to re-test those specimens with a new batch of cartridges and obtained the correct result. Are there multiple instances of the same corrective action being taken for the same problem? Why hasn’t the problem been resolved? No. Are all corrective actions documented? Yes, a corrective action is documented by a corrective action report which details the problem, investigation, findings and the correction. If temperatures are out of range for refrigerators, incubators, or other temperature-dependent equipment, is this recognized and corrected, and are the implications of improper temperatures evaluated? (For instance, controls stored in a refrigerator that is too cold may not work properly, or cultures placed in an incubator that is too warm may not grow as expected) Yes. Temperatures for refrigerators, incubators, and other temperature-sensitive equipment are monitored closely. Manual temperature checks are recorded daily, and corrective actions are immediately implemented if readings fall outside the acceptable range. For example, cool packs may be added to maintain the required 2–8°C range in a refrigerator. Have there been frequent calls to tech support or a lot of service calls?

results.snippet: Most of the time a re-test is due to specimen inhibition or a reagent issue. Specifically, we have had a batch of Cepheid Gene Xpert Xpress  Strep-A cartridges that were faulty. We had to re-test those specimens with a new batch of cartridges and obtained the correct result. Are there multiple instances of the same corrective action being taken for the same problem? Why hasn’t the problem been resolved? No. Are all corrective actions documented? Yes, a corrective action is documented by a corrective action report which details the problem, investigation, findings and the correction. If temperatures are out of range for refrigerators, incubators, or other temperature-dependent equipment, is this recognized and corrected, and are the implications of improper temperatures evaluated? (For instance, controls stored in a refrigerator that is too cold may not work properly, or cultures placed in an incubator that is too warm may not grow as expected) Yes. Temperatures for refrigerators, incubators, and other temperature-sensitive equipment are monitored closely. Manual temperature checks are recorded daily, and corrective actions are immediately implemented if readings fall outside the acceptable range. For example, cool packs may be added to maintain the required 2–8°C range in a refrigerator. Have there been frequent calls to tech support or a lot of service calls?
results.title: K1003.3.8_Data Collection Form for Corrective Actions

checks.requirement: Nucleic acid amplification procedures (eg, PCR) use appropriate physical containment and procedural controls to minimize carryover (false positive results).
checks.subject: Carryover
checks.note: NOTE: This item is primarily directed at ensuring adequate physical separation of pre- and post-amplification samples to avoid amplicon contamination. The extreme sensitivity of amplification systems requires that the laboratory take special precautions. For example, pre- and post-amplification samples should be manipulated in physically separate areas; gloves must be worn and frequently changed during processing; dedicated pipettes (positive displacement type or with aerosol barrier tips) must be used; and manipulations must minimize aerosolization. Enzymatic destruction of amplification products is often helpful, as is real-time measurement of products to avoid manual manipulation of amplification products.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory maintains a robust framework for preventing amplicon contamination as required by MIC.65500. Policy G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program establishes mandatory physical separation of pre- and post-amplification areas, dedicated lab coats, and specific pipette maintenance protocols. The TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Instructions for Use provides validated decontamination procedures (bleach, ethanol, UV light) and mandates the use of no-template controls to monitor for carryover. The NanoDrop 2000 User Manual confirms effective cleaning protocols to prevent cross-contamination during quantification. Current documentation confirms that the laboratory has integrated both procedural controls and physical containment strategies to mitigate false positives.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of maintaining physical separation of pre- and post-amplification areas and adhering to the decontamination protocols outlined in G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.
cited_documents: G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf
Instruction for Use_TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65500**: The G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program mandates physical separation of reagent preparation, sample processing, and amplification areas, requiring dedicated equipment and supplies for each. Reagents must be prepared and aliquoted per SOPs, with lot numbers documented, and added to reactions before samples, followed by immediate capping or sealing. Centrifugation is required before opening amplified materials to prevent aerosolization. Personnel must use area-specific lab coats and change gloves frequently, particularly when entering preparation zones or between samples. Waste must be disposed of promptly, and pipettes require regular calibration and cleaning. Per the TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Instructions for Use (Pub. No. MAN0028576 B), surfaces and equipment must be decontaminated using bleach, ethanol, and ultraviolet light. No-template controls are utilized to monitor for contamination, with experimental and statistical investigations triggered by positive results or suspected carryover. Additionally, the NanoDrop 2000/2000c Spectrophotometers - User Manual confirms that wiping measurement pedestals with a dry laboratory wipe effectively eliminates carryover between samples of varying concentrations.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Summary and explanation of the test The TaqPath™ COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit includes the assays and controls for a multiplex real-time
RT-PCR test for the qualitative detection of RNA from SARS-CoV-2 in nasopharyngeal and anterior
nasal specimens from individuals suspected of COVID-19 by their healthcare provider. Each kit includes the following components: Multiplexed assays that contain three primer/probe sets specific to different SARS-CoV-2 genomic
regions and primers/probes for bacteriophage MS2 MS2 Phage Control as an internal process control for nucleic acid extraction TaqPath™ COVID‑19 Diagnostic PCR Control as a positive RNA control that contains targets
specific to the SARS-CoV-2 genomic regions targeted by the assays
Results are analyzed and interpreted using COVID‑19 Interpretive Software IVD Edition. For more
information, see Chapter 6, “Analysis and results”. The workflow begins with nucleic acid extraction from upper respiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal
and anterior nasal swabs) that arrive at the testing site in transport media. Nucleic acids are isolated
and purified from the specimens using the MagMAX™ Viral/Pathogen II Nucleic Acid Isolation Kit. Nucleic acid isolation is performed via an automated process using the KingFisher™ Flex Purification
System.
policy_evidence.title: TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit Instructions for Use (Pub. No. MAN0028576 B)

policy_evidence.snippet:
2.4.6 All pipettes shall be cleaned and calibrated or calibration verified at regular intervals. 2.5 Laboratory Coats
Laboratory coats shall be dedicated to specific use areas and changed when moving between areas. 2.5.1 Gloves
To reduce the possibility of introducing amplified nucleic acid products into the clean areas, disposable gloves shall be
worn and changed when entering or reentering the amplification preparation area. Disposable gloves may be changed
between samples to prevent cross-contamination. 2.6 Biohazard and Amplicon Disposal
All nucleic acids amplification products and remnant patient samples shall be closed and disposed in the biohazard waste
bin. It is critical that all waste shall be removed as soon as possible to reduce the risk of contamination. 2.7 Monitoring
2.7.1No template control shall be run with each test to ensure the testing system is free of contaminants. In cased a system
contamination event is confirmed, investigation experiments shall be performed to identify the source of contamination. Testing environment wipe tests may be performed if necessary. Corrective action shall be taken to eliminate the problem. 2.7.2 Unexpected increase in positive results shall be investigated both experimentally and statically. Experimentally,
investigation involves in control sample, specimen handling, assay process, reagents and consumables. Statistically,
investigation includes population prevalence, specimen characteristics, historic positive distribution/pattern.
policy_evidence.title: G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program

policy_evidence.snippet: If an internal quality control process (e.g., electronic/procedural/built-in) is used instead of external control material to meet daily quality control requirements, the laboratory must have an individualized quality control plan (IQCP) approved by the laboratory director. This laboratory has been using the Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II molecular test system to detect influenza A, influenza B and RSV viruses from 11/10/2022 to 2/28/2023. Although the assay was verified in June 2022, it was not performed for clinical sample testing until 6 months later. The Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV Gen II is an integrated molecular analysis system with nucleic acid extraction and analysis all on the same well/space which is carried in an 8 sample disc. Users will just load individual specimen and reagent to the disc and the test will take care of itself. There is a built-in internal control for each sample to check the assay performance. Therefore, the external controls are not required by the  manufacturer. We started the assay by running one external positive (recommended by and separately purchased from the assay manufacturer) and one negative control (confirmed negative swab sample from past) for CLIA/CAP requirement daily when there is a test and for each new shipment of the reagent.
policy_evidence.title: XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa

policy_evidence.snippet:
Section 7- Diagnostics and Troubleshooting If the warning persists and the user visually confirms that the liquid column is forming, perform a calibration check. If
the instrument is out of calibration, contact Technical Support. Outside of the US and Canada, please contact your
local NanoDrop products distributor. Small Volume Sample Measurement This error occurs when the small sample volume feature available in the Nucleic Acid and Protein A280
applications has been selected for use with a sample a 10 mm equivalent absorbance of less than 3. 0. De-select
the small volume option, and wipe away the aliquot. Use a larger sample volume aliquot and re-measure. Sample Related Issues Sample Carryover
Simple wiping of the upper and lower measurement pedestal with a dry laboratory wipe is highly effective in
eliminating carryover for samples differing in concentration by as much as three orders of magnitude. Effect of Evaporation and Solvents
A fresh aliquot of sample should be used for each measurement. Evaporation of the sample during the
measurement cycle usually has a minimal effect on absorbance readings and may result in a 1-2% increase in
sample concentration. However, repeated measurements on the same sample aliquot will result in increasing
concentrations and or column breakage. Highly volatile solvents, such as hexane, will likely evaporate before the
measurement can be completed. Less volatile solvents such as DMSO can be used successfully.
policy_evidence.title: NanoDrop 2000/2000c Spectrophotometers - User Manual

checks.subject: Temperature Range Defined
checks.note: NOTE: For some instruments, this function is performed automatically by software provided by the manufacturer.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Compliant. The laboratory demonstrates compliance through a combination of automated monitoring and manual verification procedures. The '1_XYZ Lab Temperature and Humidity Record (Current).xlsx' confirms continuous monitoring of temperature ranges via SensoScientific probes. For incubators, the 'Binder OQ, PQ Stability data.xlsx' and 'Verification Report for Binder CO2 Incubator.docx' confirm that incubation temperatures are defined (37°C) and recorded using NIST-traceable thermometers. Additionally, the '220915 Tabletop Incubator Verification.docx' provides evidence of defined temperature verification procedures for tabletop units. The 'UTRED30-WiFi_Product_User_Guide.pdf' supports the use of automated manufacturer-provided software for temperature measurement, satisfying the requirement note.
corrective_actions: Continue current practice of maintaining NIST-traceable calibration records and automated monitoring logs for all incubation equipment.
cited_documents: Verification Report for Binder CO2 Incubator.docx
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65520**: Incubation temperatures are defined and recorded, with some instruments performing this function automatically via manufacturer-provided software. The UTRED30-WiFi Product User Guide specifies a temperature sensor measurement range of -40 °C to +99 °C and an operating temperature range of -30 °C to +70 °C. The 1_XYZ Lab Temperature and Humidity Record (Current) documents temperature ranges, such as -150 °C to -196 °C, monitored by a SensoScientific Probe. This record also shows temperature regulation via a NIST thermohygrometer. For incubators, a Binder CO2 Incubator Verification Report details calibration procedures where the incubator was set at 37°C and 5% CO2, and temperature readings were taken using a NIST thermometer. The Binder OQ, PQ Stability data further records temperature and CO2 levels for incubators set at 37°C. A Tabletop Incubator Verification outlines a procedure to measure varying temperatures at 20°C and 70°C using a reference thermometer.

checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. While the laboratory maintains valid ISO/IEC 17025:2017 calibration certificates for temperature probes (Calibration_588926, 591293, 591304, 557077), the verification report for the Binder CO2 Incubator (Verification Report for Binder CO2 Incubator.docx) indicates a significant discrepancy between the incubator's internal sensor and the NIST-traceable thermometer (mean difference of 1.8°C). The requirement mandates that incubators must maintain the appropriate temperature within the manufacturer's specified range. The current documentation does not confirm that the incubator was adjusted to account for the -1.8°C correction factor or that the unit is currently operating within the manufacturer's required tolerance for the specific assays performed.
corrective_actions: 1) Document the adjustment of the Binder CO2 incubator to align with the NIST-traceable thermometer readings.
2) Perform and document a follow-up verification study to confirm the incubator maintains temperature within the manufacturer's specified range after adjustment.
3) Update the standard operating procedure to define the corrective action process when incubator temperatures deviate from the NIST-traceable reference.

checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65530**: A Binder CO2 Incubator (XYZ ID: A0030) was verified for temperature and CO2 accuracy. The incubator was set to 37°C and 5% CO2, then allowed to stabilize for at least 12 hours. A NIST thermometer (NIST ID: TH-00) and a CO2 single gas detector (NIST ID: A0029) were used to take four readings at 10-minute intervals. The mean temperature reading from the incubator was 37°C, while the NIST thermometer recorded a mean of 35.2°C, resulting in a correction factor of -1.8°C. Calibration certificates for various temperature probes, including a Single Digi probe (Model # DTP12-1-SDS4, Serial # SDS4-112879) and Flat RTD probes (Model # RTD10-C-SRC3, Serial # SRC3-11558, SRC3-11569, SRC3-10875), indicate compliance with ISO/IEC 17025:2017. These calibrations are traceable to NIST and meet or exceed manufacturer requirements.

RT-PCR test for the qualitative detection of RNA from SARS-CoV-2 in nasopharyngeal and anterior
nasal specimens from individuals suspected of COVID-19 by their healthcare provider. Each kit includes the following components: Multiplexed assays that contain three primer/probe sets specific to different SARS-CoV-2 genomic
regions and primers/probes for bacteriophage MS2 MS2 Phage Control as an internal process control for nucleic acid extraction TaqPath™ COVID‑19 Diagnostic PCR Control as a positive RNA control that contains targets

information, see Chapter 6, “Analysis and results”. The workflow begins with nucleic acid extraction from upper respiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal
and anterior nasal swabs) that arrive at the testing site in transport media. Nucleic acids are isolated
and purified from the specimens using the MagMAX™ Viral/Pathogen II Nucleic Acid Isolation Kit. Nucleic acid isolation is performed via an automated process using the KingFisher™ Flex Purification
System.

checks.requirement: For laboratory-developed tests that generate a result based on a melting temperature (Tm), appropriately narrow temperature ranges (+/- 2.5ºC) are defined and recorded each day of use.
checks.subject: Melting Temperature - Laboratory-Developed Test
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. The laboratory performs laboratory-developed tests (LDTs) as noted in 2-wz-cv2025.pdf, but fails to meet the requirements of MIC.65550. Review of G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program confirms the lab has a validation framework, but it lacks the specific definition of melting temperature (Tm) ranges (+/- 2.5ºC) required for LDTs. Furthermore, no daily logs or records were provided to demonstrate that these temperature ranges are defined or recorded during each day of use. Documents J1002.2-CA 250425-TempLog and 2024 K1003.3.2_Test System, Instruments, Reagents, and Supplies were reviewed but found to pertain only to general environmental and storage conditions, not the specific analytical Tm monitoring required by this checklist item.
corrective_actions: 1) Define and document the acceptable melting temperature (Tm) ranges (+/- 2.5ºC) for all applicable LDTs within the test validation or standard operating procedures.
2) Implement a daily log or electronic record system to capture and verify Tm values for each day of use to ensure compliance with the defined ranges.
cited_documents: 2024 K1003.3.2_Test System, Instruments, Reagents, and Supplies
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65550**: No policies or records define or document the daily recording of narrow temperature ranges (+/- 2.5ºC) for melting temperature-based laboratory-developed tests (LDTs). Although G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program outlines general analytical performance parameters, it lacks specific melting temperature criteria, and resume 5-30-95-2 provides no operational monitoring details. Documents ID3A2025_PSR and ID3B2025_PSR identify LDTs as a manufacturer type without addressing temperature definitions, while Safety Data Sheets report no data for melting ranges. The Multi-Drug Test Cup (Urine) Package Insert AP pertains only to specimen integrity rather than LDT operational parameters. Furthermore, J1002.2-CA 250425-TempLog and 2024 K1003.3.2_Test System, Instruments, Reagents, and Supplies refer exclusively to general environmental and storage conditions rather than the required daily recording of melting temperature ranges. Consequently, no evidence exists to support the definition or daily monitoring of these specific LDT parameters.

1.3 If the test is modified from a FDA cleared or approved test including different patient population, instrument model,
software, specimen types, sample preparation method or cutoff values etc, the analytical specification is no longer be
appropriate, the validation plan needs to be in place to confirm all the specifications as for the laboratory-developed test
(LDT). 1.3.1 Clinical performance parameters include clinical validity and clinical utility. 1.3.1.1 Clinical validity includes clinical performance characteristics, such as clinical sensitivity, clinical specificity,
positive and negative predictive value in defined populations or likelihood ratios. 1.3.1.2 In genetic testing, clinical utility begins with demonstration that a particular genetic marker, mutation, or sequence
is associated with a carrier, predisposition to disease, or disease state, or is predictive of therapeutic response. In addition,
clinical utility requires demonstration that this information can positively impact the course of patient management. 1.3.2 Analytical performance parameters include accuracy, precision, reportable range, and reference interval, as well as
analytical sensitivity and limit of detection, analytical specificity, robustness (i.e. specimen stability, reagent stability),
and other important parameters that may affect assay performance (such as linearity, carryover, cross-contamination, as
appropriate and applicable).

Evidence confirms that the laboratory has established both a framework for SOP development and specific analytical guidelines for active assays.

checks.requirement: For quantitative molecular tests, methods for calculating quantitative values are adequately described in the procedure and units reported are clearly documented.
checks.subject: Calculations for Quantitative Tests
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. While G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program outlines validation requirements for quantitative tests (accuracy and precision), the laboratory has failed to provide the specific procedure (Policy/Procedure: X) that defines the calculation methods and reported units for quantitative molecular tests. The search summary confirms that while validation parameters are documented, the actual operational procedure for calculating and reporting quantitative values is missing from the provided documentation. No evidence was found to verify that technologists have access to documented calculation formulas or standardized reporting units for quantitative molecular assays.
corrective_actions: 1) Develop and implement a formal procedure (Policy/Procedure: X) that explicitly defines the mathematical formulas used for quantitative molecular test calculations.
2) Document the specific units of measure (e.g., copies/mL, IU/mL) for all quantitative molecular tests within the procedure manual.
3) Ensure the procedure is reviewed and approved by the Laboratory Director and accessible to all testing personnel.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65570**: The "Test Validation and Verification Program" G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program outlines requirements for quantitative tests, stating that accuracy should be assessed using reference material or comparison to another valid method, with a minimum of 20 samples distributed across the analytical measurement range. Precision for quantitative tests must be expressed numerically, such as coefficient of variation (CV) or standard deviation (SD) from the mean. Robustness is defined as test precision/reproducibility under small, deliberate changes in test conditions. While these documents describe how quantitative values should be assessed during validation, no specific procedure (e.g., "Policy/Procedure: X") detailing the calculation methods for quantitative values or the units reported for quantitative molecular tests was found among the provided sources. The "Direct test for Syphilis" document mentions determining the number of 60-bp repeats for the *arp* gene, but does not detail the calculation method or units for a quantitative test. Similarly, "11_Lateral Flow assays" discusses quantitative results and digitization of data but does not provide specific calculation procedures or unit documentation.

policy_evidence.document_uri: gs://xyzlapp-inspect-050526/Inspection Documents_2026/Lab Policies/G-Test Process Management/G1004.0V3-Test Validation and Verification Program.pdf
policy_evidence.snippet:
1.3.2.1 Accuracy: Accuracy can be assessed using well-characterized reference material together with appropriate
biological matrix or by comparison to another valid test method, such as through specimen exchange， and expressed as
percentage of concordance. For quantitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples with analyte concentrations distributed across
the analytical measurement range should be used. Proportionate mixtures of samples may be used to supplement the study
population. For qualitative tests, a minimum of 20 samples, including positive, negative, and low-positive samples with
concentrations near the lower level of detection should be used; equivocal samples should not be used. For certain
methods that test multiple analytes (eg, next-generation sequencing, FISH, HPLC, GC-MS, MALDI-TOF, etc.), analytic
accuracy may be established for each method (not necessarily each analyte), as appropriate.

checks.requirement: Negative results obtained for Group B Streptococcus intrapartum screening by a non-amplified DNA probe are followed up with a selective broth culture method.
checks.subject: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) Screening - Non-amplified DNA Probe
checks.note: NOTE: Direct DNA probing is insufficiently sensitive to detect light colonization and is therefore not adequate to replace culture based prenatal screening or to use in place of risk based approaches when culture results are unknown at the time of labor. An adequate rapid intrapartum test must be as sensitive as culture of vaginal and rectal swabs inoculated into selective broth media.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. The laboratory failed to provide documentation confirming that negative results from non-amplified DNA probe GBS screening are followed up with selective broth culture. The retrieved documents (1_qPCR overview 1-26-2023.pdf, Direct test for Syphilis.pdf, G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf, and SKG002-20250514-Cell Counts.pdf) focus on PCR specificity, syphilis testing, contamination protocols, and cell counting; none address GBS screening workflows or the required reflex culture policy. As the requirement mandates that direct DNA probing must be supplemented by culture to ensure sensitivity, the absence of a defined reflex policy or associated patient records constitutes a significant gap.
corrective_actions: 1) Develop and implement a formal policy requiring reflex selective broth culture for all negative GBS non-amplified DNA probe results.
2) Update the laboratory information system (LIS) to automatically trigger a culture order when a negative GBS probe result is finalized.
3) Perform a retrospective audit of GBS screening records to ensure compliance with the reflex testing requirement.
cited_documents: G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65580**: The provided documents do not contain information regarding Group B Streptococcus (GBS) intrapartum screening, non-amplified DNA probes, or follow-up selective broth culture methods. Therefore, the claim that negative results from a non-amplified DNA probe are followed up with a selective broth culture method for GBS intrapartum screening cannot be verified from the given sources. The documents discuss the specificity of TaqMan® assays, performance characteristics of direct detection and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for *Treponema pallidum* in syphilis diagnosis, and a PCR lab cross-contamination prevention program. One document also details an experiment with sample IDs, dilution factors, and cell counts.

checks.requirement: A pre-enrichment step using a selective broth enrichment culture is performed for antepartum (36 to 38 weeks gestation) vaginal/rectal swab screening for Group B Streptococcus (GBS) colonization by nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT).
checks.subject: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) Screening - Amplified Method
checks.note:
NOTE: If direct sample testing is performed, without the broth enrichment step, all antepartum samples testing negative for GBS must be followed up with a selective enrichment broth step in conjunction with culture or NAAT testing. 
  
  The utility of NAAT assays for intrapartum testing (ie, during active labor) remains unsettled. If used, it is recommended that testing only be considered for women not appropriately screened at 36 to 38 weeks and for whom no other clinical risk factors related to neonatal GBS infection are present during labor.
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Partial. While the laboratory has established a PCR cross-contamination prevention program (G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program) and an IQCP (XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa) to support molecular testing integrity, there is no specific evidence provided that confirms the mandatory pre-enrichment step for antepartum GBS screening is being performed. The retrieved documents focus on wipe tests (G1008.1-Laboratory Wipe Test Procedure and Record-210619) and general contamination protocols, but lack documentation of the specific GBS enrichment workflow or the required follow-up procedure for direct-test negatives as mandated by MIC.65590. Verification of the actual laboratory SOP for GBS screening is required to ensure compliance with the selective broth enrichment requirement.
corrective_actions: 1) Update the GBS screening SOP to explicitly include the selective broth enrichment step for antepartum samples.
2) Implement a documentation log to record the enrichment step for all antepartum GBS NAAT samples.
3) Establish a formal follow-up protocol for any direct-test negative results to ensure compliance with the enrichment requirement.
cited_documents: G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program.pdf
G1008.1-Laboratory Wipe Test Procedure and Record-210619.docx
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65590**: Policy MIC.65590 mandates a selective broth enrichment step for antepartum GBS screening via NAAT, requiring follow-up enrichment and culture or NAAT for any direct-test negatives [MIC.65590]. Intrapartum NAAT is restricted to women lacking 36-38 week screening and clinical risk factors [MIC.65590]. To ensure analytical integrity, the laboratory employs a wipe test procedure (G1008.1-Laboratory Wipe Test Procedure and Record Template; G1008.1-Laboratory Wipe Test Procedure and Record-210619) and a cross-contamination prevention program (G1008.0V2-PCR Lab Cross Contamination Prevention Program) that mandates specific tube handling, sealing, and centrifugation protocols. The IQCP (XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa) further mitigates reporting errors through rigorous personnel training, competency assessments, and standardized environmental controls, including dedicated setup areas, glove changes, and decontamination practices. These measures, alongside established preventive maintenance and instrument error protocols, support the accuracy of molecular testing, while additional documentation includes proficiency testing forms (K1003.1.6_Data Collection Form for Proficiency Testing) and procedures for unrelated assays.

It is in this period we found that we have many negative samples in our testing cohort which could act as a negative control for any potential contamination that an external negative control is used to control. checks.requirement: Laboratories performing molecular testing for the detection of M. tuberculosis directly from specimens clinically suspicious for tuberculosis perform culture on all specimens or include a recommendation for mycobacterial culture.
checks.subject: M. tuberculosis Molecular Testing
checks.note:
NOTE: Mycobacterial culture is a more sensitive method than molecular testing for the diagnosis of tuberculosis and is still considered the gold standard. When possible, a culture must be performed regardless of the molecular test result to aid in clinical diagnosis. Isolates may be required for susceptibility testing, genotyping, or to ascertain the presence of viable organisms in patients currently being treated. In the absence of a culture, a comment must be added to the report recommending culture. 
  
  This checklist item does not apply to broad multiplex or metagenomic panels that are able to detect M. tuberculosis, but in which the clinical suspicion for tuberculosis is absent.
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Patient reports or worksheets
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. The laboratory failed to provide evidence of molecular testing for M. tuberculosis. The retrieved documents (WZ-TB test result.pdf, KG-TB test results.pdf) contain only Tuberculin Skin Test (PPD) results, which do not satisfy the requirement for molecular testing documentation. No patient reports or worksheets demonstrating the inclusion of a mycobacterial culture recommendation for molecular TB testing were identified. The provided IQCP document (XYZ-MOL-Micro-IQCP-Simplexa.docx) pertains to other assays and does not address the specific reporting requirements for M. tuberculosis molecular testing.
corrective_actions: 1) Implement a mandatory report comment for all M. tuberculosis molecular tests recommending mycobacterial culture if not already performed.
2) Conduct a retrospective audit of molecular TB test reports to ensure compliance with the reporting requirement.
3) Update the laboratory information system (LIS) to automatically append the required culture recommendation to all applicable molecular test results.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65600**: The provided documents include patient test results for Tuberculin Skin Tests (TB Skin Test) for WZ and KG. These results indicate a "Negative" TB Skin Test with an induration of 0 mm. The documents explain that a negative skin test usually means no tuberculosis infection, but it can be falsely negative if recently infected, recommending re-testing in 3 months if applicable. It also advises evaluation by a primary care provider if TB symptoms persist despite a negative test. For positive skin tests, the documents recommend seeing a primary care provider and note that other tests, such as X-rays or cultures, are needed to check for active disease. No patient reports or worksheets for molecular testing for *M. tuberculosis* were found, nor were there any recommendations for mycobacterial culture in the provided documents. The documents also include an IQCP for a Simplexa Flu A/B and RSV assay and information on cross-reactivity testing for *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* in a TaqPath COVID-19 Diagnostic PCR Kit, but these do not pertain to *M. tuberculosis* molecular testing for clinical diagnosis.

policy_evidence.snippet:
Generally, NAATs using these genes show excellent specificity
across studies, ranging from 97% to 100%, whereas sensitivity
is largely dependent on the specimen source tested rather than
on the T. pallidum gene targeted (Table 3). It is important also
to remain cognizant of the different comparator reference
methods (e.g., DFM vs clinical presentation alongside serologic
results used to define primary syphilis) and national guidelines
(e.g., CDC vs Canadian vs European guidelines) used to stage
patients or define disease across these studies. The highest overall sensitivity of NAAT for T. pallidum de
tection was observed in primary lesion exudate collected by
sterile swab and ranged from 75% to 95% and 72% to 87% for the tpp47 and polA targets, respectively (Table 3) [15, 31–37]. Performance of tpp47 or polA NAATs compared with only
DFM in primary lesions showed high positive agreement, ran
ging from 87% to 95% [32, 33, 35]. Molecular testing of exudate
swabs collected from patients classified with secondary syphilis
showed a wide range in sensitivity for the tpp47 target, 20% to
86%, yet limited sensitivity by the polA NAAT (43%) (Table 3)
[15, 32, 34, 35].

checks.requirement: Detection of genotypic antimicrobial resistance markers (eg, vanA, mecA, blaKPC, etc.) is linked or attributed to a corresponding organism in the final laboratory report when molecular analysis is performed directly on patient specimens (eg, urine or respiratory specimens) or in blood culture broth. This can be accomplished through molecular detection of targets identifying the corresponding organism or by detection of resistance markers from organisms recovered in concurrent culture.
checks.subject: Antimicrobial Resistance Markers by Molecular Analysis - Clinical Validity
checks.note:
NOTE 1: The intent of this requirement is to ensure that detection of antimicrobial resistance has clinical validity. Ideally, genotypic antimicrobial resistance results will be correlated with other available results, such as identification of isolates in culture and their phenotypic AST results, with the goal of aiding in the assessment of clinical significance of such findings. There may be instances where the organism is not recovered in culture (eg, due to lack of viability) or confirmation by culture-based methods may not be possible; however, efforts should be taken to link the antimicrobial resistance gene to the organism. Resistance markers should only be reported when present with compatible/appropriate organisms. 
  
  NOTE 2: This requirement does not include either screening tests (eg, rectal swab for carbapenemase gene detection) or surveillance tests (eg, testing performed to monitor for a community- or population-level occurrence and establish incidence or prevalence of that occurrence, if results do not go back to individual patients).
checks.evidence_of_compliance:
Evidence of Compliance: 
  
  * Reports linking resistance determinants to specific organisms
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. While G1001.0V3-Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan_2025 establishes general procedures for test report accuracy and LIS validation, it does not contain specific evidence demonstrating that molecular antimicrobial resistance markers are linked or attributed to a corresponding organism in the final laboratory report as required by MIC.65630. The retrieved documents focus on general reporting, balance calibration, and hazardous material transport, but lack the specific clinical validity documentation (e.g., sample reports showing organism-resistance linkage) required to satisfy the evidence of compliance criteria. No records were verified that confirm the laboratory's process for ensuring resistance markers are only reported when present with compatible organisms.
corrective_actions: 1) Update laboratory reporting templates to explicitly link detected genotypic resistance markers to the corresponding organism identified via molecular target or concurrent culture.
2) Perform a retrospective audit of molecular resistance reports to ensure clinical validity and compliance with the linkage requirement.
3) Revise G1001.0V3 to include specific clinical validity review steps for antimicrobial resistance marker reporting.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65630**: The Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan, G1001.0V3-Laboratory Testing Process Control Plan_2025, outlines procedures for test reports and records. All test reports or information, including data from reference labs, must be stored according to H1002.0. If a report is automatically generated by LIS, its accuracy must be validated before service and re-verified every two years using Form I1003.4. A manual reporting method is required in case the LIS system is down or has errors. Reports must be reviewed and verified by the laboratory director or a qualified designee, and their content and format reviewed at least biennially. Certified reports are delivered to the ordering doctor or patient/customer via their chosen method, and any other person seeking a report must be authorized by the patient/customer using Form B1004.3. The laboratory must immediately alert the doctor if test results indicate an imminent life-threatening condition, and these critical results should be marked in the lab test menu list G1002.2. All findings and communications regarding critical results must be recorded and maintained. Test results must be reported within a predefined timeframe as per the Standard Operational Procedure Manual for each individual test.

checks.requirement: Visual or fluorescent markers are used to determine the endpoint of gel electrophoresis.
checks.subject: Visual/Fluorescent Markers
checks.gap_analysis: Status: Non-Compliant. The provided documentation does not contain evidence of standard operating procedures or validation records confirming the use of visual or fluorescent markers to determine the endpoint of gel electrophoresis. While '1_qPCR overview 1-26-2023.pdf' discusses fluorescence in the context of real-time PCR and '11. Lateral Flow Assay.docx' describes particle conjugation in lateral flow assays, neither document addresses the specific requirement for gel electrophoresis endpoint determination. No records were found verifying that markers are utilized or monitored during gel electrophoresis procedures.
corrective_actions: 1) Develop and implement a written procedure specifying the visual or fluorescent markers used to determine the endpoint of gel electrophoresis.
2) Maintain logs or validation records demonstrating that these markers are consistently used during electrophoresis runs.
3) Train laboratory staff on the specific marker protocols and document completion of this training.
checks.ai_evidence_summary: **MIC.65720**: The claim that visual or fluorescent markers are used to determine the endpoint of gel electrophoresis is not directly supported by the provided documents. However, the documents indicate that traditional PCR detection is often followed by gel electrophoresis. Real-time PCR, in contrast, uses fluorescent molecules added beforehand, with fluorescence measured after each cycle, and the signal increases with DNA amplification. Fluorescence occurs when absorbed light is re-radiated at a longer wavelength, and instruments measure this intensity in Relative Fluorescence Units (RFU). Lateral flow assays also utilize colored or fluorescent particles conjugated to antibodies for target analyte detection.
